items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How many additional access points of this class can SW1 power from its remaining budget?

exhibit.content:
SW1# show power inline
Available:370.0(w)  Used:76.4(w)  Remaining:293.6(w)

Interface Admin  Oper       Power   Device              Class Max
                            (Watts) 
--------- ------ ---------- ------- ------------------- ----- ----
Gi1/0/1   auto   on         30.0    AIR-AP2802I-E-K9    4     30.0
Gi1/0/2   auto   on         15.4    IP Phone 8841       3     30.0
Gi1/0/3   auto   on         15.4    IP Phone 8841       3     30.0
Gi1/0/4   auto   on         15.6    IP Phone 8851       3     30.0
Gi1/0/5   auto   off        0.0     n/a                 n/a   30.0

More access points of the same model are to be added. Each draws the
full 30.0 W of its class.

items.explanation: The summary line reports 293.6 W remaining, and each additional access point draws the full 30.0 W of its class, so nine fit with 23.6 W left over and a tenth would exceed the budget. Option A divides the total 370 W by 30 and ignores the 76.4 W already committed to the devices listed. Option B divides the remaining budget by 15.4 W, the draw of a phone rather than an access point. Option D subtracts one unnecessarily, as though a reserve had to be held back, which the output does not indicate.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which component must be added before PC-A and PC-B can communicate?

exhibit.content:
+--------------------+
              |     SW-ACCESS      |   Layer 2 switch
              +--+--------------+--+
                 |              |
             VLAN 10         VLAN 20
       192.168.10.0/24    192.168.20.0/24
             PC-A              PC-B

Both hosts are addressed correctly for their own VLAN and both switch
ports show connected. Neither host can reach the other. Nothing else is
attached to SW-ACCESS.

options.text: A device that routes between the VLANs, such as a router or Layer 3 switch.
A second Layer 2 switch, so that each VLAN has a dedicated switch of its own.
A wireless LAN controller to coordinate the two segments centrally.
A next-generation firewall to permit the traffic between the two VLANs.

items.explanation: A Layer 2 switch forwards only within a VLAN, and the two hosts sit in different VLANs and different subnets, so something operating at Layer 3 has to move traffic between them. Option B adds switching capacity, which was never the shortage, and would leave both VLANs just as isolated. Option C names a device that manages access points and plays no part in routing between wired segments. Option D would filter traffic that no device is currently routing at all, so permitting it changes nothing.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which addition satisfies the stated requirement?

exhibit.content:
internet
          |
    +-----+-----+
    |  ISP-RTR  |
    +-----+-----+
          |
    +-----+-----+        +------------------+
    |  EDGE-FW  |--------|  DMZ web server  |
    +-----+-----+        +------------------+
          |
    internal LAN

Requirement: traffic reaching the DMZ web server must be examined against
known exploit signatures, and any matching packet must be dropped before it
reaches the server rather than reported afterwards.

options.text: A Layer 3 switch placed in front of the server, filtering traffic with access lists.
A router access list applied inbound on the internet-facing interface of ISP-RTR.
An endpoint antivirus agent installed on the DMZ web server itself.
An IPS inspecting the traffic inline, so it can drop matching packets.

items.explanation: The requirement has two halves: match known exploit signatures, and drop the traffic before it arrives. Only an intrusion prevention system placed inline does both, since a sensor deployed out of band could detect but not stop. Option A filters on addresses and ports, which carries no signature knowledge. Option B has the same limitation and sits at the wrong point besides. Option C protects the host after the packet has already arrived, which the requirement explicitly rules out.

SRV-01

options.text: The workstation has been assigned a valid address from a DHCP scope.
No DHCP server answered, so Windows assigned a link-local address itself.
An administrator configured the address statically and omitted the gateway.
The network adapter has been disabled and holds a placeholder address.

items.explanation: The 169.254.0.0/16 range with a 255.255.0.0 mask and no gateway or DNS entries is what Windows assigns itself when DHCP goes unanswered, and the output labels it Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address rather than IPv4 Address. Option A is contradicted by that label and by the empty gateway field. Option C is ruled out because DHCP Enabled reads Yes, so the address was not entered by hand. Option D would leave the adapter reporting media disconnected rather than an address at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which subnet is this Mac attached to?

exhibit.content:
MacBook:~ user$ ifconfig en0
en0: flags=8863<UP,BROADCAST,SMART,RUNNING,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
        options=400<CHANNEL_IO>
        ether 3c:22:fb:1a:2b:3c
        inet6 fe80::1c2f:8a3b:4d5e:6f70%en0 prefixlen 64 secured scopeid 0xb
        inet 10.44.130.55 netmask 0xffffe000 broadcast 10.44.159.255
        nd6 options=201<PERFORMNUD,DAD>
        media: autoselect
        status: active

items.explanation: macOS prints the mask in hexadecimal, and 0xffffe000 expands to 255.255.224.0, a /19 whose blocks step by 32 in the third octet; 130 falls in the block beginning at 128, which the broadcast address of 10.44.159.255 confirms. Option A assumes a /24 and takes the host's own third octet as the network. Option B applies the classful /16 for the 10.0.0.0 range and ignores the mask entirely. Option D pairs the correct prefix length with an address that is not on a /19 boundary.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why can this Linux host reach its own subnet but nothing outside it?

exhibit.content:
user@host:~$ ip addr show ens192
2: ens192: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc mq state UP group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 00:0c:29:ab:cd:ef brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 172.20.14.55/26 brd 172.20.14.63 scope global ens192
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever

user@host:~$ ip route
172.20.14.0/26 dev ens192 proto kernel scope link src 172.20.14.55 metric 100

The host reaches 172.20.14.60 by address without trouble, but every
address outside 172.20.14.0/26 times out.

options.text: The routing table holds no default route, so off-subnet traffic has nowhere to go.
The interface is administratively down and cannot forward beyond the link.
The /26 prefix is too small to permit traffic to leave the local segment.
No DNS server has been configured, so remote destinations cannot be resolved by name.

items.explanation: The routing table lists only the connected 172.20.14.0/26 entry, with no default via line, so the kernel has nowhere to send anything that does not match that prefix. Option B is contradicted by the interface state, which reads UP,LOWER_UP with an address bound. Option C invents a prefix length that blocks routing; a /26 routes off-subnet as readily as any other. Option D is ruled out because the failures happen when addressing destinations numerically, which never involves DNS.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How many addresses on this host's subnet can be assigned to devices?

exhibit.content:
user@host:~$ ip addr show ens160
3: ens160: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc mq state UP group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 00:50:56:9a:33:c1 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 192.168.118.37/28 brd 192.168.118.47 scope global ens160
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
    inet6 fe80::250:56ff:fe9a:33c1/64 scope link
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever

items.explanation: The inet line reads /28, which leaves four host bits and therefore sixteen addresses in the block, of which the network address and the broadcast at 192.168.118.47 are unusable, leaving fourteen for devices. Option A counts every address in the block and forgets to deduct the two reserved ones. Option B is the figure for a /27 and comes from misreading the prefix by one bit. Option C is the figure for a /26, two bits out.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why did installing AP-D degrade performance across this floor?

exhibit.content:
Site survey of the 2.4 GHz band on one floor

    AP        Channel    Neighbouring cells overlap this AP's coverage
    ------    -------    --------------------------------------------
    AP-A            1    AP-B, AP-D
    AP-B            6    AP-A, AP-C, AP-D
    AP-C           11    AP-B
    AP-D            3    AP-A, AP-B

Users nearest AP-D report slow throughput and frequent stalls, and the
three other cells were stable before AP-D was installed.

options.text: AP-D is too close to AP-C, and both are serving the edge of the same coverage area.
AP-D uses a channel already carried by AP-A, so the two cells are duplicating traffic.
AP-D is transmitting at a higher power than the other three access points.
AP-D sits on channel 3, which overlaps both channel 1 and channel 6.

items.explanation: In the 2.4 GHz band each channel is far wider than the spacing between channel numbers, so only channels five or more apart avoid overlapping, which is why 1, 6 and 11 are the standard plan. Channel 3 sits two away from 1 and three away from 6, so AP-D interferes with AP-A and AP-B at once, matching the overlap column exactly. Option A points at AP-C on channel 11, which is eight away from AP-D and does not overlap it. Option B treats channel 3 and channel 1 as the same channel. Option C invents a power difference the survey never records.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which access point should this client associate with for the most reliable connection?

exhibit.content:
Client-side survey taken from one desk

    AP        Channel    Signal (RSSI)    Noise floor    SNR
    ------    -------    -------------    -----------    ----
    AP-1            1        -62 dBm        -92 dBm      30 dB
    AP-2            6        -57 dBm        -61 dBm       4 dB
    AP-3           11        -71 dBm        -94 dBm      23 dB

All three advertise the same SSID and the client may associate with any
of them.

options.text: AP-1, because it combines a strong signal with a quiet noise floor.
AP-2, because it shows the strongest received signal of the three.
AP-3, because channel 11 is furthest from the other two cells.
Any of the three, because all advertise the same SSID and are equivalent.

items.explanation: What matters is how far the signal rises above the noise, not its absolute strength, and AP-1's 30 dB signal-to-noise ratio is the widest margin available. Option B picks the strongest raw RSSI, but AP-2 sits in a noise floor of -61 dBm, leaving only 4 dB of usable margin, which is the trap this item is built around. Option C picks on channel separation, which affects neighbouring cells rather than this client's own link quality, and AP-3's 23 dB is still below AP-1's. Option D treats a shared SSID as meaning the radio conditions are identical.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two conclusions about CORP-WIFI and GUEST-WIFI does this scan support? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
Wireless scan taken by a laptop in the lobby

    SSID          BSSID                Channel    Security
    ----------    -----------------    -------    ------------
    CORP-WIFI     00:1a:2b:3c:4d:50          1    WPA2-Enterprise
    CORP-WIFI     00:1a:2b:3c:4d:70          6    WPA2-Enterprise
    CORP-WIFI     00:1a:2b:3c:4d:90         11    WPA2-Enterprise
    GUEST-WIFI    00:1a:2b:3c:4d:51          1    Open

options.text: The three CORP-WIFI rows are one access point reported once per channel scanned.
CORP-WIFI is served by three access points, each with its own radio identifier.
GUEST-WIFI offers the clients that join it no encryption at the link layer.
CORP-WIFI has been given the same name three times by mistake.
GUEST-WIFI must be served by a different access point from CORP-WIFI.

items.explanation: The SSID names the network and the BSSID names the radio serving it, so three BSSIDs under one SSID means three access points cooperating, which their placement on channels 1, 6 and 11 confirms; GUEST-WIFI meanwhile reads Open, so nothing protects its traffic over the air. Option A assumes a single radio was recorded repeatedly, but one radio reports one BSSID per network. Option D treats a shared SSID as an error, when sharing it is what lets a client roam. Option E is contradicted by GUEST-WIFI's BSSID sitting one digit from a CORP-WIFI radio, which is how one access point advertises two networks.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which network in this scan offers the strongest protection for traffic sent across it?

exhibit.content:
Wireless scan taken in a shared office building

    SSID          Channel    Security          Signal
    ----------    -------    --------------    --------
    OFFICE-A            1    WPA2-Personal     -48 dBm
    OFFICE-B            6    WPA3-Personal     -55 dBm
    HOTSPOT-C          11    Open              -61 dBm
    LEGACY-D            1    WEP               -67 dBm

options.text: OFFICE-A
LEGACY-D
OFFICE-B
HOTSPOT-C

items.explanation: The Security column ranks these plainly: OFFICE-B advertises WPA3, the newest of the personal modes and the strongest shown. Option A advertises WPA2, which remains sound but has been superseded by WPA3. Option B advertises WEP, which is long broken and offers protection in name only. Option D is Open, so its traffic carries no link-layer encryption at all, and its stronger signal is irrelevant to the question of protection.

       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2

       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP

C        192.168.10.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
L        192.168.10.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2

options.text: Each VRF has its own routing table, so the same prefix can exist once in each.
The router load-balances the prefix across both interfaces as equal-cost paths.
The second entry overrides the first, and only CUSTOMER-B can reach the subnet.
The prefixes differ in mask, so longest prefix match separates the two entries.

items.explanation: A VRF gives the router a separate routing and forwarding instance, so R1 maintains one table per customer and each may carry the same address space without conflict, which is what lets a provider serve two customers who both chose 192.168.10.0/24. Option B describes equal-cost paths, which apply within one table rather than across two. Option C assumes one entry wins, but both tables are shown populated and both are live. Option D looks for a mask difference, and the two prefixes are identical.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which model packages its workloads as containers, and what follows from the measurements?

exhibit.content:
Two ways of packaging the same set of applications onto one physical
server were trialled and measured.

    Property                     Model X            Model Y
    -------------------------    ---------------    ---------------
    Operating system per         one each           none; all share
    workload                                        the host's kernel
    Typical image size           several GB         tens of MB
    Time from start to serving   tens of seconds    under a second
    Isolation boundary           virtual hardware   kernel features

options.text: Model X, and its workloads start faster because no separate kernel has to boot.
Model X, because sharing virtual hardware is what defines a container runtime.
Model Y, and its workloads start faster because no guest OS has to boot.
Model Y, and each of its workloads carries a full operating system of its own.

items.explanation: Model Y runs no operating system per workload and shares the host kernel, which is exactly what a container does, and that is why its images are tens of megabytes and it serves in under a second: there is no guest system to start. Option A attaches the fast start to Model X, whose own row records tens of seconds. Option B calls virtual hardware a container property, when the exhibit lists it as Model X's isolation boundary. Option D contradicts Model Y's own row, which records no operating system per workload.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which interfaces has R3 placed in the CUSTOMER-A instance?

exhibit.content:
R3# show vrf
  Name                             Default RD            Protocols   Interfaces
  MGMT                             <not set>             ipv4        Gi0/0
  CUSTOMER-A                       65000:100             ipv4        Gi0/1,Gi0/3
  CUSTOMER-B                       65000:200             ipv4        Gi0/2

options.text: Gi0/0 and Gi0/1
Gi0/1 and Gi0/3
Gi0/2 only
Gi0/1 and Gi0/2

items.explanation: The Interfaces column lists what each instance owns, and the CUSTOMER-A row names Gi0/1 and Gi0/3, so traffic arriving on either is looked up in that instance's own table. Option A pairs a CUSTOMER-A interface with Gi0/0, which belongs to the separate MGMT instance. Option C is the single interface held by CUSTOMER-B. Option D pairs one CUSTOMER-A interface with one from CUSTOMER-B, which would defeat the separation the instances exist to provide.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does SW1 do with this frame?

exhibit.content:
SW1# show mac address-table
          Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------

Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
   1    0011.2233.4455    DYNAMIC     Gi0/1
   1    00aa.bbcc.ddee    DYNAMIC     Gi0/2
   1    0022.5566.99ab    DYNAMIC     Gi0/3
Total Mac Addresses for this criterion: 3

A frame arrives on Gi0/1 in VLAN 1, addressed to destination MAC
00de.ad00.beef. Ports Gi0/1 through Gi0/4 are all access ports in VLAN 1.

options.text: Discards it and returns an error to the sending station.
Holds it until an ARP request resolves the destination.
Sends it back out Gi0/1 toward the station that transmitted it.
Floods it out every VLAN 1 port except Gi0/1.

items.explanation: The destination 00de.ad00.beef appears nowhere in the table, making this an unknown unicast, and a switch floods those out every port in the frame's VLAN except the one it arrived on, so Gi0/2, Gi0/3 and Gi0/4 all receive a copy. Option A describes a router returning an unreachable message, which a switch does not do. Option B confuses switching with ARP, a process the sending host runs before the frame is built. Option C would send the frame back where it came from, which flooding explicitly excludes to avoid returning traffic to its source.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two statements describe how SW2 handles this frame? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
SW2# show mac address-table
          Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------

Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
   1    0011.2233.4455    DYNAMIC     Gi0/1
   1    00cc.7788.1122    DYNAMIC     Gi0/2
  20    00cc.7788.1122    DYNAMIC     Gi0/4
  20    00ff.9900.3344    DYNAMIC     Gi0/5
Total Mac Addresses for this criterion: 4

A frame arrives on Gi0/5, an access port in VLAN 20, addressed to
destination MAC 00cc.7788.1122.

options.text: It floods the frame, since the destination appears twice in the table.
It forwards the frame out GigabitEthernet0/2.
The VLAN 1 entry for that address is not a candidate for this lookup.
It forwards the frame out GigabitEthernet0/4.
It discards the frame because the destination address is ambiguous.

items.explanation: A switch looks its table up by VLAN as well as by address, so the frame arriving in VLAN 20 matches only the entry pairing 00cc.7788.1122 with Gi0/4, and the identical address in VLAN 1 belongs to a separate forwarding domain that this lookup never consults. Option A floods, which applies only when no entry matches. Option B picks that VLAN 1 entry and would leak the frame between VLANs. Option E treats two entries as a conflict, when keeping them apart is exactly what VLANs are for.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does SW3 do when PC-A's first frame arrives?

exhibit.content:
SW3# show mac address-table
          Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------

Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
   1    00bb.1122.3344    DYNAMIC     Gi0/2
   1    0099.5566.7788    DYNAMIC     Gi0/3
Total Mac Addresses for this criterion: 2

PC-A has just been plugged into Gi0/5, an access port in VLAN 1, and its
MAC address 00ee.4433.2211 appears nowhere in the table. PC-A immediately
sends a frame addressed to 00bb.1122.3344.

options.text: Floods the frame and learns nothing until 00bb.1122.3344 replies.
Forwards the frame out Gi0/2 but records PC-A only once it replies.
Records PC-A against Gi0/5 and forwards the frame out Gi0/2 only.
Records PC-A against Gi0/5 and floods the frame to every VLAN 1 port.

items.explanation: Two independent things happen to one frame: the switch reads the source address and records 00ee.4433.2211 against the ingress port Gi0/5, then looks up the destination, finds 00bb.1122.3344 already listed on Gi0/2, and forwards there alone. Option A misses the learning, which happens on the first frame from any source rather than waiting for a reply. Option B makes learning depend on a reply, when the source address of this very frame is what teaches the switch. Option D adds a flood that is unnecessary because the destination is already known.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why is the file server's MAC address missing from the table, and what follows from that?

exhibit.content:
SW4# show mac address-table
          Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------

Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
   1    0011.2233.4455    DYNAMIC     Gi0/1
   1    0044.7788.aabb    DYNAMIC     Gi0/2
Total Mac Addresses for this criterion: 2

A file server on Gi0/6 has been powered on and cabled throughout, with its
port showing connected the whole time, but it has transmitted nothing for
the last ten minutes. The switch runs the default aging time of 300
seconds. The server's MAC address is absent from the table above.

options.text: It aged out because the server sent no frames, so traffic to it is flooded.
It was removed when the port last changed VLAN and will not return.
It is retained but hidden, because the command lists only active talkers.
It was never learned at all, because a switch learns only from a device's replies.

items.explanation: A switch learns from the source address of frames a device transmits, so a station that only listens ages out after the aging timer elapses, and ten minutes exceeds the 300-second default. Frames addressed to it are then treated as unknown unicast and flooded until the server speaks again. Option B invents a VLAN change the exhibit never mentions. Option C suggests the command filters its output, but show mac address-table lists every entry held. Option D claims learning comes from replies, when it is the source address of any transmitted frame that teaches the switch.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which entry in SW5's table was configured by an administrator rather than learned from traffic?

exhibit.content:
SW5# show mac address-table
          Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------

Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
   1    0011.2233.4455    DYNAMIC     Gi0/1
   1    00aa.bbcc.ddee    DYNAMIC     Gi0/2
  10    0050.7966.6800    DYNAMIC     Gi0/7
  10    0000.0c07.ac0a    STATIC      Gi0/8
Total Mac Addresses for this criterion: 4

options.text: 00aa.bbcc.ddee on Gi0/2

items.explanation: The Type column separates the two: STATIC entries are placed in the table by configuration and never age out, while DYNAMIC entries are learned from the source addresses of arriving frames. Only 0000.0c07.ac0a on Gi0/8 reads STATIC. Options A, C and D are all marked DYNAMIC, so each was learned from traffic and each will age out if its device falls silent, which is precisely the distinction the Type column exists to record.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Compared with a classic three-tier campus design, which layer is absent here?

exhibit.content:
+-----------+     +-----------+
                | DIST-SW-1 |=====| DIST-SW-2 |
                +--+-----+--+     +--+-----+--+
                   |     \___________/     |
                   |      ___________      |
                   |     /           \     |
              +----+----+         +----+----+
              | ACC-SW-1|         | ACC-SW-2|
              +----+----+         +----+----+
                   |                   |
               user ports          user ports

DIST-SW-1 and DIST-SW-2 also terminate the site's WAN circuits and
perform all routing between VLANs. There is no further switching layer
above them.

options.text: The access layer, since the user ports attach straight to distribution.
The distribution layer, since routing happens on the same pair as the WAN.
A dedicated core layer, whose work the distribution pair absorbs instead.
None of them; access, distribution and core are all present in the drawing.

items.explanation: Two access switches feed a distribution pair that also routes between VLANs and terminates the WAN, with nothing above it, which is the collapsed-core or two-tier arrangement: the core's aggregation work has been folded into the distribution layer. Option A is contradicted by ACC-SW-1 and ACC-SW-2 carrying the user ports. Option B mistakes the distribution pair for something else, when it is the layer doing the routing. Option D counts three layers where the drawing shows two.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is consistent about the path between servers attached to any two different leaves?

exhibit.content:
+---------+                 +---------+
        | SPINE-1 |                 | SPINE-2 |
        +--+---+--+                 +--+---+--+
           |   |  \_______________     |   |
           |   \_________________ \____|   |
           |                     \ \       |
        +--+-----+          +-----+-+-+   +-------+
        | LEAF-1 |          | LEAF-2  |   | LEAF-3|
        +--------+          +---------+   +-------+
           |                     |            |
        servers               servers      servers

Every leaf connects to every spine. No leaf connects to another leaf,
and no spine connects to another spine.

options.text: Path length varies with the leaf pair, since some leaves sit closer together.
Every such path crosses one spine, so all leaf-to-leaf paths match in length.
Traffic passes directly from leaf to leaf whenever both sit in the same row.
Paths grow longer as leaves are added, because each new leaf extends the chain.

items.explanation: With every leaf attached to every spine and no leaf-to-leaf links, traffic between two leaves always goes up to a spine and back down, so the hop count is identical for every pair and latency becomes predictable no matter which servers are talking. Option A imagines physical proximity affecting the path, which the uniform wiring removes. Option C describes a direct leaf-to-leaf link the design deliberately omits. Option D expects a chain, but adding a leaf attaches it to the existing spines without lengthening any path.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which design fits these requirements?

exhibit.content:
A new eight-person office is being fitted out above a shop.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    One internet circuit, no second site
    Wired ports for eight desks and a printer
    Wireless coverage for the same eight people
    No on-site IT staff; minimum equipment to administer
    Budget covers one device, not a rack

options.text: A SOHO design on one integrated router, switch and wireless device.
A three-tier campus design with separate core, distribution and access layers.
A spine-leaf fabric with two spines, sized down for the eight users.
A dedicated WAN aggregation layer sitting between the users and the internet.

items.explanation: Eight users, one circuit, no second site and a single device of budget describe a small office or home office, where one appliance combining routing, switching and wireless covers everything and leaves almost nothing to administer. Option B builds three layers for eight desks, which the budget and the absence of on-site staff both rule out. Option C applies a data centre fabric to a workload that has no east-west traffic to speak of. Option D adds an aggregation layer for a single circuit that needs none.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which part of this drawing is the WAN?

exhibit.content:
+------------+
   branch office -------|  BR-RTR-1  |
      LAN switch        +-----+------+
                              |
                     leased circuit from
                     the service provider
                              |
                        +-----+------+
                        |  HQ-RTR-1  |------- head office LAN
                        +------------+

The circuit between the two routers is billed monthly by the provider
and crosses roughly 40 km of the provider's own infrastructure.

options.text: The branch office LAN switch and the ports it serves.
BR-RTR-1 and HQ-RTR-1 taken together as a routed pair.
The head office LAN reached through HQ-RTR-1.
The leased circuit between the two routers.

items.explanation: A WAN is the span between sites that an organisation rents rather than owns, and here that is the leased circuit crossing 40 km of the provider's infrastructure and billed monthly. Option A is a local network inside one building, which is a LAN by definition. Option C is the same on the other side. Option B names the two routers, which are the devices attaching to the WAN rather than the WAN itself; the boundary sits on the circuit between them.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which medium is the least costly one that will carry this link over the measured distance?

exhibit.content:
A 1 Gbps link is needed between two buildings on one campus. The
cable route measured along the duct is 340 m.

    Media                       Practical maximum run
    ------------------------    ---------------------
    Copper twisted pair         100 m
    Multimode fibre             550 m
    Single-mode fibre           10 km and beyond

options.text: Copper twisted pair, since 1 Gbps is well within its rated speed for this link.
Multimode fibre, which spans the distance without single-mode optics.
Single-mode fibre, the only medium rated beyond 100 m.
Copper twisted pair with a repeater placed at the midpoint of the run.

items.explanation: The run is 340 m, which is beyond copper's 100 m limit but comfortably inside multimode's 550 m, and multimode optics cost less than single-mode, so it is the cheapest medium that actually reaches. Option A ignores distance entirely and considers only speed, which copper does support but cannot deliver over 340 m. Option C would work but pays for reach the campus does not need. Option D adds active equipment mid-duct, which introduces a powered device and a failure point where a passive fibre run needs neither.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What best explains why neither port will come up?

exhibit.content:
A contractor ran copper twisted pair between the ground-floor comms
room and a cabinet on the third floor of an adjacent wing. The measured
run is 145 m. Both switch ports are configured identically and neither
comes up; swapping the transceivers and the patch leads changes nothing.

    Media                       Practical maximum run
    ------------------------    ---------------------
    Copper twisted pair         100 m
    Multimode fibre             550 m
    Single-mode fibre           10 km and beyond

options.text: The two switch ports have been left in mismatched VLANs.
The copper run needs a crossover cable rather than a straight-through one.
Autonegotiation is disabled, so the ports never agree on a speed.
The run is 45 m beyond the copper limit, so no reliable link forms.

items.explanation: Twisted pair is specified to 100 m, and this run is 145 m, so signal attenuation prevents a link establishing at all no matter what is fitted at the ends, which is exactly why swapping transceivers and leads changed nothing. Option A describes a VLAN mismatch, which leaves ports up while blocking traffic rather than keeping them down. Option B invokes cable pinout, which modern switches resolve automatically and which would not survive the swap testing already done. Option C describes a mismatch that the exhibit rules out by stating both ports are configured identically.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How do the two segments compare in the number of collision domains they create?

exhibit.content:
Segment A                          Segment B

      +-------+                          +--------+
      |  HUB  |                          | SWITCH |
      +---+---+                          +---+----+
     /   / \   \                        /   / \   \
   PC1 PC2 PC3 PC4                    PC5 PC6 PC7 PC8

Each device is attached by its own cable, and every port on both
devices is running at 100 Mbps.

options.text: Segment A has four and segment B has one, because the switch merges its ports.
Both have four, because each device is attached by its own dedicated cable.
Segment A has one and segment B has four, because each switch port is its own.
Both have one, because both devices join all their ports into a single domain.

items.explanation: A hub repeats every received signal out of all other ports, so all four stations on segment A share one collision domain regardless of having separate cables. A switch forwards selectively and each port forms its own point-to-point link, giving segment B four separate domains. Option A reverses the two devices. Option B assumes a dedicated cable is enough, but the hub's shared repeating is what defines the domain. Option D describes two hubs and ignores the switch entirely.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which port is fitted with a fibre transceiver rather than a copper connection?

exhibit.content:
SW9# show interfaces status
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/21    reception          connected    10         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/22    meeting room       connected    10         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/23    print room         connected    20         a-full  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/25    link to annexe     connected    1            full   1000 1000BaseSX

items.explanation: The Type column records the physical media, and Gi0/25 reads 1000BaseSX, an optical standard, while every other port reads 10/100/1000BaseTX, where TX denotes twisted pair. The port's description, link to annexe, fits a run between buildings. Options B and D are both copper access ports negotiating at gigabit, and option C is a copper port that settled at 100 Mbps, which reflects the device plugged into it rather than the media fitted.

options.text: A duplex mismatch between the two ends of the link.
A speed mismatch that is forcing repeated renegotiation.
A faulty cable introducing interference along its length.
Congestion, because the link is saturated in both directions.

items.explanation: SW2 is half-duplex while SW1 is full-duplex, and that pairing produces exactly this signature: the half-duplex end logs late collisions because the far end transmits whenever it likes, while the full-duplex end records CRC errors from frames SW2 truncated when it backed off. Option B is wrong because both ends agree at 100Mb/s and a speed mismatch would leave the link down rather than up. Option C would show errors on both ends without any collisions at all. Option D is ruled out because collisions and CRC errors are faults, not the queueing that congestion produces.

options.text: Autonegotiation completed, since both ends report full duplex at 1000Mb/s.
A duplex mismatch is present, because both ends are logging input errors.
The fault lies on the medium, as errors appear both ways with no collisions.
One of the two switches is running an incompatible software release.
The two ports sit in different VLANs, which is corrupting the frames.

items.explanation: Both ends agree at Full-duplex and 1000Mb/s, which only happens when negotiation succeeded, and each is receiving runts and CRC errors while logging no collisions at all, which points at the cable rather than at any setting. Option B reads input errors as proof of a duplex mismatch, but that fault leaves late collisions on the half-duplex end and neither end here is half duplex. Option D invents a software fault that would not corrupt frames on the wire. Option E describes a VLAN mismatch, which stops traffic passing rather than damaging it.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which port currently has nothing connected to it?

exhibit.content:
SW5# show interfaces status
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/1     uplink to core     connected    1          a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/2     reception PC       connected    10         a-full  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/3     meeting room       notconnect   10           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/4     printer            connected    20         a-half   a-10 10/100/1000BaseTX

options.text: Gi0/4
Gi0/3
Gi0/2
Gi0/1

items.explanation: The Status column reads notconnect only for Gi0/3, meaning the switch detects no link partner on that port, which is also why its Duplex and Speed still read auto rather than a negotiated value. Option A is connected and has negotiated half-duplex at 10Mb/s, which is unusual but is a working link. Options C and D both read connected with negotiated speeds, so each has a live partner at the far end.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does this port's state tell you, given that the same patch lead works elsewhere?

exhibit.content:
SW6# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/7
GigabitEthernet0/7 is down, line protocol is down (notconnect)
  Hardware is Gigabit Ethernet, address is 00d0.5842.c201 (bia 00d0.5842.c201)
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 100000 Kbit/sec, DLY 100 usec,
     reliability 255/255, txload 1/255, rxload 1/255
  Encapsulation ARPA, loopback not set
  Keepalive set (10 sec)
  Auto-duplex, Auto-speed, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
  ARP type: ARPA, ARP Timeout 04:00:00
     0 packets input, 52194883 bytes, 0 no buffer
     0 runts, 0 giants, 0 throttles
     0 input errors, 0 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
     0 packets output, 71029338 bytes, 0 underruns
     0 output errors, 0 collisions, 0 interface resets
     0 babbles, 0 late collision, 0 deferred

The port is not shut down in the running configuration, and the same
patch lead works when moved to a neighbouring port.

options.text: An administrator has shut the port down in the configuration.
The port is negotiating and will come up once the timers expire.
The port detects no link partner, so the fault is the far end or this port.
The port is up but has been placed in a VLAN that carries no traffic at present.

items.explanation: Down with line protocol down and a notconnect qualifier means no electrical link is detected, and since the lead is known good and no shutdown is present, the problem sits in this port or in whatever should be answering at the far end. Option A would read administratively down instead, which is the wording IOS reserves for a configured shutdown. Option B invents a negotiation delay; a port awaiting negotiation still reports a partner. Option D describes a VLAN issue, which leaves the port up and passing nothing rather than down.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Both ports were hardcoded as shown during a maintenance window. What is the result on this link?

exhibit.content:
! Two switches joined by a single copper run
!
SW7  interface GigabitEthernet0/1
      speed 100
      duplex full
!
SW8  interface GigabitEthernet0/1
      speed 1000
      duplex full
!

Both ports were previously left at their defaults and the link worked.

options.text: The link stays down, because the two ends cannot agree on a speed.
The link comes up at 100Mb/s, since the lower of the two speeds wins.
The link comes up but suffers a duplex mismatch and late collisions.
The link comes up at 1000Mb/s once SW7 renegotiates to match SW8.

items.explanation: Speed must match for an Ethernet link to establish at all, so hardcoding 100 on one end and 1000 on the other leaves both ports down; unlike duplex, speed is not something the two ends can disagree about while still passing frames. Option B invents a lowest-common-speed rule that applies to autonegotiation, which both ports have now been taken out of. Option C describes the duplex mismatch signature, but both ends here specify full duplex and never get far enough to exchange frames. Option D expects renegotiation from a port that has been hardcoded.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does the exchange with 10.1.1.201 begin carrying payload in its very first frame, while the exchange with 10.1.1.200 spends three frames before any data moves?

options.text: The 10.1.1.201 exchange had already completed its handshake before the capture began.
The switch prioritised the 10.1.1.201 traffic and forwarded its handshake unrecorded.
UDP is connectionless and sends payload at once, while TCP opens a session first.
The 10.1.1.200 exchange is retransmitting because its first two attempts were lost.

items.explanation: Frames 1 to 3 are the SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK that open a TCP connection, and only frame 4 carries a request; the UDP exchange has no such setup and puts 76 bytes of payload on the wire at once, because UDP keeps no connection state. Option A invents an earlier handshake that UDP would never have performed. Option B suggests the analyser missed frames, but both directions of the UDP exchange are present. Option D reads the three-frame opening as retransmission, though each frame carries a different flag rather than repeating one.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Segment 8815 never appears in the voice stream, and no frame recovers it. What does the capture show about how each transport handles the loss?

options.text: TCP retransmitted its own loss, while the UDP stream carried on without it.
Both transports recovered, but the UDP retransmission fell outside the captured window.
Neither transport recovered; frame 13 is a duplicate the analyser has mislabelled.
UDP recovered first because its smaller frames retransmit faster than TCP's.

items.explanation: Frame 12 acknowledges a gap and frame 13 is labelled a retransmission of the same sequence, so TCP detected the loss and resent it without the application being involved. The RTP sequence jumps from 8814 to 8816 with nothing resending 8815, because UDP offers no recovery and leaves the decision to the application, which for voice is to move on. Option B expects a UDP retransmission the protocol cannot perform. Option C dismisses a retransmission the capture states plainly. Option D reverses which transport recovers and invents a size-based advantage.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which service is the one best carried over UDP, and for what reason?

exhibit.content:
Three services are being moved onto a new link

    Service              Requirement
    -----------------    ----------------------------------------
    File synchronise     Every byte must arrive, order matters,
                         a pause of a second or two is acceptable
    Live voice call      A lost sample is better discarded than
                         delivered late; delay must stay minimal
    Database replica     Missing records are unacceptable and the
                         receiver must detect any gap

options.text: File synchronise, because bulk transfers benefit from the lower per-segment overhead.
Live voice call, because a late sample is worthless and retransmitting one adds delay.
Database replica, because the receiver detects gaps itself and needs no transport help.
All three, because UDP's smaller header improves throughput on any type of traffic.

items.explanation: Voice is the one requirement that prefers loss to delay: a sample that arrives after its playback moment is useless, so the retransmission TCP would perform actively hurts, which is why UDP suits it. Option A picks a service whose stated requirement is that every byte arrives in order, which is exactly what TCP provides. Option C describes a service that calls missing records unacceptable, so it needs guaranteed delivery rather than gap detection alone. Option D generalises a header saving into a universal rule and ignores every stated requirement.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which transport protocol carries the name lookup in frames 21 and 22?

exhibit.content:
Capture of a workstation opening a file share
No.  Time      Source          Destination     Protocol  Length  Info
21   4.100000  192.168.7.30    192.168.7.10    DNS       78      Standard query A files.example.internal
22   4.100944  192.168.7.10    192.168.7.30    DNS       122     Standard query response A 192.168.7.60
23   4.101550  192.168.7.30    192.168.7.60    TCP       74      52310 > 445 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=64240 Len=0 MSS=1460
24   4.101988  192.168.7.60    192.168.7.30    TCP       74      445 > 52310 [SYN, ACK] Seq=0 Ack=1 Win=65535 Len=0

options.text: TCP
ICMP
ARP
UDP

items.explanation: Frames 21 and 22 are a single query and a single response with no session setup around them, which is the shape of a UDP exchange; the analyser names the application protocol in its column, and the transport underneath it is connectionless. Option A is what frames 23 and 24 use, and their SYN and SYN-ACK flags show the contrast plainly. Option B is a control protocol that carries no name lookups. Option C resolves addresses at layer 2 within a segment and appears nowhere in this capture.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is the broadcast address of the subnet that GigabitEthernet0/1 belongs to?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description accounting LAN
 ip address 192.168.20.100 255.255.255.224
 no shutdown
!

items.explanation: A 255.255.255.224 mask is a /27, so subnets step in blocks of 32 and .100 falls in the block running from .96 to .127; the last address, .127, is the broadcast. Option B is the network address of the next subnet, an error of exactly one address past the boundary. Option C is the broadcast for the whole /24 and ignores that the interface is subnetted at all. Option D is the last usable host address, which sits one below the broadcast.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does PC1 get no reply from PC2 even though both are cabled to the same switch?

exhibit.content:
! Two hosts on one switched segment, no router present
!
PC1   IPv4 address . . . : 192.168.10.70
      Subnet mask  . . . : 255.255.255.192

PC2   IPv4 address . . . : 192.168.10.130
      Subnet mask  . . . : 255.255.255.192

PC1 can reach 192.168.10.65 but gets no reply from PC2.

options.text: 192.168.10.130 is the broadcast address of the subnet PC1 occupies.
PC2's address lies outside the private range and requires translation.
The /26 mask places the two hosts in different subnets.
Both hosts resolve to the same network address, so their addresses conflict.

items.explanation: 255.255.255.192 is a /26, giving blocks of 64: PC1's .70 sits in the .64 to .127 subnet while PC2's .130 sits in .128 to .191, so the two need a router between them despite sharing a switch. That PC1 reaches .65 confirms its own subnet works. Option A is wrong because the broadcast of PC1's subnet is .127. Option B misapplies private addressing, since all of 192.168.0.0/16 is private. Option D describes an address conflict, which would need the two hosts to share one address.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which set of subnets satisfies every host requirement without overlapping?

exhibit.content:
Address block available for the branch:  172.16.8.0/22

    Segment            Hosts required
    ---------------    --------------
    User LAN                      500
    Voice LAN                     200
    Server LAN                    100
    Management LAN                 50

The four segments must be carved from the block with no overlap.

items.explanation: Each segment needs the smallest subnet that still fits it: 500 hosts need a /23 giving 510, 200 need a /24 giving 254, 100 need a /25 giving 126, and 50 need a /26 giving 62. Placed in descending order from 172.16.8.0 those four tile the /22 exactly. Option A starts with a /24, which offers only 254 addresses and cannot hold 500 hosts. Option B opens with the entire /22, leaving nothing for the other three. Option C assigns a /24 at 172.16.11.0 that swallows the /26 placed at 172.16.11.128.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two addresses in this subnet cannot be given to a host? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! R4 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.10.10.65 255.255.255.192
 no shutdown
!

items.explanation: A 255.255.255.192 mask is a /26, so the interface sits in the block from 10.10.10.64 to 10.10.10.127; the first of those is the network address and the last is the broadcast, and neither may be assigned. Option A is the router's own address, already in use as an ordinary host address. Option C is the highest usable host address, one below the broadcast. Option E sits comfortably inside the usable range.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which subnet mask meets the host requirement while producing the largest number of subnets?

exhibit.content:
192.168.5.0/24
        +---------+---------+---------+---------+
            |           |         |         |
        +---+---+   +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+
        | Sales |   |Support| |Finance| |  Ops  |
        +-------+   +-------+ +-------+ +-------+
         60 hosts    60 hosts  60 hosts  60 hosts

Every segment must hold 60 hosts, and the design must leave room for
as many equally sized subnets as the block allows.

items.explanation: Sixty hosts need at least 62 usable addresses, which a /26 provides, and a /26 divides the /24 into four subnets, exactly matching the four segments. Option B is a /27 with only 30 usable addresses and cannot hold 60 hosts. Option D is a /28 with 14 usable and falls further short still. Option C is a /25, which does hold 126 hosts but splits the block into only two subnets, leaving two segments with nowhere to go.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which subnet does the address on GigabitEthernet0/1 belong to?

exhibit.content:
R6# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     10.1.1.1        YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     172.18.45.200   YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down

GigabitEthernet0/1 is configured with the mask 255.255.248.0.

items.explanation: A 255.255.248.0 mask is a /21, which steps in blocks of 8 in the third octet, giving boundaries at 32, 40 and 48; the address 172.18.45.200 falls in the block starting at 40 and running to 47.255. Option A treats the host's own third octet as the network number, which only holds when the mask lands on a /24. Option B picks the previous block and is the answer for anything from 172.18.32.0 to 172.18.39.255. Option D uses a block of 4, which would be a /22 rather than a /21.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which interface has been disabled by an administrator rather than failing on its own?

exhibit.content:
R7# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     10.30.1.1       YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     10.30.2.1       YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Loopback0              7.7.7.7         YES manual up                    up

options.text: GigabitEthernet0/0
Loopback0
GigabitEthernet0/1
GigabitEthernet0/2

items.explanation: The Status column reads administratively down only for GigabitEthernet0/2, and that wording means a shutdown command is in the configuration rather than a cable or carrier fault, which would show simply as down. Options A and C both read up in Status and Protocol and are carrying traffic normally. Option B is a loopback, which stays up because it is a virtual interface and has no physical layer to lose.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why did R8 reject the address configured on GigabitEthernet0/1?

exhibit.content:
R8(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R8(config-if)# ip address 10.1.0.1 255.255.0.0
R8(config-if)# exit
R8(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R8(config-if)# ip address 10.1.5.1 255.255.255.0
% 10.1.5.0 overlaps with GigabitEthernet0/0
R8(config-if)#

options.text: The mask 255.255.255.0 is invalid for an address in the 10.0.0.0 range.
10.1.5.0/24 falls inside the 10.1.0.0/16 already assigned to another interface.
A router may hold only one address from a given classful network at a time.
The second address was entered before the first interface was brought up.

items.explanation: GigabitEthernet0/0 owns 10.1.0.0 through 10.1.255.255, and 10.1.5.0/24 sits wholly inside that span, so accepting it would leave R8 with two interfaces claiming the same addresses; IOS blocks the overlap and names the conflicting interface. Option A treats the mask as illegal, but a /24 is fine in that space and the error text mentions overlap rather than the mask. Option C invents a classful limit that vanished with CIDR. Option D points at ordering, which the error message never mentions.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why can this host reach its own segment but nothing beyond it?

exhibit.content:
C:\> ipconfig

Windows IP Configuration

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:

   Connection-specific DNS Suffix  . : example.internal
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.30.200
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.192
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.30.129

The host reaches other stations on its own segment but nothing beyond it.

options.text: The subnet mask is too long to permit traffic to leave the local segment.
The default gateway address is the broadcast address of the host's subnet.
The host address is reserved and cannot originate routed traffic.
The default gateway lies in a different subnet from the host.

items.explanation: A 255.255.255.192 mask gives blocks of 64, so the host at .200 sits in the subnet from .192 to .255 while the configured gateway at .129 sits in the block from .128 to .191; a host can only send to a gateway inside its own subnet, so off-net traffic has nowhere to go. Option A invents a mask length that blocks routing. Option B is wrong because the broadcast for this host's subnet is .255. Option C treats .200 as reserved, but it is an ordinary usable address here.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which site's block is publicly routable and therefore would not require translation at the border?

exhibit.content:
Branch address blocks proposed for a new deployment

    Site            Block
    ------------    ------------------
    Manchester      10.14.0.0/16
    Leeds           172.20.0.0/16
    Bristol         172.32.0.0/16
    Cardiff         192.168.44.0/24

All four sites reach the internet through one border router.

items.explanation: The private space in the 172 range is 172.16.0.0/12, which runs from 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, so Bristol's 172.32.0.0/16 sits just past the end of it and is ordinary public address space. Option A falls inside 10.0.0.0/8 and is private. Option B at 172.20.0.0 sits comfortably within the /12 and is private too, which is exactly what makes the pair worth comparing. Option D falls inside 192.168.0.0/16 and is private.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does the proposed address fail the design standard?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - proposed addressing for the new data centre
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 description data centre core
 ip address 172.32.10.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
!

The design standard requires every internal segment to use address space
reserved for private use.

options.text: The private range in that space ends at 172.31.255.255.
The private range in that space ends at 172.16.255.255.
Addresses beginning 172.32 are reserved for multicast rather than unicast.
Only 10.0.0.0/8 and 192.168.0.0/16 are private; no 172 block qualifies.

items.explanation: The reserved block is 172.16.0.0/12, whose twelve network bits leave the second octet free to run from 16 through 31, so 172.32.10.1 falls one step outside private space and is publicly assigned. Option B stops the range at the end of 172.16, treating the /12 as though it were a /16 and shrinking the space sixteenfold. Option C confuses this with the multicast range, which begins at 224.0.0.0. Option D denies that any 172 block is private, which would make 172.16.0.0/12 itself public.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which interface on the border router carries an address drawn from private space?

exhibit.content:
BORDER1# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     203.0.113.2     YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     10.8.8.1        YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     198.51.100.7    YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/3     172.32.4.1      YES manual up                    up

options.text: GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/1
GigabitEthernet0/2
GigabitEthernet0/3

items.explanation: GigabitEthernet0/1 holds 10.8.8.1, which sits inside 10.0.0.0/8 and is the only private address in the output. Option A is 203.0.113.2, a publicly assigned address. Option C is 198.51.100.7, also public. Option D is the trap: 172.32.4.1 looks like the familiar private 172 space, but private use stops at 172.31.255.255, so that address is public as well.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which entry is the shortest valid form of the recorded address?

exhibit.content:
An address has been recorded in full, unabbreviated form:

    2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:0AB0:0000:00CD

It must be entered into the documentation in its shortest valid form.

items.explanation: Leading zeros in a group are dropped and the single longest run of all-zero groups is replaced by a double colon, which here is the three groups before 0AB0, giving 2001:DB8::AB0:0:CD. Option A uses two double colons, which is invalid because the expansion would then be ambiguous. Option C loses a digit from 0AB0, turning it into AB and producing a different address entirely. Option D drops leading zeros correctly but never applies the double colon, so it is valid yet not the shortest form.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which global unicast address does GigabitEthernet0/0 build for itself?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::/64 eui-64
 no shutdown
!

The burned-in address of GigabitEthernet0/0 is 001a.2b3c.4d5e.

options.text: 2001:DB8:ACAD:1:1A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
2001:DB8:ACAD:1:21A:2BFE:FF3C:4D5E
2001:DB8:ACAD:1:21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
2001:DB8:ACAD:1:21A:2BFF:FE4D:5E3C

items.explanation: Modified EUI-64 splits the MAC in half, inserts FFFE between the two halves, and inverts the seventh bit of the first byte, turning 00 into 02; 001A2B and 3C4D5E therefore become 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E under the configured prefix. Option A skips the bit inversion and leaves the first byte as 00, which is the single commonest omission. Option B writes the inserted value as FEFF rather than FFFE. Option D transposes the final two groups of the interface identifier.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which entry correctly expresses the /64 segment for VLAN 30?

exhibit.content:
The organisation has been allocated 2001:DB8:ACAD::/48 and subnets it
into /64 segments, one per VLAN.

    VLAN 10   segment 1
    VLAN 20   segment 2
    VLAN 30   segment 7   <- being configured now

items.explanation: A /48 allocation fixes the first three groups and leaves the fourth free as a subnet identifier, so segment 7 is written 2001:DB8:ACAD:7::/64. Option B alters the third group from ACAD to ACAE, which falls outside the allocation altogether. Option C keeps the right address but labels it /48, the length of the whole allocation rather than one segment. Option D places the 7 in the interface identifier instead of the subnet field, describing a host address rather than a subnet.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which interface is up but has no address that can be routed off the local link?

exhibit.content:
R4# show ipv6 interface brief
GigabitEthernet0/0     [up/up]
    FE80::21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
GigabitEthernet0/1     [up/up]
    FE80::21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5F
    2001:DB8:ACAD:9::1
GigabitEthernet0/2     [administratively down/down]
    unassigned

options.text: GigabitEthernet0/1
Loopback0
GigabitEthernet0/2
GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: GigabitEthernet0/0 shows up/up but lists only an FE80 address, and link-local addresses are confined to the link they sit on, so nothing can be routed to it from elsewhere. Option A carries a 2001 global address in addition to its link-local and is fully reachable. Option C is administratively down and unassigned, so it fails the up part of the question rather than the addressing part. Option B names an interface that does not appear in this output at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why do the link-local pings succeed while the global ones fail?

exhibit.content:
! R1 and R2 are cabled directly to one another
!
R1  interface GigabitEthernet0/0
     ipv6 address 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1/64
!
R2  interface GigabitEthernet0/0
     ipv6 address 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::1/64
!

Each router can ping the other's link-local address, but a ping to the
other's global address fails.

options.text: Link-local addresses are always reachable, but global addresses require DHCPv6.
The two global addresses sit in different /64 prefixes, so they need routing.
The global addresses lack an EUI-64 interface identifier and cannot be pinged.
Global addresses require ipv6 unicast-routing on both routers before any ping.

items.explanation: The fourth group differs, making the prefixes 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::/64 and 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::/64, so the two globals are on separate subnets and would need a router between them. Link-local pings still work because FE80 addresses are scoped to the shared link and do not depend on the prefixes at all, which is exactly what makes the fault look intermittent. Option A invents a DHCPv6 dependency for statically configured addresses. Option C treats EUI-64 as mandatory, but a manually written identifier is fine. Option D would prevent transit routing, not a directly connected ping.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which single command should be added under GigabitEthernet0/0?

exhibit.content:
! R6 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 no shutdown
!

GigabitEthernet0/0 must take its prefix from the router advertisements
already being sent on the segment and build its own interface identifier,
without any DHCPv6 server involved.

options.text: ipv6 address autoconfig
ipv6 address dhcp
ipv6 address 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1/64
ipv6 enable
ipv6 unicast-routing

items.explanation: Stateless address autoconfiguration takes the prefix from a router advertisement and appends an interface identifier the device generates itself, which is precisely what the requirement describes. Option B requests an address from a DHCPv6 server, which the requirement rules out explicitly. Option C hardcodes the prefix instead of learning it, so the address would not follow a renumbering. Option D brings IPv6 up but yields a link-local address only, leaving no global address. Option E is a global command enabling forwarding for the whole router and cannot be entered against an interface.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which global unicast address has been configured on GigabitEthernet0/1?

exhibit.content:
R7# show ipv6 interface brief
GigabitEthernet0/0     [up/up]
    FE80::2D0:58FF:FE12:3401
    2001:DB8:CAFE:10::1
GigabitEthernet0/1     [up/up]
    FE80::2D0:58FF:FE12:3402
    2001:DB8:CAFE:20::1
Loopback0              [up/up]
    FE80::2D0:58FF:FE12:3400
    2001:DB8:CAFE:FF::1

options.text: 2001:DB8:CAFE:FF::1

items.explanation: Each block lists its interface first and its addresses beneath, and the second entry under GigabitEthernet0/1 is the global address 2001:DB8:CAFE:20::1. Option A belongs to GigabitEthernet0/0, the block directly above, which is the classic error of reading the right field from the neighbouring block. Option B is the correct block's link-local rather than its global address. Option D is the loopback's global address, taken from the block below.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which address is a unique local address, routable inside the organisation but never across the internet?

exhibit.content:
Addresses observed on one segment during a survey

    Host        Address
    --------    ---------------------------
    SRV-A       2001:DB8:ACAD:1::10
    SRV-B       FD3A:9C21:4E7B:1::10
    SW-MGMT     FE80::20C:29FF:FEAB:CDEF
    (group)     FF02::1

options.text: FE80::20C:29FF:FEAB:CDEF

items.explanation: Unique local addresses come from FC00::/7 and are written in practice beginning FD, so FD3A:9C21:4E7B:1::10 is the one that routes within the organisation while being filtered at its edge. Option A begins with 2001 and falls in 2000::/3, the global unicast space that is routable across the internet. Option B begins FE80 and is link-local, which cannot be routed off its own link at all. Option C begins FF and is a multicast group address rather than a unicast address for any single host.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two of the joined groups would an ordinary IPv6 host join as well, not only a router? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
R2# show ipv6 interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  IPv6 is enabled, link-local address is FE80::21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
  Global unicast address(es):
    2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1, subnet is 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::/64
  Joined group address(es):
    FF02::1
    FF02::2
    FF02::1:FF00:1
  MTU is 1500 bytes

options.text: FE80::21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E

items.explanation: FF02::1 is the all-nodes group, which every IPv6 interface joins whatever its role, and FF02::1:FF00:1 is the solicited-node group derived from the low-order bits of the interface's own unicast address, which hosts and routers alike use for neighbour discovery. Option B is the all-routers group and marks this interface as a router's. Option C is the link-local unicast address rather than a group. Option E is the global unicast address, also not a group.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which link-local address does this interface form for itself?

exhibit.content:
! Host NIC details
!
    Burned-in address . . . : 000c.29ab.cdef
    IPv6 routing  . . . . . : enabled on the segment

The interface has just been brought up and has not yet received a router
advertisement, so it has formed only its link-local address.

options.text: FE80::20C:29FF:FEAB:CDEF
FE80::C:29FF:FEAB:CDEF
FE80::20C:29FE:FFAB:CDEF
FE80::20C:29FF:FECD:EFAB

items.explanation: A link-local address is FE80 followed by an interface identifier built by modified EUI-64: the MAC splits into 000C29 and ABCDEF, FFFE goes between them, and the seventh bit of the first byte inverts so 00 becomes 02. Option B leaves the first byte uninverted and then drops its leading digit, losing the 02 entirely. Option C writes the inserted value as FEFF instead of FFFE. Option D rotates the final three octets of the MAC rather than keeping their order.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which address would this host use as the source when contacting a server elsewhere on the internet?

exhibit.content:
PC1> ipconfig

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:

   IPv6 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 2001:DB8:ACAD:1:2C4A:9B11:78D3:5E02
   Temporary IPv6 Address. . . . . . : 2001:DB8:ACAD:1:9017:E3B2:44AC:1F65
   Link-local IPv6 Address . . . . . : FE80::2C4A:9B11:78D3:5E02
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : FE80::1

items.explanation: A host with both a stable and a temporary global address prefers the temporary one as the source for connections it starts outward, which is what the privacy extension exists to do, so the 9017 address is used. Option D is the stable global address and serves inbound connections rather than outbound ones. Option A is link-local and cannot leave the segment. Option B is link-local too and belongs to the router, appearing here only as the default gateway.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which VLAN has GigabitEthernet0/3 been assigned to?

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which ports have never been moved out of the default VLAN?

Option A names ports that appear on the SALES and VOICE rows, so both have been configured. Option B names the single port belonging to SERVERS. items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which pair of interface commands meets the requirement for Gi0/4?

exhibit.content:
! SW1 - GigabitEthernet0/4 as it stands today
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/4
 description spare port, to be handed to the server team
 no shutdown
!

VLAN 30 already exists on SW1. Gi0/4 must carry untagged traffic for a
single server in VLAN 30 and must never negotiate a trunk.

options.text: switchport mode access, then switchport access vlan 30
switchport access vlan 30, then switchport mode trunk
switchport mode access, then switchport voice vlan 30
switchport mode dynamic auto, then switchport access vlan 30

items.explanation: Setting the mode to access fixes the port so it never negotiates a trunk, and the access vlan command places its untagged traffic in VLAN 30, which is exactly what a single server needs. Option B assigns the VLAN and then makes the port a trunk, which would tag traffic the server cannot read. Option C configures a voice VLAN, meant for the tagged traffic of an IP phone rather than a server. Option D leaves the port willing to negotiate, which the requirement forbids.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How does SW1 handle the traffic arriving from the two devices on Gi0/1?

exhibit.content:
! SW1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 switchport voice vlan 20
!

An IP phone is cabled to Gi0/1, and a PC is cabled into the switch port
on the back of that phone.

options.text: Both devices send tagged frames, the PC in VLAN 10 and the phone in VLAN 20.
Both devices send untagged frames, and the switch places all of it in VLAN 10.
The PC sends untagged frames into VLAN 10; the phone tags its own for VLAN 20.
The port turns into a trunk and carries VLANs 10 and 20 tagged in both directions.

items.explanation: A port with both an access VLAN and a voice VLAN carries two kinds of traffic at once: whatever arrives untagged lands in the access VLAN, while the phone is told through CDP to tag its own traffic for the voice VLAN. Option A would require the PC to tag, which an ordinary host does not do. Option B ignores the voice VLAN entirely. Option D describes a trunk, and the configuration reads switchport mode access, which the voice VLAN does not change.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why can VLAN 20 hosts not reach their gateway while VLAN 10 hosts can?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - router on a stick
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 30
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
!
----------------------------------------------------------
SW1 carries VLANs 10 and 20 across the trunk to R1. Hosts in VLAN 10
reach 192.168.10.1 without trouble. Hosts in VLAN 20 cannot reach
192.168.20.1 at all.

options.text: A subinterface number must match the VLAN ID before encapsulation takes effect.
The trunk to R1 needs switchport nonegotiate before subinterfaces will pass traffic.
Each subinterface needs its own no shutdown command before it will forward.
The second subinterface tags for VLAN 30, which the trunk does not carry.

items.explanation: The VLAN a subinterface serves is set by the encapsulation dot1Q value, not by the subinterface number, and the second one reads 30 while the trunk carries only VLANs 10 and 20, so nothing tagged for VLAN 20 ever reaches a matching subinterface. Option A inverts that relationship: the number is a label and is conventionally matched for readability alone. Option B names a command affecting trunk negotiation rather than tagging. Option C is wrong because subinterfaces follow the state of the physical interface, which is already up.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which approach gives the two VLANs reachability to each other on SW-CORE?

exhibit.content:
+----------------+
                     |  SW-CORE (L3)  |
                     +---+--------+---+
                         |        |
                     VLAN 10   VLAN 20
                 192.168.10.0/24  192.168.20.0/24

SW-CORE is a Layer 3 switch. Both VLANs exist in its VLAN database and
both have active access ports. No router is attached, and hosts in the
two VLANs must be able to reach each other.

options.text: Create interface vlan 10 and interface vlan 20, then apply switchport mode access to each.
Enable ip routing, then give interface vlan 10 and interface vlan 20 an address.
Create a subinterface per VLAN with encapsulation dot1Q and an address on each.
Convert one physical port per VLAN into a routed port and address each of them.

items.explanation: A Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs using switched virtual interfaces, one per VLAN, but only once ip routing is enabled globally; without it the SVIs act as management interfaces and forward nothing. Option A applies a switchport command to a virtual interface, which has no physical port to switch. Option C describes router-on-a-stick, which belongs on a router across a trunk rather than on the switch itself. Option D consumes two physical ports and still leaves the VLANs unrouted.

options.text: No access port in VLAN 30 is up, so nothing brings the SVI into service.
The Vlan30 interface is missing a no shutdown command in the configuration.
VLAN 30 has not been created in the switch's VLAN database.
ip routing has not been enabled, so only one SVI may be active at a time.

items.explanation: An SVI follows its VLAN, coming up only while at least one access port in that VLAN is up or a trunk carries it; the VLAN 30 row lists no ports at all, while VLAN 10 lists two, which is the whole difference between the two interfaces. Option B is ruled out by the note that neither SVI carries a shutdown. Option C is contradicted by VLAN 30 appearing in the VLAN table as active. Option D invents a one-SVI limit, and the exhibit states ip routing is already on.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why can the two hosts not reach each other across the trunk?

switchport access vlan 40. The trunk joining the two switches is up
and allows every VLAN. A host on each of those two ports cannot

options.text: Spanning tree has placed VLAN 40 into a blocking state on the trunk link.
The two switches disagree about the native VLAN configured on the trunk.
VLAN 40 does not exist on SW2, so its port cannot become active in it.
The two hosts sit in different subnets and require a router between them.

items.explanation: A VLAN has to exist in a switch's own database before a port can join it, and SW2's table lists only VLANs 1 and 10; assigning its Gi0/1 to VLAN 40 therefore leaves that port inactive no matter what the trunk allows. Option A blames spanning tree, but a blocked VLAN would still appear in SW2's table. Option B describes a native VLAN mismatch, which affects untagged traffic rather than a VLAN missing entirely. Option D assumes different subnets, when both hosts are meant to share VLAN 40.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why has no trunk formed between the two switches?

exhibit.content:
! SW1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1

!
----------------------------------------------------------
! SW2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode dynamic auto
!

Both interfaces are up and the cable between them is known good, yet
show interfaces trunk lists nothing on either switch.

options.text: Both ports are set to dynamic auto, so neither one asks to become a trunk.
Dynamic auto requires 802.1Q to be stated explicitly before it will negotiate.
The two ports are in different VLANs, which blocks trunk negotiation.
A trunk cannot form until an access VLAN is removed from both interfaces.

items.explanation: Dynamic auto waits to be asked: it accepts a trunk if the far end proposes one but never proposes one itself, so two ports both set to auto sit in access mode indefinitely. Setting either side to trunk or dynamic desirable resolves it. Option B invents an encapsulation prerequisite that negotiation handles on its own. Option C misapplies VLAN membership, which does not govern whether negotiation happens. Option D describes removing configuration neither interface carries.

discovered on GigabitEthernet0/1 (99), with SW2 GigabitEthernet0/1 (1).
SW1#

The trunk between the two switches reports trunking on both sides and
tagged VLANs pass across it normally.

options.text: The trunk drops and no VLAN can cross it until the two ends agree.
Tagged frames for VLAN 99 are discarded by SW2 as belonging to an unknown VLAN.
Both switches move every VLAN into spanning tree blocking as a safety measure.
Untagged frames from VLAN 99 on SW1 arrive in VLAN 1 on SW2.

items.explanation: Each end leaves its own native VLAN untagged and assumes anything untagged belongs to that VLAN, so with 99 on one side and 1 on the other the two VLANs are quietly bridged into one broadcast domain. Option A expects the trunk to fail, but the exhibit states it reports trunking and tagged VLANs still pass, which is what makes this fault hard to spot. Option B describes tagged traffic, which is unaffected. Option C invents a spanning tree response that no switch takes to a native VLAN mismatch.

VLAN 20 is absent from the list of VLANs allowed on the trunk.
The trunk's native VLAN of 1 prevents any even-numbered VLAN from crossing.
Spanning tree has blocked VLAN 20 on this link to prevent a loop.

items.explanation: The Vlans allowed on trunk section reads 1,10,30, so frames tagged for VLAN 20 are dropped at the trunk regardless of the VLAN existing and having active ports at both ends. Option A blames pruning, but a pruned VLAN would still be listed as allowed and would appear in the allowed-and-active section. Option C invents a rule about even-numbered VLANs. Option D blames spanning tree, which would show the VLAN as allowed but missing only from the forwarding section.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which set of commands configures Gi0/24 to meet the stated requirement?
