The uplink must be a trunk that never relies on negotiation, must tag

switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q, switchport mode trunk, switchport trunk native vlan 99
switchport mode access, switchport access vlan 99, switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q

items.explanation: The three requirements map onto three commands: dot1q sets the tagging, mode trunk fixes the port so it does not depend on negotiation, and the native vlan command moves untagged traffic to 99. Option A leaves the port at dynamic desirable, which still negotiates. Option B omits the encapsulation and adds nonegotiate, which suppresses DTP frames but leaves the tagging method unset on a switch that supports more than one. Option D configures an access port, which carries a single VLAN untagged and tags nothing.

options.text: The second command replaced the list instead of extending it.
A trunk accepts at most one allowed-VLAN command per interface.
VLAN 40 does not exist, so the switch cleared the list as invalid.
The list was reset because the interface was not shut down first.

items.explanation: switchport trunk allowed vlan sets the list outright, so entering it a second time discards whatever went before; extending a list requires the add keyword, as in switchport trunk allowed vlan add 40. Option B invents a one-command limit, when the command may be issued repeatedly and simply overwrites each time. Option C blames a missing VLAN, but an allowed list may name VLANs that do not yet exist. Option D adds a shutdown requirement the command does not have.

items.explanation: Administrative Mode records what was configured and Operational Mode what the port actually became; dynamic auto will accept a trunk but never ask for one, so ending in static access means nothing on the far end proposed one either. options.text: No trunk will form, because both ends are configured statically.
VLAN 30 is allowed on SW7 but not on SW8, so its frames are dropped at SW8.
The encapsulation differs between the two ends, so tagged frames are unreadable.
Untagged traffic crosses between VLAN 99 and VLAN 1, merging two domains.
VLANs 10 and 20 will be pruned because the native VLANs disagree.

items.explanation: Two independent faults sit in these configurations: the allowed lists differ, so VLAN 30 leaves SW7 tagged and is discarded by SW8, and the native VLANs differ, so untagged frames cross between VLAN 99 and VLAN 1 and silently join the two. Option A is wrong because two ends both set to trunk form one readily. Option C invents an encapsulation difference that neither configuration states. Option E attaches pruning to the native VLAN, which governs untagged traffic rather than which VLANs are carried.

The links to SW2 are trunks, and CDP is exchanged only on access ports.
SW2 needs an IP address on a management interface before CDP will operate.

items.explanation: The message CDP is not enabled means the global process is off, so SW2 neither sends nor accepts advertisements; its neighbours still list it because they hold entries learned before it stopped, or because the direction is simply one-way. Option B invents a version incompatibility that CDPv2 does not create. Option C is wrong because CDP runs on trunks and access ports alike. Option D adds an addressing requirement CDP does not have, since it works at Layer 2.

items.explanation: The s flag against Gi0/2 marks it suspended, which is what happens when a member's configuration does not match its partner's, and here the allowed VLAN lists differ by one VLAN. Option B is contradicted by Po1 showing SU, so the bundle is up and running on Gi0/1 alone at half the intended bandwidth, which is what makes this fault easy to miss. Option D invents a one-member limit that would defeat the feature. Option E describes the H flag, which is absent here.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which change lets the port-channel take the address?

exhibit.content:
! SW6 - a Layer 3 switch aggregating two links to R1
!
interface Port-channel1
 ip address 10.9.9.1 255.255.255.252
!
interface range GigabitEthernet0/1 - 2
 channel-group 1 mode active
!

The port-channel refuses the ip address command, reporting that the
interface is a switchport.

options.text: Apply switchport mode trunk to the port-channel before addressing it.
Apply no switchport to Port-channel1 and to both member interfaces.
Move the address onto the member interfaces and leave the bundle unaddressed.
Change the member interfaces to channel-group 1 mode passive.

items.explanation: A Layer 3 EtherChannel needs the logical interface and its members taken out of switching with no switchport before an address will be accepted, and doing it on the port-channel alone leaves the members mismatched. Option A moves further into Layer 2, which is the opposite of what the error asks for. Option C addresses the members individually, which defeats the aggregation. Option D changes the LACP mode, which affects negotiation and has no bearing on whether the interface routes.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which command applied to both interfaces meets the requirement?

exhibit.content:
! SW7 - the two links to be bundled
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode trunk
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 switchport mode trunk
!

The two links must be aggregated into one logical trunk using LACP,
with SW7 actively initiating the negotiation.

options.text: channel-group 1 mode active
channel-group 1 mode desirable
channel-protocol lacp
channel-group 1 mode on

items.explanation: Active is the LACP mode that initiates the negotiation, which is precisely what the requirement asks SW7 to do, and applying it to both interfaces places them in the same group. Option B is the PAgP equivalent and would not speak LACP. Option C selects a protocol but creates no group, so no bundle forms from it alone. Option D forces the channel up without any negotiation, so nothing verifies that the far end agrees before traffic is committed to the bundle.

options.text: SW1 is the root, since its Bridge ID priority matches the Root ID priority.
SW1 is the root, because one of its ports is designated and forwarding.
SW1 is the secondary root and assumes the role if the current root fails.
SW1 is not the root, because the Root ID names a different address.

items.explanation: A bridge is the root only when the Root ID and Bridge ID describe the same bridge, and here the priorities match at 32778 while the addresses differ, so the root is another switch. Option A rests on the priorities alone, which is the trap: a tie in priority is normal and the address then decides. Option B misreads a designated port, which almost every switch has. Option C invents a secondary role that this output never records.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two statements describe how SW-C settles on a root port? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
+-------------+
                    |  ROOT-SW    |
                    +--+-------+--+
                       |       |
              cost 4   |       |   cost 4
                       |       |
                 +-----+--+ +--+-----+
                 |  SW-A  | |  SW-B  |
                 +-----+--+ +--+-----+
                       |       |
                 Gi0/1 |       | Gi0/2
                    +--+-------+--+
                    |    SW-C     |
                    +-------------+

Both of SW-C's paths reach the root at a total cost of 8. SW-A's bridge
ID is 32778.0022.2222.2222 and SW-B's is 32778.0033.3333.3333. The two
links from SW-C use port priority 128 with port numbers 1 and 2.

options.text: Both ports become root ports, and SW-C shares the load across them.
Cost to the root is compared first, and here the two paths tie at 8.
The tie falls to the neighbour advertising the lower bridge ID, so Gi0/1 wins.
The tie falls to the neighbour advertising the higher bridge ID, so Gi0/2 wins.
SW-C holds a fresh root election whenever two paths tie on cost.

items.explanation: Spanning tree compares cost to the root first, and with both paths at 8 that decides nothing, so the next comparison applies: the bridge ID of the neighbour sending the BPDU, where SW-A's 0022.2222.2222 beats SW-B's 0033.3333.3333 and Gi0/2 becomes an alternate port. Option A describes equal-cost load sharing, which routing protocols do and spanning tree deliberately does not. Option D applies the comparison backwards, since lower always wins. Option E invents a re-election that the tie-breakers exist to avoid.

The extra ten counts the ports this switch holds in the forwarding state.
The VLAN ID is carried in the priority field as the system ID extension.
32778 is the value the root advertised, and SW1 has adopted it.

items.explanation: Rapid PVST+ runs one instance per VLAN, so the bridge ID reserves part of the priority field for the VLAN number, and the output spells it out as priority 32768 sys-id-ext 10. That is why every VLAN on this switch shows a slightly different priority. Option A ties the value to how many VLANs exist, which would change as VLANs are added. Option B connects it to port states, which the priority does not track. Option D has the switch adopting the root's priority, when a bridge always advertises its own.

SW3's configured priority drops to 24576, so its bridge ID now wins.
SW3's priority is set to zero, the only value that guarantees the role.
Nothing changes for VLAN 10 until the present root bridge is reloaded.

items.explanation: The root primary macro lowers the configured priority for that VLAN to 24576, well below the current root's 32768, and since priority is compared before the address SW3 wins the election immediately. Its bridge ID then displays as 24586 once the VLAN's system ID extension is added. Option A invents a shared role that spanning tree has no concept of. Option C describes what root primary would do only if a competing bridge were already at 24576. Option D expects a reload, but the election reruns as soon as the new BPDU is sent.

Learning addresses while it counts down to a forwarding state.
Sitting administratively disabled after a shutdown command.
Blocking, while holding an alternate path toward the root bridge.

items.explanation: The row reads Altn for role and BLK for state, so the port has a valid path to the root but is kept out of forwarding to avoid a loop, ready to take over if the root port fails. Option A describes the Desg role that Gi0/3 carries. Option B describes the LRN state, which appears while a port transitions rather than while it holds steady. items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What risk does this configuration create, given what Gi0/5 is actually plugged into?

exhibit.content:
SW5(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/5
SW5(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW5(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW5(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
%Warning: portfast should only be enabled on ports connected to a single
host. Connecting hubs, concentrators, switches, bridges, etc... to this
interface when portfast is enabled, can cause temporary bridging loops.
Use with CAUTION

SW5(config-if)#

Gi0/5 has in fact been patched into an access port on another switch,
not to an end device.

options.text: The port forwards at once, so a loop can form before any BPDU is acted on.
The port is err-disabled the moment the neighbouring switch sends a BPDU.
The port refuses to negotiate a trunk for as long as PortFast is applied.
None, because PortFast is ignored on any port that reaches another switch.

items.explanation: PortFast moves an access port straight into forwarding without waiting through the listening and learning stages, which is safe for a single host but not for a link to another switch: traffic flows before spanning tree has had a chance to block anything, which is exactly what the warning describes. Option B describes BPDU guard, which is not configured here. Option C invents an interaction with trunk negotiation. Option D claims the switch detects what is attached, when only BPDU guard turns that detection into protection.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What happened on Gi0/5?

exhibit.content:
SW6#
*Aug 22 10:02:44.118: %SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port
GigabitEthernet0/5 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port.
*Aug 22 10:02:44.121: %PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on
Gi0/5, putting Gi0/5 in err-disable state
SW6#

Gi0/5 is an access port configured with spanning-tree portfast and
spanning-tree bpduguard enable.

options.text: A loop was detected across the port, and it was shut to break the loop.
The neighbour advertised a superior root, so the port was held blocking.
Something sending BPDUs was plugged into a PortFast access port.
BPDUs stopped arriving on the port, so it was disabled as unsafe.

items.explanation: BPDU guard exists to enforce the assumption PortFast makes, namely that only an end device sits on the port; the moment a BPDU arrives, that assumption is broken and the port is err-disabled rather than left to form a loop. Option A describes the outcome BPDU guard prevents rather than what it detects. Option B describes root guard, which blocks rather than err-disables. Option D describes loop guard, which reacts to BPDUs stopping rather than starting.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What did SW7 receive on Gi0/2 to trigger this message?

exhibit.content:
SW7#
*Aug 22 10:41:07.552: %SPANTREE-2-ROOTGUARD_BLOCK: Root guard blocking
port GigabitEthernet0/2 on VLAN0010.
SW7#

GigabitEthernet0/2 faces a switch administered by another team. Until a
moment ago it was a normal designated port carrying traffic.

options.text: Nothing; the port stopped receiving BPDUs from its neighbour altogether.
A BPDU advertising a bridge better than the current root bridge.
A BPDU on a port that had been configured with PortFast.
Two devices claiming the designated role for the same segment.

items.explanation: Root guard protects the topology's shape: it allows a neighbour to participate normally until that neighbour claims a better root, at which point the port is moved to root-inconsistent and blocks, which is why a port facing another team's switch is the classic place to apply it. Option A describes loop guard's trigger. Option C describes BPDU guard, which err-disables rather than blocking. Option D describes a condition spanning tree resolves by election rather than by guarding.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which feature keeps Gi0/3 from forwarding in this situation?

exhibit.content:
+-------------+
                    |   ROOT-SW   |
                    +--+-------+--+
                       |       |
                       |       |
                 +-----+--+ +--+-----+
                 |  SW-D  |-|  SW-E  |
                 +--------+ +--------+
                    Gi0/3 blocking on SW-E

SW-E's Gi0/3 has been blocking correctly for months. A fault develops in
one direction of that fibre pair, so SW-E stops receiving BPDUs on Gi0/3
while its own transmissions still reach SW-D. Without protection Gi0/3
would age out its stored BPDU, decide no better path exists, and begin
forwarding, closing a loop.

options.text: BPDU guard, which err-disables a port as soon as a BPDU reaches it.
PortFast, which leaves the port out of the spanning tree calculation.
Root guard, which stops the neighbour from claiming the root role.
Loop guard, which holds the port blocking once BPDUs stop arriving.

items.explanation: Loop guard covers exactly this case: a non-designated port that has been receiving BPDUs and then stops is moved to loop-inconsistent rather than being allowed to age out its stored BPDU and start forwarding, which is what would close the loop on a unidirectional fault. Option A reacts to a BPDU arriving, and the problem here is one no longer arriving. Option B describes a feature for host ports that would make the situation worse. Option C guards against a neighbour claiming the root, which is not what is happening.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which wireless architecture fits these requirements?

exhibit.content:
Requirements for a new wireless deployment

    Fourteen sites, 180 access points in total
    One wireless policy applied everywhere, changed centrally
    Clients must roam between APs at a site without reauthenticating
    The team will not log in to individual access points
    Hardware is to be owned and hosted by the organisation

options.text: Autonomous access points, each configured through its own interface.
A centralised controller with lightweight access points joined to it.
A cloud-managed deployment, with the controller hosted by the vendor.
A mesh of bridge-mode access points relaying between the fourteen sites.

items.explanation: One policy applied centrally, roaming handled between APs, no logging in to individual units and hardware owned on site all point to a controller-based split-MAC design. Option A would mean touching 180 devices for every change and offers no controller to coordinate a roam. Option C matches every requirement except the last, since a cloud deployment puts the control plane in the vendor's hands rather than the organisation's, which is the detail that separates the two. Option D describes a way of linking sites rather than an architecture for serving clients.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two functions stay on the access point rather than moving to the controller? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
A lightweight access point has joined its controller. The two now
divide the work of serving a client between them.

    Function
    -------------------------------------------------------
    Transmitting beacons and probe responses
    Acknowledging frames from clients at the radio
    Encrypting and decrypting frames on the air interface
    Deciding whether a client may associate
    Applying the security policy configured for the WLAN
    Managing the client's roam from one AP to the next

options.text: Deciding whether a client may associate
Acknowledging frames from clients at the radio
Applying the security policy configured for the WLAN
Transmitting beacons and probe responses
Managing the client's roam from one AP to the next

items.explanation: The split divides work by how time-critical it is: anything that must answer within microseconds stays on the radio, so the AP keeps beaconing, probe responses, acknowledgements and encryption, while slower decisions move upstream. Options A and C are policy decisions the controller makes once and applies everywhere. Option E is coordination between two APs, which only something seeing both of them can do. That is why an AP in local mode stops serving clients when it loses its controller.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which access point mode meets the branch requirement?

exhibit.content:
A branch office holds twelve access points and reaches the wireless
controller across a WAN circuit at the head office.

When that circuit fails, staff at the branch must keep using the local
wireless network, and their traffic must stay on the branch LAN rather
than being carried anywhere else.

options.text: Monitor mode, so the access points keep scanning while the circuit is down.
Local mode, which is the default and needs no change for this.
FlexConnect mode, which puts client traffic onto the branch LAN.
Bridge mode, so the APs relay to one another until the WAN returns.

items.explanation: FlexConnect exists for exactly this: the AP keeps serving clients and puts their traffic straight onto the local LAN, so a WAN failure between branch and controller does not take the wireless network down with it. Option A stops client service entirely, which is the opposite of the requirement. Option B tunnels all client traffic to the controller, so the branch loses wireless the moment the circuit fails. Option D links wired segments together and does not address controller reachability.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which mode should be applied to that access point?

exhibit.content:
Access point mode reference

    Mode           What the radio does
    -----------    ---------------------------------------------------
    Local          Serves clients, and scans off-channel briefly
    FlexConnect    Serves clients, can switch traffic locally
    Monitor        Serves no clients; listens full time
    Sniffer        Captures frames and forwards them to an analyser
    Bridge         Provides a wireless link between two wired segments

An access point is to be dedicated to detecting rogue devices and
measuring interference across the band. It must never carry client
traffic.

options.text: Monitor
Bridge
Sniffer
FlexConnect

items.explanation: Monitor is the mode that takes an AP out of client service and leaves its radio listening across the band full time, which is what rogue detection and interference measurement need. Option C also carries no clients, but it captures frames for an external analyser rather than reporting rogues and interference to the controller. Option B provides a wireless link between wired segments. Option D keeps serving clients, which the requirement forbids outright.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which statement correctly identifies the two units?

exhibit.content:
Two access points recovered from a storeroom

    Property                     Unit A                Unit B
    -------------------------    ------------------    ---------------
    Holds its own full config    yes                   no
    Configured over              its own web page      a controller
    Behaviour with no            keeps serving         will not serve
    controller reachable         clients               clients
    Typical deployment size      one or two units      dozens upward

options.text: Unit A is autonomous and Unit B is lightweight, needing a controller.
Unit B is autonomous, which is why it depends on a controller being reachable.
Both are lightweight; the difference is only which controller software they run.
Unit A is a mesh access point and Unit B is configured for FlexConnect.

items.explanation: Unit A carries its own full configuration, is administered through its own web page and keeps working with no controller, which describes an autonomous access point. Unit B holds no configuration and will not serve clients without a controller, which is the defining trait of a lightweight one. Option B reverses the two, and depending on a controller is precisely what autonomous means it does not do. Option C denies a difference the table records in four rows. Option D applies deployment modes that the table never mentions.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How should the switch port serving AP-21 be configured?

exhibit.content:
CAPWAP tunnel
        +--------+   ................................   +---------+
        |  AP-21 |===[ SW-ACC ]=====[ SW-DIST ]=========|   WLC   |
        +--------+                                      +---------+
       lightweight,                                      10.50.0.5
       local mode

AP-21 advertises three SSIDs, mapped on the controller to VLANs 10, 20
and 30. The access point itself is addressed from the management VLAN,
VLAN 50. All client traffic is carried inside CAPWAP to the WLC.

options.text: As a trunk allowing VLANs 10, 20 and 30, one for each advertised SSID.
As a trunk allowing VLANs 10, 20, 30 and 50, with 50 as the native VLAN.
As an access port in VLAN 50, where the AP itself is addressed.
As a routed port with an address in each of the three client VLANs.

items.explanation: A lightweight AP in local mode wraps every client frame in CAPWAP and sends it to the controller, so the switch never sees VLAN 10, 20 or 30 on that link; the only traffic on the wire belongs to the AP itself, which lives in VLAN 50. An access port is therefore correct and a trunk would carry nothing extra. Options A and B follow the reasoning that several SSIDs must mean several VLANs on the cable, which holds for an autonomous AP but not behind a controller. Option D would need the AP to route, which it does not.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which switchport configuration does the link to this autonomous access point require?

exhibit.content:
+-----------+
        |   AP-07   |-----------[ SW-ACC ]
        +-----------+
        autonomous

AP-07 holds its own configuration and no controller is deployed. It
advertises three SSIDs and bridges each one directly onto the wired
network as VLAN 10, VLAN 20 and VLAN 30 respectively.

options.text: As an access port in VLAN 10, with the other two SSIDs tunnelled inside it.
As a trunk carrying VLANs 10, 20 and 30 down to the access point.
As an access port in a management VLAN, since the AP holds its own config.
As a routed port, because an autonomous access point performs its own routing.

items.explanation: An autonomous access point has no controller to tunnel to, so it tags each SSID's traffic onto the wire itself and the switch must carry all three VLANs, which requires a trunk. Option A would collapse three separate networks into one and there is no tunnel here to carry the others. Option C describes the correct answer for a lightweight AP in local mode, which is the contrast worth holding onto. Option D has the AP routing between the VLANs, which it bridges rather than routes.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How should the four controller ports and the switch side be configured?

exhibit.content:
A wireless controller is being cabled into the distribution layer.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Four controller ports go to the same distribution switch pair
    The four are to act as one logical link, surviving any one failure
    Every WLAN interface on the controller must reach the switches
    The controller's LAG implementation does not negotiate with LACP

options.text: Four separate access ports, one per WLAN interface on the controller.
One EtherChannel with LACP active on the switch side to negotiate the bundle.
Four separate trunks, letting the controller balance across them itself.
One EtherChannel set to mode on, carrying a trunk for the WLAN interfaces.

items.explanation: The requirements ask for one logical link that survives a failure, so the four ports bundle into an EtherChannel, and they must carry several WLAN interfaces, so that bundle is a trunk. Because the controller's LAG does not negotiate, the switch side has to be forced on rather than left to LACP. Option B is the right shape but relies on a negotiation the exhibit says will not happen, leaving the ports unbundled. Option A gives one VLAN per port and no resilience. Option C leaves four independent links with no bundle at all.

    SW1>

options.text: The session was encrypted, and the analyser has decrypted it using a stored key.
The password shown is a hash, so the capture reveals nothing an attacker could reuse.
The capture was taken on the device itself, which is why the payload is readable.
Credentials crossed the network in clear text, readable by anyone capturing.

items.explanation: Telnet carries its payload with no encryption at all, so reassembling the frames yields the username and password exactly as typed, which is why SSH replaced it for device management. Option A credits an encryption the protocol never applied. Option B hopes the value is a hash, but the reassembled stream shows the characters the operator entered. Option C suggests the capture point explains the readability, when a capture anywhere along the path would show the same thing.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which access control protocol fits these requirements, and why?

exhibit.content:
An access control server is being chosen for the network team.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Junior staff may log in to switches but run only show commands
    Senior staff get full privileges on the same devices
    Every command a user types must be recorded centrally
    The entire exchange with the server must be encrypted, not just
    the password field

options.text: RADIUS, because it combines authentication with authorisation in one exchange.
TACACS+, which separates authorisation and logs each command.
RADIUS, because it is an open standard and therefore records more detail.
Either one, since both handle per-command authorisation in the same way.

items.explanation: Two requirements decide this: different privilege levels for different staff on the same device, and a record of every command typed, which needs authorisation and accounting handled separately from authentication. TACACS+ does that and encrypts the whole payload rather than the password alone. Option A names the very property that makes RADIUS unsuitable here, since combining the two leaves no room for per-command control. Option C substitutes openness for capability. Option D denies a difference that is the heart of the comparison.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which access method lets the engineer reach the switch now?

exhibit.content:
A distribution switch has become unreachable. Its uplinks are down,
its management VLAN interface does not answer, and no routing protocol
adjacency to it remains. The switch itself is powered on and its status
lights are normal.

An engineer is standing in the room with the switch and a laptop.

options.text: SSH to the management VLAN interface, once a laptop is on the same subnet.
HTTPS to the device's web interface from the laptop over a patch lead.
The console port, using a cable directly from the laptop to the switch.
Telnet from the laptop, since Telnet needs no working routing protocol.

items.explanation: Console access is out of band: it needs no address, no VLAN and nothing on the network to be working, which is exactly why it remains available when everything else on the device has failed. Options A, B and D all depend on the switch being reachable over the network, and the exhibit states the uplinks are down and the management interface does not answer. Option D also assumes Telnet somehow bypasses that, when it needs IP reachability just as SSH does.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why are SSH connections refused when the keys have been generated?

exhibit.content:
! SW4 - relevant configuration
!
hostname SW4
ip domain-name example.internal
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
!
username netadmin privilege 15 secret Wr3nch-Harbour-42
!
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input telnet
!

Attempts to reach SW4 over SSH are refused, while Telnet connects and
prompts for credentials normally.

options.text: The vty lines accept Telnet only, so SSH is never offered on them.
The RSA key is too short, and SSH requires a modulus above 2048 bits.
The username needs privilege level 15 removed before SSH will accept it.
A domain name must be set after the key is generated, not before.

items.explanation: Generating a key makes SSH possible but does not enable it: the vty lines decide what they will listen for, and transport input telnet excludes SSH entirely. Changing that line to transport input ssh is the fix, and doing so also stops the clear-text option. Option B invents a length requirement, and 2048 exceeds the 768-bit minimum comfortably. Option C confuses privilege level, which governs what an account may do after logging in. Option D reverses the correct order, since the domain name must exist before the key can be generated at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two weaknesses remain in SW5's management configuration? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! SW5 - relevant configuration
!
ip http server
no ip http secure-server
!
line con 0
 password 7 08701E1D5D4C53
 login
!
line vty 0 15
 transport input ssh
 login local
!

options.text: The web interface answers over plain HTTP rather than being secured.
The vty lines still permit Telnet alongside SSH.
The console password is held with a reversible encoding rather than a hash.
No password has been set on the console line at all.
Local authentication has been left off the vty lines.

items.explanation: ip http server is on while ip http secure-server is off, so anything sent to the web interface crosses in clear, and the console password carries the type 7 marker, which is an obfuscation that is trivially reversed rather than a hash. Option B is contradicted by transport input ssh, which excludes Telnet. Option D is contradicted by the password line under line con 0, weak though its storage is. Option E is contradicted by login local on the vty lines.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why can no client see or join this WLAN?

exhibit.content:
WLC GUI  -  WLANs > Edit > CORP-WIFI

Tab: General
    Profile Name                  CORP-WIFI
    SSID                          CORP-WIFI
    Status                        Disabled
    Radio Policy                  All
    Interface/Interface Group     vlan10-corp
    Broadcast SSID                Enabled

Tab: Security > Layer 2
    Layer 2 Security              WPA+WPA2
    WPA2 Policy                   Enabled
    WPA2 Encryption               AES
    Authentication Key Mgmt       PSK

The access points are joined and healthy, VLAN 10 is reachable, and the
pre-shared key has been distributed. No client can see or join CORP-WIFI.

options.text: Broadcast SSID is enabled, which hides the network from ordinary clients.
The WLAN's Status is Disabled, so it is never advertised.
The Radio Policy of All prevents the WLAN binding to any single band.
WPA2 with PSK cannot be used together with an interface group.

items.explanation: A WLAN is only pushed to the access points once its Status is Enabled, so with it disabled the SSID is never advertised no matter how complete the rest of the configuration is. Option A reverses the meaning of Broadcast SSID, which when enabled makes the network visible rather than hiding it. Option C misreads Radio Policy, where All means both bands carry the WLAN rather than none. Option D invents a conflict; WPA2 with a pre-shared key on a mapped interface is an ordinary combination.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two statements describe what a guest experiences on this WLAN? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
WLC GUI  -  WLANs > Edit > GUEST-WIFI

Tab: General
    Profile Name                  GUEST-WIFI
    SSID                          GUEST-WIFI
    Status                        Enabled
    Interface/Interface Group     vlan90-guest

Tab: Security > Layer 2
    Layer 2 Security              None

Tab: Security > Layer 3
    Layer 3 Security              Web Policy
    Web Policy                    Authentication

options.text: They are prompted for a pre-shared key when they associate.
They cannot associate at all until a Layer 2 security method is set.
They associate with no key, and their traffic crosses the air unencrypted.
A browser is intercepted and credentials are demanded before access is granted.
Their traffic becomes encrypted once web authentication succeeds.

items.explanation: Layer 2 Security reads None, so association needs no key and nothing protects the radio link, while the Layer 3 Web Policy intercepts the browser and demands credentials before granting access. Option A describes a pre-shared key the configuration does not set. Option B is contradicted by this being an ordinary working guest arrangement. Option E is the tempting error: web authentication decides who may pass traffic and never turns on link-layer encryption, so guest traffic stays readable throughout.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which change on the controller addresses the reported audio problem?

exhibit.content:
WLC GUI  -  WLANs > Edit > VOICE-WIFI

Tab: General
    Profile Name                  VOICE-WIFI
    SSID                          VOICE-WIFI
    Status                        Enabled
    Interface/Interface Group     vlan20-voice

Tab: QoS
    Quality of Service (QoS)      Silver (best effort)
    Application Visibility        Disabled
    WMM Policy                    Allowed

Handsets on this WLAN report choppy audio whenever the office data
network is busy. Wired QoS is already trusting and prioritising the
voice VLAN correctly end to end.

options.text: Disable the WMM Policy, so voice frames are no longer queued behind data.
Enable Application Visibility so the controller can identify the voice stream.
Set Quality of Service on this WLAN to Platinum, the profile intended for voice.
Move the WLAN to the data interface so it shares the wired queue already trusted.

items.explanation: The wired path is already prioritising voice, so the gap is over the air: this WLAN sits on Silver, the best-effort profile, and voice needs Platinum, which is the profile the controller reserves for it. Option A removes the very mechanism that gives voice frames preferential radio access. Option B adds visibility and reporting without changing how frames are queued. Option D moves voice onto the data network, which would undo the separation that makes the wired prioritisation work.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does the Maximum Allowed Clients value of 0 mean for this WLAN?

exhibit.content:
WLC GUI  -  WLANs > Edit > CORP-WIFI

Tab: Advanced
    Enable Session Timeout        1800 seconds
    Client Exclusion              Enabled, 60 seconds
    Maximum Allowed Clients       0
    Aironet IE                    Enabled
    P2P Blocking Action           Disabled
    Client Load Balancing         Disabled

options.text: No limit is applied; clients are capped by hardware alone.
The WLAN is closed to clients until an administrator raises the figure.
Clients are admitted one at a time as earlier sessions time out.
The value is ignored while Client Exclusion remains enabled.

items.explanation: On this page zero is the value meaning unlimited rather than none, so the WLAN accepts clients up to whatever the access points and controller can carry. Option B reads zero literally, which would silently take a working WLAN out of service and is the reason the convention is worth knowing. Option C invents a queueing behaviour tied to the session timeout above it. Option D links the field to Client Exclusion, which governs how long a misbehaving client is locked out rather than how many may join.

options.text: 110 is the administrative distance of the entry; the OSPF cost shown for it is 74.
110 is the OSPF cost of the entry; the administrative distance shown for it is 74.
110 is the hop count that OSPF inherited from the RIP entry above it in the table.
110 is a composite metric, because OSPF entries are not assigned an administrative distance.

items.explanation: The bracket prints [administrative distance/metric]. For 192.168.40.0/24 that is [110/74], so 110 is the administrative distance and 74 is the OSPF cost. Option B simply reverses the two fields, the single commonest misreading of this output. Option C imports the hop-count metric idea from the RIP entry [120/3] above and applies it to OSPF, confusing one protocol's metric type with another's. Option D asserts that OSPF has no administrative distance, when every installed entry is selected using one.

The six child entries are subnets of 10.0.0.0/8 and use three different masks.
R4 is summarising the six child subnets of 10.0.0.0/8 into three advertised routes.
Three of the six child subnets were learned from a classful protocol that discarded the mask.

options.text: 10.1.1.0/30, because a static next hop must sit on a directly connected subnet.
10.1.1.4/30, because that entry's range covers the next hop 10.1.1.6.
10.1.1.1/32, because the local route identifies the router's own outgoing interface.

Option A describes a floating route held out of the table, but a backup path with a worse distance would not be printed here at all. Option B reads duplication as instability, yet both paths show a matching 00:31:16 uptime, which indicates stability rather than flapping. Option C invents a numerically-lowest-next-hop tie-break, borrowing a bridge-ID style comparison that OSPF does not apply to installed routes.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Both prefixes were learned from the same neighbour, 10.9.9.2. Which conclusion does the administrative distance shown for 192.168.80.0/24 support?

exhibit.content:

Both routes, because R6 load-shares whenever two protocols offer the same prefix.
The RIP route, because its updates arrive more often than OSPF link-state refreshes.

items.explanation: When two sources offer the same prefix, IOS compares administrative distance first and installs the more trustworthy source. The exhibit prints distance 110 for the OSPF entry, and RIP's 120 is higher, so the OSPF route stays. Option B compares a hop count with an OSPF cost, but metrics from different protocols have no common scale. Option C invents cross-protocol load sharing, which does not occur. The better-trusted OSPF entry is installed and the static waits in reserve, appearing only if OSPF withdraws the prefix. Option B assumes statics always win, which is true only at their default distance of 1. Option C would require equal distance and equal cost. items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Both paths from R1 to 192.168.70.0/24 are inside OSPF area 0. Which path does R1 install, based on the costs shown?

options.text: The path through R2, with a total cost of 21.
The path through R3, with a total cost of 11.
Both paths, because OSPF always load-shares across available paths.
The path through R2, because it has the lower administrative distance.

items.explanation: OSPF sums the outgoing interface costs along each path. Through R2 the total is 10 plus 10 plus 1, which is 21; through R3 it is 5 plus 5 plus 1, which is 11. The lower total wins, so R1 installs the path through R3. Option A adds the costs correctly but then selects the higher total. Option C assumes load sharing without checking that the costs are unequal. Option D invokes administrative distance to separate two routes learned from the same protocol, where it is identical and decides nothing.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R15 receives advertisements for 172.20.40.0/24 from both EIGRP and OSPF, and the OSPF advertisement carries a cost of 3. Why did R15 install the entry shown rather than the OSPF one?

R15# show ip route 172.20.40.0
Routing entry for 172.20.40.0/24
  Known via "eigrp 100", distance 90, metric 3072, type internal

      Loading 1/255, Hops 1

options.text: Because EIGRP updates arrive faster than OSPF LSAs, so EIGRP populated the table first.
Because the EIGRP route is internal, and internal routes are always preferred over OSPF.
Because metrics are compared only when two routes carry the same prefix length.
Because administrative distance is compared first, and EIGRP's 90 beats OSPF's 110.

items.explanation: The exhibit prints distance 90 for the EIGRP entry. When two protocols offer the same prefix, IOS compares administrative distance before it ever looks at a metric, so EIGRP wins and the OSPF cost of 3 is never weighed against 3072. Option A substitutes timing for distance. Option B invents a rule about internal routes that would apply within EIGRP, not between protocols. Option C states a condition that is already satisfied here, since both advertisements carry the same /24.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R1 must reach every host in the 172.16.8.0 through 172.16.11.255 range by way of R2, using one static route. Which command configures it?

Option B is a /23 and covers only 172.16.8.0 through 172.16.9.255, leaving half the range unreachable, a boundary error of exactly one block. Option C is a /24 and covers only the first quarter. Option D supplies the wildcard mask 0.0.3.255, which belongs in an access list; the ip route command expects a subnet mask.

items.explanation: A Cisco router drops IPv6 transit traffic until ipv6 unicast-routing is enabled globally; the interface still holds an address and answers pings addressed to itself, which is exactly why the fault looks like a routing problem. Option A would be required only for a link-local next hop, and this next hop is global. Option C is wrong because IOS derives a link-local address automatically. Option D confuses a host route's length with the /64 the destination network genuinely uses.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Every destination for which R3 holds no specific route must be sent to the ISP router at 203.0.113.1. Which command achieves that?

items.explanation: A default route is the prefix 0.0.0.0 with the mask 0.0.0.0, which matches every destination and loses every longest-match comparison, so it applies only when nothing more specific exists. Option A is a real command, but it applies to a device with IP routing disabled, such as a Layer 2 switch, and is ignored on a routing router. Option B pairs the all-zeros network with a host mask, matching only the address 0.0.0.0. Option D marks a classful network as a candidate default and does not create this route.

Option A writes the IPv4 default prefix into an IPv6 command, mixing the two address families. Option B uses ::/128, which is the unspecified address as a host route and matches nothing useful. Option C pairs the right prefix with the IPv4 command keyword, which IOS will not accept for an IPv6 destination.

The route is refused, because Ethernet interfaces cannot appear in an ip route command.
R9 installs the route with an administrative distance of 0 rather than the usual 1.

items.explanation: Naming a broadcast interface tells R9 the destination is reachable out that port but not which neighbour to address, so it ARPs for the remote destination itself and forwards only if a neighbour answers on that host's behalf through proxy ARP. Option B is wrong because the command is accepted. Option C repeats the common belief that an exit-interface static becomes a connected route with distance 0; it still carries 1, though it is displayed as directly connected. Option D invents load sharing that no single static route performs.

Option A enables IPv4 routing, which is on by default and has no effect on IPv6 traffic. Option D points at a link-local next hop without the exit interface, which IOS rejects as ambiguous. Option E would replace the manually configured address with an autoconfigured one, changing the interface rather than establishing the route.

ipv6 route 2001:DB8:ACAD:3::/64 2001:DB8:ACAD:12::2
ipv6 route 2001:DB8:ACAD:3::/64 2001:DB8:ACAD:24::2 5
R11#
R11# show ipv6 route static
IPv6 Routing Table - default - 6 entries
Codes: C - Connected, L - Local, S - Static, U - Per-user Static route
       B - BGP, R - RIP, H - NHRP, I1 - ISIS L1
       I2 - ISIS L2, IA - ISIS interarea, IS - ISIS summary, D - EIGRP
       EX - EIGRP external, ND - ND Default, NDp - ND Prefix, DCE - Destination
       NDr - Redirect, RL - RPL, O - OSPF Intra, OI - OSPF Inter
       OE1 - OSPF ext 1, OE2 - OSPF ext 2, ON1 - OSPF NSSA ext 1

S   2001:DB8:ACAD:3::/64 [1/0]

options.text: The second route was refused at configuration time as a duplicate prefix.
The second route is active but this command displays only the first path.
Both routes are in use and the displayed output has simply been truncated.
The second route has a higher distance and waits as a backup.

items.explanation: The second command ends in 5, which sets its administrative distance to 5 against the first route's default of 1, making it an IPv6 floating static that installs only if the primary is withdrawn. Option A is wrong because IOS accepts several statics for one prefix precisely so backups can exist. Option B invents a display limit; the command lists every installed static. Option C treats the single entry as truncation, but the table reports its entry count and the primary is genuinely the only installed path.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which next-hop address has R12 recorded for the 2001:DB8:ACAD:9::/64 prefix?

exhibit.content:
R12# show ipv6 route static
IPv6 Routing Table - default - 8 entries
Codes: C - Connected, L - Local, S - Static, U - Per-user Static route
       B - BGP, R - RIP, H - NHRP, I1 - ISIS L1
       I2 - ISIS L2, IA - ISIS interarea, IS - ISIS summary, D - EIGRP
       EX - EIGRP external, ND - ND Default, NDp - ND Prefix, DCE - Destination
       NDr - Redirect, RL - RPL, O - OSPF Intra, OI - OSPF Inter
       OE1 - OSPF ext 1, OE2 - OSPF ext 2, ON1 - OSPF NSSA ext 1
