S   2001:DB8:ACAD:7::/64 [1/0]
     via 2001:DB8:ACAD:12::2
S   2001:DB8:ACAD:9::/64 [1/0]
     via 2001:DB8:ACAD:34::2
S   ::/0 [1/0]
     via 2001:DB8:FEED:1::1

items.explanation: In show ipv6 route output the next hop appears on the indented via line beneath its prefix, and the one under 2001:DB8:ACAD:9::/64 reads 2001:DB8:ACAD:34::2. Option A takes the via line belonging to the 2001:DB8:ACAD:7::/64 entry above it, the classic error of reading the right field from the neighbouring block. Option B belongs to the ::/0 default entry below. Option D assumes the next hop is the first address inside the destination prefix, which the output never states.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R13 must reach 2001:DB8:ACAD:9::/64 through the neighbour whose link-local address is FE80::2, reached over GigabitEthernet0/0. Which command is accepted and produces that route?

options.text: ipv6 route 2001:DB8:ACAD:9::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0 FE80::2
ipv6 route 2001:DB8:ACAD:9::/64 FE80::2 GigabitEthernet0/0
ipv6 route 2001:DB8:ACAD:9::/64 FE80::2
ipv6 route 2001:DB8:ACAD:9::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: When the next hop is link-local the exit interface must come first, then the address, because FE80::2 alone does not say which link it sits on. Option B carries exactly the right keywords in the wrong order, which IOS will not parse. Option C omits the interface altogether and is rejected outright for that reason. Option D names only the interface, which IOS accepts but leaves R13 relying on neighbour discovery for every destination across a multi-access link rather than pointing at R14.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R14 must reach all four branch subnets through 10.1.1.2 using a single static route that covers those four and nothing beyond them. Which command does that?
items.explanation: Four consecutive /24s starting at a multiple of four summarise to a /22, and 255.255.252.0 anchored at 172.16.20.0 spans 172.16.20.0 through 172.16.23.255 exactly. Option A is a /23 and reaches only the first two subnets. Option C uses the right mask but the wrong base, covering 172.16.16.0 through 172.16.19.255, none of which are branch subnets. Option D is a /21 spanning 172.16.16.0 through 172.16.23.255, which does include all four but drags in four subnets that were not meant to be covered.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The 192.168.77.0/24 block is unassigned, and traffic addressed to it should be dropped by R15 instead of being handed to the ISP. Which command achieves that?

exhibit.content:
R15# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       i - IS-IS, su - IS-IS summary, L1 - IS-IS level-1, L2 - IS-IS level-2
       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       a - application route
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
      192.168.1.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        192.168.1.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        192.168.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
      203.0.113.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        203.0.113.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        203.0.113.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: Null0 is a virtual interface that discards everything sent to it, so a static route pointing there gives the block a longer match than the default and drops the traffic locally. Option A names 0.0.0.0 as a next hop, which does not identify the discard interface. Option B borrows the blackhole keyword used by other vendors; IOS does not accept it. Option C removes a route that was never configured, leaving the default to keep carrying the traffic to the ISP, which is the behaviour being eliminated.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The route was meant to cover only 192.168.16.0/24, but the mask was mistyped. What is the effect of the command as entered?

exhibit.content:
! R16 - relevant configuration
!
ip route 192.168.16.0 255.255.240.0 10.1.1.2
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1
!

Traffic for every 192.168.x.x destination other than 192.168.16.0/24 is
expected to leave by the default route.

options.text: It covers only 192.168.16.0 through 192.168.16.255, exactly as intended.
It also captures 192.168.17.0 through 192.168.31.255, bypassing the default.
It is rejected at entry, because the address and mask are inconsistent.
It covers the whole of 192.168.0.0 through 192.168.255.255, capturing every private prefix.

items.explanation: 255.255.240.0 is a /20, and a /20 anchored at 192.168.16.0 spans sixteen values in the third octet, 16 through 31. Traffic to any of those now follows 10.1.1.2 rather than the default. Option A describes the /24 that was intended but not the mask that was typed. Option C expects a rejection, but 16 is a valid multiple of 16 so the pair is consistent and IOS accepts it silently, which is what makes the error hard to spot. Option D describes a /16, two steps broader than the mask shown.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The default entry reads 'is directly connected' rather than naming a next hop. What does that tell you about how it was configured?

exhibit.content:
R17# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       i - IS-IS, su - IS-IS summary, L1 - IS-IS level-1, L2 - IS-IS level-2
       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       a - application route
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is 0.0.0.0 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 is directly connected, Serial0/0/0
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        10.1.1.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0

options.text: The default route was learned dynamically from the service provider.
The default route carries an administrative distance of 0, as connected routes do.
R17 must ARP for every remote destination reached across that link.
The default route was configured with an exit interface instead of a next hop.

items.explanation: A static route configured with only an exit interface is displayed as directly connected, which is why the entry names Serial0/0/0 and no via address. Option A is ruled out by the S code, which marks a static route rather than a learned one. Option B repeats the frequent belief that this display form implies distance 0; the route still carries the static default of 1. Option C describes what happens on a multi-access link, but a point-to-point serial interface has one possible receiver and uses no ARP.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which entry in R18's table is a statically configured host route?

exhibit.content:
R18# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       i - IS-IS, su - IS-IS summary, L1 - IS-IS level-1, L2 - IS-IS level-2
       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       a - application route
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 5 subnets, 4 masks
C        10.1.1.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
S        10.60.0.0/16 [1/0] via 10.1.1.2
S        10.60.5.7/32 [1/0] via 10.1.1.2
S        10.70.0.0/20 [1/0] via 10.1.1.2

items.explanation: A host route carries the all-ones mask, and the only entry that is both coded S and written /32 is 10.60.5.7/32. Option B is a static route but a /16 network route covering 65,534 addresses. Option C is the trap: it is a /32, but its code is L, meaning IOS created it automatically for the router's own interface address rather than an administrator configuring it. Option D is a static /20 network route, broader still than option B.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. No router ID has been set under the OSPF process. Which value does R1 adopt as its router ID when OSPF starts?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface Loopback0
 ip address 1.1.1.1 255.255.255.255
!
interface Loopback1
 ip address 9.9.9.9 255.255.255.255
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!

items.explanation: With no router-id command, OSPF prefers the highest IPv4 address on any active loopback, and 9.9.9.9 outranks 1.1.1.1. Option A assumes Loopback0 wins because of its interface number, but the comparison is on address value, not interface order. Option B is the highest physical interface address, which is consulted only when no loopback exists. Option D would mean OSPF failed to pick an ID, in which case the process refuses to start rather than running with zeros.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. An engineer sets a router ID on R2, but the verification command still reports the old value. Which action makes the configured value take effect?

exhibit.content:
R2# show ip ospf | include Routing Process
 Routing Process "ospf 1" with ID 10.1.2.1
R2#
R2# configure terminal
Enter configuration commands, one per line.  End with CNTL/Z.
R2(config)# router ospf 1
R2(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2
% OSPF: Reload or use "clear ip ospf process" command, for this to take effect
R2(config-router)# end
R2#
R2# show ip ospf | include Routing Process
 Routing Process "ospf 1" with ID 10.1.2.1

options.text: Clear the OSPF process with clear ip ospf process, or reload the router.
Re-enter the router-id command from interface configuration mode instead.
Remove and re-add the network statement so OSPF re-reads its configuration.
Configure a loopback with address 2.2.2.2 so the ID is derived from it.

items.explanation: A router ID is chosen when the OSPF process starts and is then held for the life of that process, which is why IOS prints the reload-or-clear notice visible in the exhibit. Option B invents an interface-level version of the command, which does not exist; router-id is a router-configuration command. Option C touches the network statement, which changes which interfaces run OSPF but never re-runs ID selection. Option D would matter only if no ID had been configured at all, and it still would not apply without restarting the process.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Both interfaces are up on the same link, yet no adjacency forms. Which two differences in the output explain it? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
R1# show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 10.1.1.1/30, Area 0, Attached via Network Statement
  Process ID 1, Router ID 1.1.1.1, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DR, Priority 1
  Designated Router (ID) 1.1.1.1, Interface address 10.1.1.1
  No backup designated router on this network
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5
  Neighbor Count is 0, Adjacent neighbor count is 0
----------------------------------------------------------
R2# show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 10.1.1.2/30, Area 0, Attached via Network Statement
  Process ID 1, Router ID 2.2.2.2, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DR, Priority 1
  Designated Router (ID) 2.2.2.2, Interface address 10.1.1.2
  No backup designated router on this network
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 5, Dead 20, Wait 20, Retransmit 5
  Neighbor Count is 0, Adjacent neighbor count is 0

options.text: The hello intervals differ between the two interfaces.
The two routers advertise different router IDs on the segment.
The dead intervals differ between the two interfaces.
Both interfaces report State DR, so neither will accept the other.
The interface cost of 1 is too low for a broadcast network type.

items.explanation: OSPF requires both the hello and the dead interval to match before neighbours will form, and R1 uses 10 and 40 where R2 uses 5 and 20, so each discards the other's hellos. Option B inverts a requirement, since router IDs must differ rather than match. Option D mistakes a symptom for a cause: each claims DR precisely because neither has seen the other. Option E invents a minimum cost, and cost never governs whether an adjacency forms.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The link between R1 and R2 is up and both routers run OSPF in area 0, yet no adjacency forms. What prevents it?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!
----------------------------------------------------------
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.5 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 2
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 network 10.1.1.4 0.0.0.3 area 0
!

options.text: The two routers have conflicting router IDs on the shared segment.
The OSPF process IDs differ, and they must match for an adjacency to form.
The hello intervals differ because only one router sets them explicitly.
The two interfaces do not sit in the same IPv4 subnet.

items.explanation: With a /30 mask, 10.1.1.1 belongs to 10.1.1.0/30 while 10.1.1.5 belongs to 10.1.1.4/30, so the addresses look adjacent but the interfaces are on different subnets and OSPF will not peer across them. Option B names the process IDs 1 and 2, which is the most tempting distractor here: the process ID is locally significant and need not match. Option A is wrong because 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2 differ, which is what OSPF requires. Option C invents a timer difference neither configuration shows.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which router is elected designated router on the shared segment?

exhibit.content:
10.1.1.0/24  (broadcast segment)
      +---------+---------------+---------------+---------------+
                |               |               |               |
            +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+
            |  R1   |       |  R2   |       |  R3   |       |  R4   |
            +-------+       +-------+       +-------+       +-------+
        router-id 1.1.1.1   4.4.4.4         3.3.3.3         2.2.2.2
        ip ospf priority 1  priority 1      priority 5      priority 0

All four routers are powered on at the same moment and no adjacency
has formed yet.

options.text: R1
R2
R3
R4

items.explanation: DR election compares interface priority first and only falls back to the highest router ID on a tie. R3 carries priority 5, above every other router, so it becomes DR regardless of its router ID. Option B is the trap: R2 holds the highest router ID at 4.4.4.4 and would win only if all priorities were equal. Option A has neither the highest priority nor the highest ID. Option D is configured with priority 0, which bars it from becoming DR or BDR at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R5 joins a segment where the DR and BDR were elected hours earlier. What happens to the designated router role?

exhibit.content:
10.1.1.0/24  (broadcast segment)
      +---------+---------------+---------------+---------------+
                |               |               |               |
            +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+
            |  R1   |       |  R2   |       |  R3   |       |  R5   |
            +-------+       +-------+       +-------+       +-------+
        router-id 1.1.1.1   4.4.4.4         3.3.3.3         5.5.5.5
        priority 1          priority 1      priority 5      priority 10

R3 was elected DR and R2 BDR some hours ago. R5 has just now been
cabled to the segment and brought up.

options.text: R3 stays designated router, because OSPF elections are not preemptive.
R5 becomes designated router at once, since its priority is the highest present.
R5 becomes backup designated router and is promoted at the next hello interval.
The election is rerun, making R5 designated router and R3 backup designated router.

items.explanation: OSPF elections are non-preemptive: once a DR and BDR are established, a newly arrived router with a better priority does not displace them, and R5 becomes a DROTHER until the DR fails. Option B applies the priority comparison that governs only a fresh election. Option C invents a promotion path through the BDR role, but the sitting BDR keeps its place too. Option D assumes any topology change reruns the election, which would cause exactly the churn that non-preemption exists to prevent.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R7 must be prevented from ever becoming the designated router or backup designated router on GigabitEthernet0/0, while continuing to run OSPF there. Which command accomplishes that?

exhibit.content:
R7# show ip ospf interface brief
Interface    PID   Area            IP Address/Mask    Cost  State Nbrs F/C
Gi0/0        1     0               10.1.1.1/24        1     DR    3/3
Gi0/1        1     0               10.1.2.1/30        1     P2P   1/1

options.text: R7(config-router)# priority 0
R7(config-if)# ip ospf priority 0
R7(config-if)# ip ospf priority 255
R7(config-router)# passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: Priority is an interface setting, and the value 0 removes the router from the election while leaving OSPF running on the link. Option A has the right keyword and value but is entered in router configuration mode, where priority is not a valid command. Option C sets 255, the highest priority, which makes the router almost certain to become DR, the opposite of the requirement. Option D silences OSPF on the interface entirely, so no adjacency would form at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The neighbour reached over Serial0/0/0 shows FULL with no role after the slash. What does that indicate about the link?

exhibit.content:
R8# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   FULL/BDR        00:00:36    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0
3.3.3.3           1   FULL/DR         00:00:33    10.1.1.3        GigabitEthernet0/0
4.4.4.4           0   FULL/  -        00:00:38    10.2.2.2        Serial0/0/0

options.text: The neighbour has not finished exchanging its link-state database with R8.
The OSPF priority on that neighbour's interface has been set to zero.
The designated router for that segment has not been elected yet.
The link uses a point-to-point network type, which elects no DR or BDR.

items.explanation: OSPF elects a DR and BDR only on multi-access networks; on a point-to-point link there is no role to print, so the state shows FULL with a dash. Option A misreads FULL, which is the final state and confirms the databases are already synchronised. Option B is tempting because the Pri column reads 0, but that is what a point-to-point interface reports, not evidence of a configured priority. Option C would leave the neighbours in a transitional state rather than FULL.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which network statement enables OSPF on GigabitEthernet0/0 in area 0 without also enabling it on GigabitEthernet0/1?

exhibit.content:
! R9 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.1.1.65 255.255.255.192
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 9.9.9.9
!

OSPF must be enabled on GigabitEthernet0/0 in area 0, and on no other
interface.

options.text: network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 1

items.explanation: The network statement takes a wildcard mask, and a /30 corresponds to 0.0.0.3, which matches 10.1.1.0 through 10.1.1.3 and so covers GigabitEthernet0/0 alone. Option A supplies a subnet mask where the command expects a wildcard; IOS reads the value as a wildcard anyway, so the match bears no relation to the /30 link. Option B widens the match to 10.1.1.0 through 10.1.1.255, which also picks up 10.1.1.65 on GigabitEthernet0/1 and violates the requirement. Option D has the correct wildcard but places the interface in area 1, breaking the single-area design.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is the effect of R10's configuration on the 10.1.1.0/30 link?

exhibit.content:
! R10 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 10.10.10.10
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!

A neighbouring router is correctly configured for area 0 on the far end
of the 10.1.1.0/30 link.

options.text: R10 advertises the 10.1.1.0/30 prefix into OSPF but forms no adjacency on that link.
R10 stops advertising 10.1.1.0/30 and forms no adjacency on that link.
R10 forms the adjacency normally but withholds the 10.1.1.0/30 prefix.
R10 is unaffected, because passive-interface applies only to distance-vector protocols.

items.explanation: A passive interface stops OSPF from sending or accepting hellos on that link, so no adjacency can form, while the network statement still causes the prefix to be advertised into the area. Option B misses that half: suppressing hellos does not withdraw the prefix. Option C reverses the behaviour entirely. Option D confuses OSPF with RIP or EIGRP, where the command exists as well; it is equally effective under OSPF, which is exactly why misapplying it silently breaks adjacencies.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which neighbour is acting as the designated router on GigabitEthernet0/0?

exhibit.content:
R11# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
5.5.5.5           1   FULL/DROTHER    00:00:31    10.1.1.5        GigabitEthernet0/0
6.6.6.6           2   FULL/DR         00:00:34    10.1.1.6        GigabitEthernet0/0
7.7.7.7           1   FULL/BDR        00:00:39    10.1.1.7        GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: The State column carries the neighbour's role after the slash, and 6.6.6.6 is the row that reads FULL/DR. Option A is the DROTHER row, a neighbour that took no role in the election. Option C is the BDR, which stands by rather than serving as DR. Option D quotes an address from the Address column instead of the Neighbor ID column, which is a different field entirely and belongs to the 5.5.5.5 row.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R1 and R2 share an up/up link but never become neighbours. Which two configuration differences account for that? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf hello-interval 10
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!
----------------------------------------------------------
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf hello-interval 5
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 1
!

options.text: The two routers have been given identical router IDs.
The two interfaces have been addressed in different subnets.
The interfaces have been placed in different OSPF areas.
The configured hello intervals do not match.
One of the two interfaces has been configured as passive.

items.explanation: Two routers must agree on the area and on their hello and dead timers before an adjacency will form; R1 uses area 0 with hello 10 while R2 uses area 1 with hello 5, so both checks fail. Option A is wrong because the IDs 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2 are properly distinct. Option B is wrong because 10.1.1.1 and 10.1.1.2 both sit inside 10.1.1.0/30. Option E describes a command that appears in neither configuration.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The adjacency between R13 and its neighbour never advances beyond the state shown. Which cause does the remaining output point to?

exhibit.content:
R13# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   EXSTART/DR      00:00:35    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0

R13# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0 | include MTU
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,
R13#
----------------------------------------------------------
R14# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0 | include MTU
  MTU 9000 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,

options.text: The interface MTU values on the two routers do not match.
The dead interval expired before the databases could be exchanged.
Both routers claim the designated router role for the segment.
The neighbour's router ID duplicates one already known to R13.

items.explanation: An adjacency that halts at EXSTART or EXCHANGE points at the database exchange itself, and the two interfaces report 1500 and 9000 bytes, so the routers cannot agree on a payload size and the exchange never completes. Option B is wrong because an expired dead interval drops the neighbour out of the table rather than freezing it in EXSTART. Option C describes a condition that resolves through election rather than stalling the exchange. Option D would prevent the neighbour from being listed at all rather than holding it mid-exchange.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The OSPF process on R14 carries no network statements, and the design calls for enabling OSPF directly on the interface instead. Which command does that?

exhibit.content:
! R14 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 14.14.14.14
!

options.text: R14(config-router)# network GigabitEthernet0/0 area 0
R14(config-if)# ip ospf 1 area 0
R14(config-if)# ospf 1 area 0
R14(config-router)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0 area 0

items.explanation: The interface-level form is ip ospf followed by the process ID and the area, entered under the interface, and it enables OSPF on that interface without any network statement. Option A keeps the network keyword, which expects an address and wildcard rather than an interface name. Option C drops the leading ip, so IOS does not recognise the command. Option D tries to nest an interface command inside router configuration mode, mixing the two modes that the interface-level form exists to separate.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What OSPF cost does R15 assign to Serial0/0/0?

exhibit.content:
R15# show interfaces Serial0/0/0 | include BW
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1544 Kbit/sec, DLY 20000 usec,
R15#
R15# show ip ospf | include Reference bandwidth
 Reference bandwidth unit is 100 mbps

items.explanation: Cost is the reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth, so 100,000,000 divided by 1,544,000 gives 64.77, and OSPF discards the remainder to leave 64. Option C rounds the quotient up to 65 instead of truncating, which is the single commonest arithmetic slip on this calculation. Option A is the cost a link at or above the reference bandwidth receives, since the formula floors at 1. Option B quotes the reference bandwidth itself rather than the result of the division.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. From which neighbour has R16 most recently received OSPF routing information?

exhibit.content:
R16# show ip protocols
*** IP Routing is NSF aware ***

Routing Protocol is "ospf 1"
  Outgoing update filter list for all interfaces is not set
  Incoming update filter list for all interfaces is not set
  Router ID 16.16.16.16
  Number of areas in this router is 1. 1 normal 0 stub 0 nssa
  Maximum path: 4
  Routing for Networks:
    10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
    10.1.2.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
  Routing Information Sources:
    Gateway         Distance      Last Update
    2.2.2.2              110      00:00:19
    3.3.3.3              110      00:14:52
  Distance: (default is 110)

items.explanation: The Last Update column counts elapsed time since the update arrived, so the smaller figure is the more recent one, and 2.2.2.2 at nineteen seconds beats 3.3.3.3 at almost fifteen minutes. Option B reads the larger elapsed time as the more recent, inverting the column's meaning. Option C quotes R16's own router ID, which identifies the local router rather than a source. Option D takes a value from the Routing for Networks list, which records what R16 advertises, not who it hears from.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The neighbour has been sitting in the state shown for several minutes. What does that state indicate?

exhibit.content:
R17# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   INIT/DROTHER    00:00:31    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0

options.text: The neighbour finished exchanging databases but has not installed the routes.
R17 has seen the neighbour's hello, but the neighbour has not yet seen R17's.
The two routers disagree over which of them is the designated router.
The dead interval has expired and the neighbour is being removed from the table.

items.explanation: INIT means hellos are arriving in one direction only: R17 has heard the neighbour, but has not yet seen its own router ID listed in the neighbour's hello, so the relationship cannot advance to two-way. It usually points at something filtering traffic in one direction. Option A describes FULL, the state that follows a completed exchange. Option C describes an election dispute, which does not hold a neighbour at INIT. Option D is contradicted by the Dead Time of 31 seconds still counting down.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which OSPF cost does R18 apply to traffic leaving Serial0/0/0?

exhibit.content:
R18# show ip ospf interface brief
Interface    PID   Area            IP Address/Mask    Cost  State Nbrs F/C
Gi0/0        1     0               10.1.1.1/30        1     DR    1/1
Se0/0/0      1     0               10.1.2.1/30        64    P2P   1/1
Lo0          1     0               18.18.18.18/32     1     LOOP  0/0

items.explanation: The Cost column on the Serial0/0/0 row reads 64, which is the value OSPF adds when a path leaves by that interface. Option A takes the cost from the GigabitEthernet0/0 row, reading the right column on the wrong line. Option B quotes 110, which is OSPF's administrative distance and never appears in this output at all. Option D assumes an unlisted interface costs nothing, but every OSPF-enabled interface carries a cost of at least 1.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Both ends of this Ethernet link have been set to the point-to-point network type. What will show ip ospf neighbor report once the adjacency settles?

exhibit.content:
! R19 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf network point-to-point
!
----------------------------------------------------------
! R20 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf network point-to-point
!

Both routers place the interface in area 0 and use default timers.

options.text: A designated router and backup are still elected, but the hello timers halve.
No adjacency forms, because Ethernet interfaces cannot use that network type.
The adjacency reaches FULL, but no link-state advertisements cross the link.
No designated router is elected, and the state shows FULL with no role.

items.explanation: Changing the network type to point-to-point tells OSPF to treat the segment as having exactly two routers, so the election is skipped entirely and the neighbour prints as FULL with a dash where a role would otherwise appear. Option A keeps an election that the network type removes. Option B assumes the type is tied to the physical medium, but it is a software setting commonly applied to Ethernet links carrying only two routers. Option C would leave the routers with no shared topology, which FULL rules out.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R20's loopback carries a /24 mask, yet its neighbour installs the prefix as a /32. What accounts for the difference?

exhibit.content:
! R20 - relevant configuration
!
interface Loopback0
 ip address 10.9.9.9 255.255.255.0
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 20.20.20.20
 network 10.9.9.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
!
----------------------------------------------------------
R21# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       i - IS-IS, su - IS-IS summary, L1 - IS-IS level-1, L2 - IS-IS level-2
       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       a - application route
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 3 subnets, 2 masks
C        10.1.1.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
O        10.9.9.9/32 [110/2] via 10.1.1.1, 00:06:18, GigabitEthernet0/0

options.text: The wildcard mask in the network statement forced the advertised length to /32.
OSPF summarised the loopback prefix to its classful boundary before advertising.
OSPF advertises a loopback as a host route unless the network type is changed.
R21 applied its own mask, because the two routers sit in different areas.

items.explanation: OSPF treats a loopback as a stub host and advertises it as a /32 no matter what mask the interface carries, which is why R21 installs 10.9.9.9/32; setting the interface to the point-to-point network type is what restores the configured length. Option A confuses the wildcard, which selects which interfaces participate, with the length that gets advertised. Option B describes summarisation to a classful boundary, which would produce a shorter prefix rather than a longer one. Option D invokes an area difference that the single-area configuration rules out.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which address should hosts on the 10.1.1.0/24 segment carry as their default gateway?

exhibit.content:
R1# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/0       1    110 P Active  local           10.1.1.3        10.1.1.1

items.explanation: Hosts point at the virtual address the group presents, listed in the Virtual IP column as 10.1.1.1, which survives a failover because the standby router adopts it. Option A is R1's own interface address, and pointing hosts there would strand them the moment R1 failed, which is the entire problem an FHRP exists to solve. Option B is the standby router's real address and has the same weakness. Option D reads the Pri column value of 110 as though it were part of an address.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which virtual MAC address does R2 use for this HSRP group?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.0
 standby version 1
 standby 10 ip 10.1.1.1
 standby 10 priority 110
 standby 10 preempt
!

items.explanation: An HSRP version 1 virtual MAC is 0000.0C07.AC followed by the group number in hexadecimal, and group 10 in hex is 0a, giving 0000.0c07.ac0a. Option A writes the group as the literal digits 10, producing 0000.0c07.ac10, which is a genuine virtual MAC but belongs to group 16. Option C uses the 0000.5E00.01 range, which identifies VRRP rather than HSRP. Option D is the group 1 address, ignoring the configured group number entirely.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which role does each router hold once R1 has recovered?

exhibit.content:
10.1.1.0/24
        +-----------------+------------------+
                |                   |
            +---+---+           +---+---+
            |  R1   |           |  R2   |
            +-------+           +-------+
          10.1.1.2            10.1.1.3
          priority 110        priority 100
          no preempt          no preempt

Virtual IP 10.1.1.1, HSRP group 1 on both routers.

R1 was active. Its uplink failed, R2 took over, and R1 has now
recovered and re-formed its HSRP relationship with R2.

options.text: R2 stays active and R1 becomes standby, despite R1's higher priority.
R1 resumes the active role at once, because its priority is the higher of the two.
Both routers hold the active role until the next hello exchange separates them.
R1 stays out of the group until preemption is configured on R2.

items.explanation: Priority decides an election, but without the preempt keyword a returning router cannot displace a sitting active router, so R2 keeps the role and R1 settles for standby. Option B applies the priority comparison to a group that has already elected, which is what preemption exists to enable and neither router has it. Option C describes a split-active state that the hello exchange prevents. Option D inverts the requirement: preemption would be needed on R1, the router trying to take over, not on R2.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does PC1 experience after R1 loses power?

options.text: PC1 must be reconfigured with R2's interface address as its gateway.
PC1 has to renew its DHCP lease to be issued a new default gateway.
PC1 loses reachability until its ARP cache expires and it re-resolves.
PC1 keeps the same gateway, as R2 takes over the virtual IP and MAC.

items.explanation: The standby router assumes both the virtual IP address and the virtual MAC address, so the entry already cached by PC1 stays valid and forwarding resumes without any change on the host. That property is the whole purpose of a first hop redundancy protocol. Option A would require touching every host, which is precisely what the protocol avoids. Option B assumes a DHCP dependency PC1 does not have, since its gateway is static. Option C is the most tempting error: it would be true if only the IP moved, but the virtual MAC moves with it.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Once both routers have finished negotiating, which one forwards traffic sent to 10.1.1.1?

exhibit.content:
10.1.1.0/24
        +-----------------+------------------+
                |                   |
            +---+---+           +---+---+
            |  R1   |           |  R2   |
            +-------+           +-------+
          10.1.1.2            10.1.1.3
          standby 1 priority 90    standby 1 priority 120
          standby 1 preempt        standby 1 preempt

Both routers use virtual IP 10.1.1.1 in HSRP group 1 and are
brought up at the same time.

options.text: R1, because it holds the lower interface address on the segment.
Both routers share the load, since each is configured to preempt.
R2, because its configured priority is the higher of the two.
Whichever router completed boot first and claimed the virtual address.

items.explanation: HSRP elects the router with the numerically higher priority, so R2's 120 beats R1's 90 and R2 becomes active while R1 stands by. Option A applies a lowest-address tie-break, which HSRP consults only when priorities are equal, and even then it prefers the higher address. Option B assumes load sharing between the two, but a single HSRP group has exactly one forwarder. Option D describes what would happen without preemption, yet both routers carry the preempt keyword, so the higher priority asserts itself regardless of boot order.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Tracked object 1 transitions to Down. What follows?

exhibit.content:
R6# show standby GigabitEthernet0/0 1
GigabitEthernet0/0 - Group 1
  State is Active
    2 state changes, last state change 01:42:11
  Virtual IP address is 10.1.1.1
  Active virtual MAC address is 0000.0c07.ac01
    Local virtual MAC address is 0000.0c07.ac01 (v1 default)
  Hello time 3 sec, hold time 10 sec
  Preemption enabled
  Active router is local
  Standby router is 10.1.1.3, priority 100 (expires in 8.352 sec)
  Priority 110 (configured 110)
    Track object 1 state Up decrement 20

Both routers are configured with standby 1 preempt.

options.text: R6's priority falls to 90, and the router at 10.1.1.3 preempts to become active.
R6's priority falls to 90, but R6 stays active because it already owns the role.
R6 leaves the group entirely and stops responding to the virtual IP address.
R6's priority is unaffected, since tracking influences only the routing table.

items.explanation: The tracking statement decrements R6's priority by 20 when the object goes down, taking 110 to 90, which is below the standby router's 100; because both routers are configured to preempt, the router at 10.1.1.3 then takes the active role. Option B ignores preemption, which is exactly what makes the decrement useful. Option C overstates the effect, as a lowered priority demotes the router rather than removing it. Option D denies the decrement the exhibit prints on the Track object line.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. In group 5, which device currently holds the active role?

exhibit.content:
R7# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/0       5    100 P Standby 10.1.5.4        local           10.1.5.1
Gi0/1       6    120 P Active  local           10.1.6.4        10.1.6.1

options.text: R7 itself

items.explanation: On the group 5 row the Active column names 10.1.5.4 while the Standby column reads local, so the peer is forwarding and R7 is standing by. Option A reverses the two columns, a slip made easy by R7 being active in the other group listed. Option B quotes the Virtual IP for group 5, which identifies the group rather than the device holding the role. Option C takes the address from the group 6 row, reading the correct column from the wrong line.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. A host on the segment resolves its default gateway. Which MAC address does it cache?

exhibit.content:
R8# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/0       1    110 P Active  local           10.1.1.3        10.1.1.1

R8# show standby GigabitEthernet0/0 1 | include virtual MAC
  Active virtual MAC address is 0000.0c07.ac01

----------------------------------------------------------
R8 burned-in address on Gi0/0 is 00d0.5842.1c01
R9 burned-in address on Gi0/0 is 00d0.5842.7f22

options.text: ffff.ffff.ffff

items.explanation: An ARP request for the virtual IP is answered with the group's virtual MAC, 0000.0c07.ac01, which is why the cached entry stays correct after a failover moves the role to the other router. Option A is R8's burned-in address; a host that cached it would lose reachability the moment R8 failed, defeating the redundancy. Option C is R9's burned-in address and has the same flaw. Option D is the broadcast address, which never appears as the resolved result of an ARP request.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Both routers share the 10.1.1.0/24 segment and both are up. Which two outcomes result from the configurations shown? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.0
 standby 1 ip 10.1.1.1
 standby 1 priority 110
!
----------------------------------------------------------
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.3 255.255.255.0
 standby 2 ip 10.1.1.1
 standby 2 priority 100
!

options.text: The routers negotiate a single group and elect R1 as the active router.
Each router becomes the active router for its own group.
Both routers answer ARP for 10.1.1.1 with different virtual MACs.
Neither router responds to traffic addressed to 10.1.1.1.
R1 suppresses R2's group because it holds the higher configured priority.

items.explanation: HSRP routers only negotiate with peers in the same group number, so R1 in group 1 and R2 in group 2 never see each other; each declares itself active for its own group, and each answers for 10.1.1.1 with the virtual MAC derived from its own group number. Option A assumes the shared virtual IP is enough to pair them, when the group number is what binds peers. Option D contradicts both routers being active. Option E applies a priority comparison across groups that never communicate.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which public address has been given to the host at 10.1.1.77?
items.explanation: The Inside local column carries the private address and the Inside global column the public one it is presented as, so the row for 10.1.1.77 shows 203.0.113.9. Option A belongs to 10.1.1.50, the row above, which is the classic wrong-row read. Option C is an Outside global address, meaning the server being contacted rather than anything on the inside. Option D is an inside local address and never appears on the internet at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two commands are missing, leaving R2 translating nothing? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
ip nat inside source list 1 pool NAT-POOL overload
ip nat pool NAT-POOL 203.0.113.9 203.0.113.14 netmask 255.255.255.248
access-list 1 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description inside LAN
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 description toward the ISP
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
!

Hosts on 10.1.1.0/24 reach the ISP router but nothing beyond it. R2's
translation table is empty.

options.text: A wider pool, since six addresses cannot serve the whole inside subnet
An access list permitting the outside subnet rather than the inside one
ip nat inside under GigabitEthernet0/1
ip nat outside under GigabitEthernet0/0
ip nat outside under GigabitEthernet0/1

items.explanation: NAT acts only on traffic crossing from an interface declared inside to one declared outside, and neither declaration is present, so the pool and the access list are never consulted and the table stays empty. Option A misjudges the pool, since overload lets six addresses serve a whole subnet. Option B reverses which side the list describes. Option E puts the outside declaration on the LAN interface, which would leave the pair the wrong way round and translate nothing still.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What explains the pattern the users are reporting?

exhibit.content:
! R3 - relevant configuration
!
ip nat pool NAT-POOL 203.0.113.9 203.0.113.14 netmask 255.255.255.248
ip nat inside source list 1 pool NAT-POOL
access-list 1 permit 10.3.3.0 0.0.0.255
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.3.3.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
 ip nat outside
!

The subnet holds around forty active workstations. Each morning the
first few users reach the internet without trouble; the rest are
unable to, until someone else's session ends.

options.text: Without overload, the pool gives one address per host and holds only six.
The access list permits a /24, which is wider than the pool can support.
The pool's netmask is wrong, so only the first few addresses are usable.
The inside and outside interfaces have been declared the wrong way round.

items.explanation: A pool without the overload keyword hands each inside host its own public address for the life of its translation, and this pool holds six, so the seventh user onward is refused until an earlier translation expires. Adding overload lets all forty share the pool by port. Option B blames the access list, which correctly names the subnet to translate. Option C misreads the netmask, which describes the pool addresses rather than limiting how many are handed out. Option D is contradicted by the interface declarations, which are correct.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which command creates the mapping the requirement describes?

exhibit.content:
A web server sits on the inside network at 10.9.9.20 and must be
reachable from the internet at the fixed public address 203.0.113.20.

The mapping must hold whether or not the server has traffic in flight,
so that inbound connections can find it at any time.

options.text: ip nat inside source list 1 pool WEB overload
ip nat outside source static 203.0.113.20 10.9.9.20
ip nat inside source static 10.9.9.20 203.0.113.20

items.explanation: A static inside source entry ties one inside local address to one inside global address permanently, which is what lets an inbound connection find the server without the server having spoken first. Option A builds a dynamic mapping, so no entry exists until the server originates traffic. Option B translates in the outside source direction, which rewrites addresses on the far side rather than presenting an inside host publicly. Option D defines a pool without any command referring to it.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why do only the hosts on one of the two inside subnets reach the internet?

exhibit.content:
! R5 - relevant configuration
!
ip nat inside source list 7 pool NAT-POOL overload
ip nat pool NAT-POOL 203.0.113.9 203.0.113.14 netmask 255.255.255.248
access-list 7 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 ip address 10.1.2.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
 ip nat outside
!

Hosts on 10.1.1.0/24 reach the internet. Hosts on 10.1.2.0/24 do not,
though they route to R5 correctly and R5 has a default route.

options.text: GigabitEthernet0/2 is missing the ip nat inside declaration.
Access list 7 permits 10.1.1.0/24 only, so 10.1.2.0/24 is untranslated.
A router supports one inside interface per NAT configuration.
The pool has to be widened considerably before a second subnet can be translated.

items.explanation: The access list decides which traffic NAT acts on, and list 7 names 10.1.1.0/24 alone, so packets from 10.1.2.0/24 pass through untranslated and their private source address is dropped upstream. Adding a line for the second subnet resolves it. Option A is contradicted by Gi0/2 carrying the declaration already. Option C invents a one-interface limit. Option D points at the pool, which overload makes ample for both subnets.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What do the pool figures at the foot of this output indicate?

exhibit.content:
R6# show ip nat statistics
Total active translations: 4 (1 static, 3 dynamic; 3 extended)
Peak translations: 61, occurred 00:22:14 ago
Outside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0
Inside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/1
Hits: 91744  Misses: 0
Expired translations: 57
Dynamic mappings:
-- Inside Source
[Id: 1] access-list 7 pool NAT-POOL refcount 3

    start 203.0.113.9 end 203.0.113.14
    type generic, total addresses 6, allocated 6 (100%), misses 214

options.text: The pool is healthy, since the hit counter is high and misses read zero.
Six translations have expired, which is why the pool shows fully allocated.
The static entry has consumed the pool, leaving nothing for dynamic use.
The pool is fully allocated, and 214 attempts have found no address free.

items.explanation: The pool line reads allocated 6 of 6 at 100 per cent with 214 misses, meaning every address is in use and that many translation attempts have been turned away, so the pool needs widening or an overload keyword. Option A quotes the Hits and Misses counters higher up, which describe packets matching existing translations rather than the pool's capacity. Option B misreads the expired count, which is a lifetime total. Option C blames the static entry, which is counted separately from the dynamic pool.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How far is R1 from the authoritative source of this time?

exhibit.content:
R1# show ntp status
Clock is synchronized, stratum 3, reference is 10.1.1.1
nominal freq is 250.0000 Hz, actual freq is 249.9990 Hz, precision is 2**18
reference time is EB1A2C44.6C2A1E30 (09:14:12.422 UTC Sun Aug 23 2026)
clock offset is 0.4120 msec, root delay is 1.82 msec
root dispersion is 12.11 msec, peer dispersion is 0.92 msec

options.text: It is the authoritative source, which is what stratum 3 records.
One step, since it takes its time directly from 10.1.1.1.
Three steps, which is what a stratum of 3 counts.
Sixteen steps, the value NTP uses when counting from a reference clock.

items.explanation: Stratum counts distance from the reference clock, so a device reporting stratum 3 sits three steps away, taking its time from a stratum 2 peer which took it from a stratum 1 source attached to the reference itself. Option A describes stratum 1. Option B counts only the hop to its own peer and ignores what lies beyond it, which is what the number exists to record. Option D quotes 16, the value that means unsynchronised rather than a distance.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which command configures R2 as the requirement describes?

exhibit.content:
R2 is to take its time from the public source at 203.0.113.30 and
must not offer itself as a time source to anything else.

options.text: ntp server 203.0.113.30
ntp master 3
ntp source 203.0.113.30

items.explanation: ntp server names an upstream source to synchronise from and leaves the device a client, which is precisely the requirement. Option B makes the router an authoritative source of its own, which the requirement forbids. Option C establishes a symmetric relationship in which either device may synchronise the other. Option D sets which address the router uses when sending NTP packets and selects no source at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does this state cost the team, given that traffic and logging both continue?

exhibit.content:
R3# show ntp status
Clock is unsynchronized, stratum 16, no reference clock
nominal freq is 250.0000 Hz, actual freq is 250.0000 Hz, precision is 2**18
reference time is 00000000.00000000 (00:00:00.000 UTC Mon Jan 1 1900)
clock offset is 0.0000 msec, root delay is 0.00 msec

R3 is forwarding traffic normally and its syslog server is receiving
messages from it without interruption.

options.text: Routing decisions become unreliable, since protocols timestamp their updates.
The syslog timestamps R3 sends cannot be trusted or correlated.
Nothing measurable, because stratum 16 still keeps time to within a second.
SSH sessions will be refused, as key exchange depends on an accurate clock.

items.explanation: Stratum 16 with no reference means the clock is running free, so every timestamp R3 stamps on a log message is its own guess; the messages arrive but cannot be lined up against events on any other device, which is exactly when an incident timeline is needed. Option A ties routing to timestamps, which the protocols in scope here do not depend on. Option C treats stratum 16 as a working state rather than the marker for unsynchronised. Option D invents a dependency SSH does not have.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which command makes that router the reference for the site?

exhibit.content:
A site has no reachable external time source. One router with an
accurate hardware clock is to become the reference for the other
devices at that site, which will then take their time from it.

options.text: ntp server 127.127.1.1 on each of the other devices
ntp peer, entered on every device including the reference
ntp update-calendar on the router with the accurate clock
ntp master, entered on the router with the accurate clock

items.explanation: ntp master tells a router to declare itself an authoritative time source using its own clock, which is what an isolated site needs when no external source is reachable; the other devices then point at it with ntp server. Option A has each device treat its own internal clock as the source, so nothing is shared. Option B builds symmetric relationships with no agreed reference. Option C copies NTP time into the hardware calendar, which assumes synchronisation rather than establishing it.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which service is at fault here?

exhibit.content:
C:\> ping 10.9.9.20

Pinging 10.9.9.20 with 32 bytes of data:
Reply from 10.9.9.20: bytes=32 time=2ms TTL=126
Reply from 10.9.9.20: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=126

C:\> ping files.example.internal
Ping request could not find host files.example.internal. Please check
the name and try again.

The workstation holds a valid address, mask and default gateway, and
10.9.9.20 is the host registered as files.example.internal.

options.text: DHCP, since the workstation must have been issued incorrect parameters.
Routing, because the reply to the name-based attempt never came back.
DNS, as the address is reachable but the name cannot be resolved to it.
Neither; the server is refusing requests that arrive by name only.

items.explanation: The numeric ping succeeds, which proves addressing, routing and the server itself are all working, and the failure message says the name could not be found rather than that the host did not answer, so resolution is the only step that broke. Option A is contradicted by the working ping, which needs a correct address, mask and gateway. Option B is ruled out by the same reply. Option D invents a server behaviour, and the request never reached the server at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which service delivers all four of those items to a workstation?

exhibit.content:
A new subnet is being brought into service. The team wants every
workstation on it to receive, without anyone visiting a desk:

    an address from the correct range
    the subnet mask for that range
    the address of the gateway to leave the subnet
    the addresses of the two name servers

options.text: DNS, which returns the addressing a client needs along with names.
DHCP, which supplies the address together with the other parameters.
ARP, which discovers each of these values from the local segment.
DHCP for the address, with the remaining three set by hand on each host.

items.explanation: A DHCP offer carries the address and the options alongside it, so mask, gateway and name servers arrive in the same exchange, which is what makes bringing a subnet into service a matter of configuring one scope. Option A gives DNS a role it does not have, since it maps names to addresses. Option C describes ARP, which resolves an address to a MAC within one segment. Option D splits the work unnecessarily and would need the desk visits the requirement rules out.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which address would this host contact to turn a hostname into an address?

exhibit.content:
C:\> ipconfig /all

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:

   DHCP Enabled. . . . . . . . . . . : Yes
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 10.20.30.44(Preferred)
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Lease Obtained. . . . . . . . . . : Sunday, 23 August 2026 08:14:02
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 10.20.30.1
   DHCP Server . . . . . . . . . . . : 10.20.30.10
   DNS Servers . . . . . . . . . . . : 10.20.30.10
                                       10.20.30.11

items.explanation: The DNS Servers line names 10.20.30.10 first, and that is where a name lookup goes; the same host also happens to run DHCP, which is common but incidental. Option B is the default gateway, used to leave the subnet rather than to resolve names. Option C is the workstation's own address. Option D is the subnet mask, which is not an address the host contacts at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which description correctly names the two methods?

exhibit.content:
Two ways of learning that an interface has failed

    Method A   The management station asks each device every five
               minutes whether its interfaces are up, and compares
               the answer with the previous one

    Method B   The device sends a message to the management station
               the moment the interface changes state, without being
               asked

options.text: A is a trap and B is polling, since the device answers each request.
Both are polling, differing only in how often the station asks.
Both are traps, because each ends with the station learning of the fault.
A is polling and B is a trap, sent by the device on its own initiative.

items.explanation: Polling has the manager ask on a schedule and wait for an answer, which is method A, while a trap is sent by the agent the moment something happens, which is method B; the practical difference is that a trap arrives at once whereas polling can leave a fault unnoticed for most of an interval. Option A reverses the two. Option B ignores that method B involves no request. Option C calls both traps by looking at the outcome rather than what initiates the message.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is the audit most likely to have objected to?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
snmp-server community publicRO RO
snmp-server community privateRW RW
snmp-server host 10.9.9.50 version 2c publicRO
!

An audit has flagged this configuration. The management traffic crosses
a shared campus network on its way to 10.9.9.50.

options.text: Version 2c sends its community strings in clear, including the writable one.
Two communities are configured where SNMP permits only one per device.
The host statement names a single station, so no redundancy exists.
Read-only access is inadequate for monitoring and should be writable.

items.explanation: Under version 2c the community string is the whole of the authentication and travels unencrypted, so anyone capturing the traffic reads it, and a read-write string in that position lets them change the device rather than merely observe it. Version 3 with authentication and privacy is the answer. Option B invents a limit on communities. Option C raises availability rather than the security concern an audit would flag. Option D argues for wider access, which is the opposite of hardening.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which SNMP version satisfies all three requirements?

exhibit.content:
Monitoring requirements for a new deployment

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Management traffic must be unreadable to anyone capturing it
    The identity of the management station must be verifiable
    Individual accounts, not one shared string for the whole estate

options.text: Version 1
Version 3
Version 2c
No version offers all three

items.explanation: Version 3 adds authentication and privacy on a per-user basis, so the traffic is encrypted, the sender can be verified, and each operator holds their own credential rather than sharing a string. Options A and C both authenticate with a community string sent in clear, which fails the first two requirements and offers no notion of an individual account. Option D is contradicted by version 3 being designed for exactly this set of concerns.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which part of this message names the facility that raised it?

exhibit.content:
A message arrives at the syslog server from a switch.

    %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/7,
    changed state to down

    Level  Keyword          Meaning
    -----  --------------   ------------------------------
      0    emergencies      system unusable
      1    alerts           immediate action needed
      2    critical         critical condition
      3    errors           error condition
      4    warnings         warning condition
      5    notifications    normal but significant
      6    informational    informational message
      7    debugging        debugging output

options.text: UPDOWN
LINEPROTO
GigabitEthernet0/7

items.explanation: A syslog message is built as facility, then severity, then mnemonic, so LINEPROTO is the facility, 5 is the severity and UPDOWN is the mnemonic naming the specific event. Option A is that mnemonic. Option B is the severity, which places the message at notifications. Option D is a value from the message text, describing what the event concerns rather than which subsystem reported it.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two of the four messages reach the syslog server? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
logging host 10.9.9.40
logging trap 4
!

Four messages are generated on R2 in the next minute:

    %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down
    %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by netadmin on vty0
    %OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Process 1, Nbr 2.2.2.2 on Gi0/1 from FULL to DOWN
    %SYS-2-MALLOCFAIL: Memory allocation of 4096 bytes failed

    Level  Keyword          Meaning
    -----  --------------   ------------------------------
      0    emergencies      system unusable
      1    alerts           immediate action needed
      2    critical         critical condition
      3    errors           error condition
      4    warnings         warning condition
      5    notifications    normal but significant
      6    informational    informational message
      7    debugging        debugging output

options.text: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down
%SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by netadmin on vty0
%OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Process 1, Nbr 2.2.2.2 on Gi0/1 from FULL to DOWN
%SYS-2-MALLOCFAIL: Memory allocation of 4096 bytes failed
None of them, since logging trap 4 excludes every level shown

items.explanation: logging trap 4 forwards everything at level 4 or more severe, and severity counts downward, so levels 0 through 4 are sent while 5 through 7 are discarded; that captures the level 3 link message and the level 2 memory failure. Options B and C both sit at level 5, notifications, and are dropped, which is how a trap level set too low silently loses configuration and adjacency changes. Option E inverts the scale, treating a higher number as more severe.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which message should be dealt with first, and why?

exhibit.content:
Two messages arrive within the same second from the same router.

    %SYS-2-MALLOCFAIL: Memory allocation of 4096 bytes failed
    %SYS-6-LOGGINGHOST_STARTSTOP: Logging to host 10.9.9.40 started

    Level  Keyword          Meaning
    -----  --------------   ------------------------------
      0    emergencies      system unusable
      1    alerts           immediate action needed
      2    critical         critical condition
      3    errors           error condition
      4    warnings         warning condition
      5    notifications    normal but significant
      6    informational    informational message
      7    debugging        debugging output

options.text: The LOGGINGHOST message, since level 6 outranks level 2 on this scale.
Neither is urgent; both sit in the routine half of the severity range.
Both equally, as messages from one facility carry the same weight.
The MALLOCFAIL message, because level 2 is nearer the severe end.

items.explanation: Severity runs from 0 as the most serious to 7 as the least, so the level 2 memory allocation failure is a critical condition while the level 6 logging notice is informational housekeeping. Option A reads the scale backwards, which is the mistake this item exists to catch. Option B places level 2 in the routine half, when the table marks it critical. Option C treats the shared SYS facility as making them equivalent, but the facility says which subsystem spoke rather than how much it matters.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. At which severity level was this message recorded?

exhibit.content:
A message recorded on the syslog server

    %SEC-6-IPACCESSLOGP: list 110 denied tcp 10.20.4.55(51204) ->
    10.90.1.10(22), 1 packet

    Level  Keyword          Meaning
    -----  --------------   ------------------------------
      0    emergencies      system unusable
      1    alerts           immediate action needed
      2    critical         critical condition
      3    errors           error condition
      4    warnings         warning condition
      5    notifications    normal but significant
      6    informational    informational message
      7    debugging        debugging output

items.explanation: The severity is the number between the facility and the mnemonic, so SEC-6-IPACCESSLOGP is level 6, informational, which is the usual level for an access list logging a match. Option A is the access list number taken from the message text. Option B and option D are severities that appear nowhere in this message; the value 1 is the packet count at the end of the line, which is a different number entirely.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does the same server answer one VLAN and not the other?

exhibit.content:
VLAN 30                      VLAN 99
    clients ---[ SW-L3 ]------------------------[ DHCP-SRV ]
              10.30.0.1                          10.99.0.10

The DHCP server holds a scope for 10.30.0.0/24. Clients on VLAN 30 send
their requests and receive nothing. A workstation moved onto VLAN 99
obtains an address from the same server immediately.

options.text: A DHCP request is a broadcast and does not leave VLAN 30.
The scope for 10.30.0.0/24 must be defined on the VLAN 30 interface itself.
DHCP works only where the server and the client share an IP subnet by design.
The clients need a static address before they can request a dynamic one.

items.explanation: A client with no address starts by broadcasting, and a broadcast stops at the boundary of its own VLAN, so a server one subnet away never hears it; the workstation moved onto VLAN 99 succeeds because it is then in the same broadcast domain. A relay configured with ip helper-address forwards the request as a unicast. Option B misplaces the scope, which lives on the server. Option C states a limitation that relays exist to remove. Option D reverses the process entirely.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two facts describe the helper address this design needs? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! SW-L3 - relevant configuration
!
interface Vlan30
 description client VLAN
 ip address 10.30.0.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface Vlan99
 description server VLAN
 ip address 10.99.0.1 255.255.255.0
!

The DHCP server at 10.99.0.10 must serve clients in VLAN 30.

options.text: It belongs on interface Vlan99, where the server sits.
It belongs on interface Vlan30, where the clients broadcast.
Its value is 10.30.0.1, the gateway the clients already use.
Its value is 10.99.0.10, the address of the DHCP server.
It must be applied on both interfaces so each direction works.

items.explanation: The helper address goes on the interface that receives the clients' broadcasts, which is Vlan30, and names where those requests should be forwarded, which is the server at 10.99.0.10. Option A places it on the server side, where no client broadcast ever arrives. Option C points the relay back at the router's own address. Option E adds a statement on an interface with nothing to relay, which would forward the server's own broadcasts toward the clients.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which command lets R3 accept whatever address the provider offers?

exhibit.content:
! R3 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 description circuit to the service provider
 no shutdown
!

The provider issues this circuit's address by DHCP and will not supply a
static allocation. R3 must take whatever address the provider offers,
including the default route that comes with it.

options.text: ip helper-address from the provider's first-hop router
ip address dhcp
ip address negotiated 198.51.100.0 255.255.255.0
ip dhcp pool WAN followed by a network statement

items.explanation: ip address dhcp puts the interface into client mode, so it requests an address from the provider and installs the default route that accompanies the lease, which is exactly what the circuit requires. Option A configures a relay, which forwards other devices' requests rather than making a request of its own. Option C invents a command; negotiation of this kind is not how IOS expresses it. Option D turns the router into a DHCP server handing out addresses, which is the opposite role.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which interface obtained its address from a DHCP server?

exhibit.content:
R4# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     198.51.100.37   YES DHCP   up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     10.4.4.1        YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down

options.text: GigabitEthernet0/1
GigabitEthernet0/2
Neither of the two up interfaces
GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: The Method column records how each address arrived, and Gi0/0 reads DHCP while carrying a live address. Option A reads manual, meaning an operator typed the address into the configuration. Option B is unassigned and administratively down, so it has requested nothing. Option C is contradicted by the DHCP entry on Gi0/0, and the Method column exists precisely so this distinction is visible without reading the configuration.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which QoS mechanism should be applied to the backup stream?

exhibit.content:
A branch uploads nightly backups across a circuit it shares with
interactive traffic.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    The backup stream must be held to 4 Mbps on average
    Bursts above that must be smoothed out rather than discarded
    Retransmitting lost backup data wastes the circuit twice over
    A little extra delay on the backup traffic is acceptable

options.text: Shaping, which buffers the excess and releases it at the agreed rate.
Policing, which enforces the rate by discarding whatever exceeds it.
Classification, which identifies the backup stream so it can be counted.
Congestion avoidance, which drops early to keep queues from filling.

items.explanation: Shaping holds traffic above the rate in a queue and releases it later, so a burst is delayed rather than lost, which suits a backup that tolerates delay but wastes the circuit if it has to retransmit. Option B meets the rate requirement but does so by discarding, which is what the third and fourth lines rule out. Option C identifies traffic without limiting it, so nothing enforces the rate. Option D deliberately drops to signal senders to slow down, again losing data.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Where should classification and marking take place?

exhibit.content:
+--------+          +--------+          +--------+
   IP phone ------| SW-ACC |----------| SW-DIST|----------| R-EDGE |
                  +--------+          +--------+          +--------+

The phone marks its own voice traffic. Voice must receive priority at
every hop across the campus and out to the WAN, and no hop should have
to inspect the traffic deeply to work out what it is carrying.

options.text: At R-EDGE, so one device decides the policy for the whole campus.
At every hop, each re-examining the traffic and marking it again.
Nowhere; priority should be applied by queueing without any marking.
As close to the source as possible, with later hops trusting the mark.

items.explanation: Marking once at the edge, at the trust boundary where the phone attaches, lets every subsequent hop read a field in the header and queue accordingly rather than inspecting payload, which is the whole point of a per-hop behaviour. Option A leaves the campus hops with nothing to act on until the traffic reaches the WAN. Option B repeats expensive work at each device and risks the hops disagreeing. Option C removes the signal that queueing depends on.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which command must be entered before the key can be generated?

exhibit.content:
SW1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
% Please define a domain-name first.

SW1(config)#

The switch has been given the hostname SW1 and a username with a secret.
The vty lines are already set to transport input ssh.

options.text: ip ssh version 2, which selects the key format to generate
ip domain-name followed by the organisation's domain
crypto key zeroize rsa, to clear any partially built key
service password-encryption, so the key is stored protected

items.explanation: An RSA key pair is labelled with the device's fully qualified name, so IOS needs both a hostname and a domain name before it can build one, and the error names the missing half directly. Option A selects the protocol version, which is set after a key exists rather than before. Option C erases keys, and there is none to erase. Option D encrypts passwords in the configuration and has no bearing on key generation.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What should the version setting be changed to, and why?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
hostname R2
ip domain-name example.internal
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ip ssh version 1
!
username netadmin privilege 15 secret Wr3nch-Harbour-42
!
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
!

A security review has asked for the version setting to be revisited.

options.text: Change it to 2, which closes known weaknesses in the older protocol.
Leave it at 1, since version 2 requires a key of at least 4096 bits.
Remove the line, so the device negotiates whichever version the client offers.
Change it to 2, which is required before login local will be accepted.

items.explanation: Version 1 has structural weaknesses that version 2 was written to address, and a device with a 2048-bit key can run version 2 without any other change, so pinning to 2 is the correct outcome of the review. Option B invents a key length requirement. Option C leaves the device willing to fall back to version 1 whenever a client asks, which is the situation being closed. Option D ties the version to local authentication, which works under either.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which transfer method meets these requirements?

exhibit.content:
An IOS image is to be copied onto twelve routers across a WAN.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Only named accounts may retrieve the image from the server
    A partial transfer over a lossy circuit must be detectable
    The server already refuses anonymous connections

options.text: TFTP, which is lighter and therefore better suited to a WAN circuit.
Either, because both prompt for credentials before transferring.
TFTP, provided the server is configured to demand a username.
FTP, since it authenticates the user and runs over a connection.

items.explanation: FTP asks for a username and password before the transfer and runs over TCP, so the session is acknowledged and an incomplete transfer is apparent, which covers all three requirements.
