Option A picks the lighter protocol but TFTP has no concept of an account, so a server refusing anonymous access will refuse it. Option B credits TFTP with credentials it does not support. Option C expects a TFTP server to demand a username, which the protocol gives it no way to do.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does the absence of any credential prompt tell you?

exhibit.content:
R2# copy tftp: flash:
Address or name of remote host []? 10.9.9.60
Source filename []? c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.157-3.M4b.bin
Destination filename [c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.157-3.M4b.bin]?
Accessing tftp://10.9.9.60/c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.157-3.M4b.bin...

At no point was a username or password requested.

options.text: The router cached credentials from an earlier transfer to the same server.
The server has been left misconfigured and should have demanded a login.
TFTP carries no authentication, so anyone reaching the server may fetch the file.
The prompt appears only once the transfer has finished and is verified.

items.explanation: TFTP has no mechanism for a username or password at all, so the transfer begins as soon as the filename is supplied and any device that can reach the server may retrieve or replace files there. Option A invents credential caching for a protocol with no credentials. Option B blames the server, when the omission is inherent to the protocol rather than a configuration choice. Option D postpones a prompt that never comes.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which part of this account describes the vulnerability?

exhibit.content:
Incident summary - finance office workstation

    The machine was running a document reader two versions behind, with
    a published flaw in the way it parses embedded fonts.

    A crafted document arrived by email. When the user opened it, code
    inside the file used that font-parsing flaw to run commands.

    The group behind the campaign has targeted finance departments
    across the sector for the past two years.

options.text: The group that has been targeting finance departments for two years.
The unpatched font-parsing flaw in the document reader.
The crafted document that carried the code to the user.
The commands that ran on the workstation once the file was opened.

items.explanation: A vulnerability is the weakness itself, and here that is the flaw in how the outdated reader parses fonts; it existed before anyone tried to use it and would still exist if nobody had. Option A is the threat, meaning the actor with the intent and capability to act. Option C is the exploit, the crafted artefact that leverages the weakness. Option D is the impact, which is what resulted rather than what allowed it.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which response removes the vulnerability rather than reducing its exposure?

exhibit.content:
A public-facing server runs a version of its application with a
published remote code execution flaw. The vendor released a fixed
version three weeks ago.

Four responses have been proposed while the incident is open.

options.text: Rate-limit inbound connections to the server at the perimeter firewall.
Move the server to a different public address and update the records.
Increase how often the server's logs are reviewed by the operations team.
Apply the vendor's fixed version to the application.

items.explanation: Patching eliminates the flaw, so there is nothing left to exploit however the traffic arrives; every other option leaves the weakness in place and only makes reaching it harder or noticing it faster. Option A slows an attack without preventing it. Option B relies on the address not being rediscovered, which scanning defeats within hours. Option C improves detection after the fact rather than removing the cause.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is the limitation of the protection the team has put in place?

exhibit.content:
After the third compromise of the same application server, the team
added a signature to the intrusion prevention system that matches the
exact request pattern used in the attacks. Blocking took effect
immediately and no further compromises have occurred this week.

The application itself has not been updated. The vendor's patch is
still waiting for a change window.

options.text: The flaw remains, so a variant the signature does not match still works.
An intrusion prevention system cannot inspect traffic bound for a server.
Signatures stop matching after thirty days and have to be rewritten.
The block also turns away the legitimate users of the application.

items.explanation: A signature matches one observed pattern, so it buys time but leaves the underlying weakness intact; anyone who alters the request enough to miss the signature reaches the same flaw. It is a compensating control, useful until the patch lands rather than instead of it. Option B is wrong because an inline sensor inspects exactly this traffic. Option C invents an expiry that signatures do not have. Option D describes a false positive, which the exhibit gives no sign of.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which row of this record describes the exploit?

exhibit.content:
Incident record

    Element                Detail
    -------------------    --------------------------------------------
    Actor                  A group known to target logistics firms
    Weakness               Default administrative credentials left in
                           place on an internet-facing appliance
    Method used            An automated script that tried the vendor's
                           documented default credentials
    Outcome                Administrative access to the appliance
    Response taken         Credentials changed, management moved to an
                           internal-only address

options.text: Actor
Weakness
Method used
Response taken

items.explanation: An exploit is the means by which a weakness is turned into access, which the record files under Method used: the script that submitted the documented default credentials. Option A is the threat, the group with intent. Option B is the vulnerability, namely the credentials left unchanged. Option D is the mitigation applied afterwards, which closed the weakness rather than using it.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two settings on the Layer 2 security tab meet the requirement? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
A new WLAN called BRANCH-STAFF is being created on the controller.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Clients join with a passphrase, not an individual account
    Data must be protected with AES rather than TKIP
    No RADIUS server is available at this site
    The WLAN maps to the existing vlan30-staff interface

options.text: Authentication Key Mgmt set to 802.1X
WPA2 Encryption set to AES
Layer 2 Security set to None
Authentication Key Mgmt set to PSK
WPA2 Encryption set to TKIP

items.explanation: A passphrase rather than individual accounts means the key management is PSK, and protecting data with AES means the WPA2 encryption is AES, so those two together satisfy the requirement without any RADIUS server. Option A selects 802.1X, which needs the RADIUS server the site does not have. Option C removes security altogether. Option E selects TKIP, the older cipher the requirement rules out by name.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does every association attempt fail?

exhibit.content:
WLC GUI  -  WLANs > Edit > BRANCH-STAFF

Tab: General
    Profile Name                  BRANCH-STAFF
    SSID                          BRANCH-STAFF
    Status                        Enabled
    Interface/Interface Group     vlan30-staff

Tab: Security > Layer 2
    Layer 2 Security              WPA+WPA2
    WPA2 Policy                   Enabled
    WPA2 Encryption               AES
    Authentication Key Mgmt       802.1X
    PSK Format                    not configured

No RADIUS server is configured on this controller. Clients see the SSID
and attempt to join, but every association fails.

options.text: The WLAN Status is Enabled before the security settings were completed.
AES cannot be selected while the WLAN maps to a tagged VLAN interface.
Key management is 802.1X, which needs a RADIUS server that is absent.
The interface vlan30-staff has to be created after the WLAN, not before.

items.explanation: 802.1X hands authentication to a RADIUS server, and none is configured, so the exchange never completes and every client is refused even though the SSID is advertised correctly; switching key management to PSK and setting a passphrase resolves it. Option A treats enabling the WLAN as premature, but a WLAN must be enabled to be advertised at all. Option B invents a conflict between AES and a mapped interface. Option D invents an ordering requirement for the interface.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What do these settings confirm about how clients join this WLAN?

exhibit.content:
WLC GUI  -  WLANs > Edit > BRANCH-STAFF

Tab: Security > Layer 2
    Layer 2 Security              WPA+WPA2
    WPA Policy                    Disabled
    WPA2 Policy                   Enabled
    WPA2 Encryption               AES
    Authentication Key Mgmt       PSK
    PSK Format                    ASCII

options.text: They authenticate individually against a RADIUS server using AES.
They supply a shared passphrase, and their data is protected with AES.
They join without any credential, since only the format has been set.
They supply a passphrase, but the older WPA cipher protects their data.

items.explanation: Authentication Key Mgmt reads PSK, so every client presents the same passphrase, and WPA2 Encryption reads AES with the WPA policy disabled, so the newer cipher protects the traffic. Option A describes 802.1X, which these settings do not select. Option C ignores the PSK setting, and the ASCII format line describes how the passphrase is entered rather than replacing it. Option D is contradicted by WPA Policy reading Disabled, which leaves only WPA2 with AES in use.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which security programme element most directly addresses what happened here?

exhibit.content:
Incident summary

    Fourteen staff across five departments received a message that
    appeared to come from the payroll system, warning that their bank
    details needed reconfirming before the month end.

    Nine followed the link and entered their network credentials into a
    page that closely resembled the real portal.

    The page was hosted outside the organisation. No software flaw was
    involved at any point.

options.text: A user awareness programme on recognising messages of this kind.
Role-specific technical training for the network and server engineers.
Tighter physical access control at the entrances to the building.
A policy raising the minimum length of every user's password.

items.explanation: Nothing technical failed: the staff were persuaded, so the gap is whether people across the organisation can recognise a convincing imitation, which is what an awareness programme addresses. Option B trains a small technical group on tasks, which would not have reached the nine people who entered credentials. Option C guards the premises, and the page was hosted elsewhere entirely. Option D lengthens passwords that were handed over willingly, so their strength never mattered.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which element of the security programme failed in this incident?

exhibit.content:
Incident summary

    A visitor waited by the rear entrance and followed an employee
    through the door as it closed behind them. They then walked to the
    second-floor communications room, whose door was propped open with a
    fire extinguisher, and connected a small device to a spare switch
    port before leaving.

    Every switch in the room has a strong enable secret and permits SSH
    management only.

options.text: Password management, since the enable secret should be rotated more often.
Awareness training, because staff should lock their screens when away.
Physical access control, at both the rear door and the communications room.
Device hardening, as management access should have been restricted further.

items.explanation: The intruder never needed a credential: they were let through one door by following someone and found another propped open, so the failure is physical and occurs twice over. Option A hardens a secret that was never tested. Option B names a real habit, but no unattended workstation features in the account. Option D is contradicted by the switches already being restricted to SSH with a strong secret, which did nothing to stop a cable being plugged in.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which gap is the one that role-specific training addresses?

exhibit.content:
Three gaps identified in an internal review

    Gap
    -------------------------------------------------------------
    A  Staff cannot reliably tell a genuine internal message from a
       convincing imitation
    B  The two engineers who will run the new firewall have never
       configured that product and are unsure of its rule syntax
    C  Server room doors are left on the latch during deliveries

options.text: Gap A
Gap B
Gap C
None of the three

items.explanation: Training equips a particular role to perform a task correctly, and gap B is exactly that: two named engineers who need working knowledge of a product they will operate. Option A is a matter of general recognition across all staff, which awareness covers. Option C is a physical control at a door rather than anything taught. Option D is contradicted by gap B being a textbook training need.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which value does R1 accept at the privileged EXEC prompt?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
enable password Harbour42
enable secret Wr3nch-Harbour-42
!
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
!

options.text: Wr3nch-Harbour-42, because enable secret takes precedence.
Harbour42, because enable password is the older command and is read first.
Either value, since both commands populate the same credential store.
Neither, because configuring both together disables privileged access.

items.explanation: When both are present the secret always wins, and the older enable password is ignored entirely; the secret is also stored as a hash rather than recoverable text, which is why it replaced the earlier command. Option B assumes configuration order decides, when precedence is fixed regardless of where each line sits. Option C treats them as one store, but they are separate and only one is consulted. Option D invents a lockout that would make the pair impossible to configure safely.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two conclusions should the reviewer draw now that the configuration has left the building? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
service password-encryption
!
username backup password 7 08701E1D5D4C53
username netadmin secret 9 $9$Xk2mQvR8LpT4c0$hV1nZ7yW3sK
!

The configuration was reviewed after a contractor was given a copy of it
for a documentation exercise.

options.text: The backup account's password can be recovered from the file as it stands.
service password-encryption has made both credentials safe to share.
The netadmin credential is stored as a hash and is not recoverable that way.
Both credentials are held as plain text and both must be changed.
The netadmin credential is the one at immediate risk of exposure.

items.explanation: Type 7 is an obfuscation rather than a hash and is reversed in seconds with freely available tools, so the backup password is effectively public, while the netadmin secret is stored as type 9, a genuine hash that does not give its input back. Option B treats service password-encryption as real protection, which is the misconception this item targets. Option D ignores the difference the two type numbers record. Option E reverses which of the two is exposed.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why are the credentials rejected on every attempt?

exhibit.content:
! R3 - relevant configuration
!
hostname R3
ip domain-name example.internal
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
!
enable secret Wr3nch-Harbour-42
!
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
!

No engineer can log in over SSH. The connection is accepted and then the
credentials are rejected, whatever is typed.

options.text: The RSA key must be regenerated after the domain name is set.
login local checks a local user database, and no username is configured.
transport input ssh has to be paired with transport output ssh to work.
The enable secret has to be removed before local logins will be accepted.

items.explanation: login local tells the line to authenticate against locally configured usernames, and this configuration defines none, so every attempt fails no matter what is typed; adding a username with a secret resolves it. Option A reverses the ordering, since the domain name must exist before the key is generated and this configuration does that correctly. Option C invents a pairing requirement, as transport output governs outbound sessions from the device. Option D confuses the enable secret, which guards privileged mode after login rather than login itself.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does this message indicate about the vty configuration?

exhibit.content:
R4(config)# line vty 0 4
R4(config-line)# login
R4(config-line)# transport input telnet
R4(config-line)# end
R4#

An engineer then tries to connect from a workstation:

    % Password required, but none set

    [Connection to 10.4.4.1 closed by foreign host]

options.text: The device is refusing Telnet because only SSH is permitted on those lines.
The vty lines have run out of free sessions and are turning connections away.
login was configured without a line password, so the device refuses access.
The connection was closed because no enable secret has been configured yet.

items.explanation: The plain login command tells the line to check a password configured on that line, and when none exists IOS refuses the session outright rather than letting anyone in unauthenticated, which is the safe behaviour and exactly what the message reports. Option A is contradicted by transport input telnet permitting the protocol used. Option B describes exhausted vty sessions, which produce a different refusal. Option D points at the enable secret, which is consulted only after a successful login.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which account can enter privileged EXEC mode without supplying a further credential?

exhibit.content:
R5# show running-config | include ^username
username helpdesk privilege 1 secret 9 $9$Lm4pQ2xR7vN9a0$cW8tY
username netadmin privilege 15 secret 9 $9$Kd7nB3wS5hJ2f0$pR6uX
username monitor privilege 1 secret 9 $9$Zq9cV4tG8mL1e0$nD3sA
username backup privilege 1 secret 9 $9$Rt5xH6yK2bF7d0$jM4wQ

options.text: netadmin
helpdesk
backup
monitor

items.explanation: Privilege level 15 places an account straight into privileged EXEC on login, and netadmin is the only one configured with it. Options B, C and D are all set to privilege 1, which lands them in user EXEC and requires the enable secret before they can go further. All four store their credential as type 9, so the difference between them is the privilege level rather than how the password is held.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which weakness does this policy leave open?

exhibit.content:
Extract from a draft password policy

    Minimum length              twelve characters
    Composition                 upper case, lower case, digit, symbol
    Maximum age                 ninety days, enforced
    Account lockout             after ten failed attempts
    Reuse                       not addressed
    Second factor               not required

options.text: Composition rules become unnecessary once a maximum age is enforced.
Ninety days is far too long an interval between forced changes.
Enforced rotation without any composition rule leaves passwords guessable.
Nothing prevents a user returning to a password they have used before.

items.explanation: The policy sets length, composition, age and lockout but says nothing about reuse, so a user can cycle through a handful of passwords and return to the first, which makes the ninety-day rotation largely decorative. Option A treats the two as alternatives when they address different attacks. Option B challenges an interval the policy does enforce and which is not the gap. Option C describes a policy with no composition rule, which this one plainly has.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which scheme is genuinely multifactor?

exhibit.content:
Four schemes proposed for administrative logins

    Scheme   First credential        Second credential
    ------   --------------------   ---------------------------
    W        A password             An answer to a chosen question
    X        A password             A code from a hardware token
    Y        A password             A second, longer password
    Z        A fingerprint          A facial scan

options.text: Scheme W
Scheme X
Scheme Y
Scheme Z

items.explanation: Multifactor means credentials from different categories, and only scheme X combines something known with something held, so stealing the password alone leaves an attacker short of the token. Option A pairs a password with a security answer, which is a second thing known and often easier to research than the password. Option C is two passwords, one category twice. Option D pairs two biometrics, which are both something you are, and neither can be reissued if copied.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which approach satisfies every line of the requirement?

exhibit.content:
A field deployment of two hundred devices needs to authenticate to
the management platform.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    No shared value that is identical across the estate
    A stolen device must not yield anything reusable elsewhere
    Credentials must be revocable for one device on its own
    No human types anything during the device's enrolment

options.text: A certificate issued to each device by an internal authority.
One pre-shared key, distributed to all two hundred devices.
A long password per device, rotated on a quarterly schedule.
A biometric enrolment recorded against each device's serial number.

items.explanation: A per-device certificate is unique, carries no secret that works anywhere else, can be revoked individually, and is issued during enrolment without anyone typing a credential, which covers all four lines. Option B fails the first two outright, since one stolen device yields the key for the estate. Option C is unique per device but still a typed secret and a rotation burden across two hundred units. Option D applies a human characteristic to hardware, which has nobody to measure.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which VPN arrangement fits these requirements?

exhibit.content:
A manufacturer is joining its two sites over the internet.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Both sites have a permanent circuit and a router at the edge
    The link must be up continuously, not raised per session
    Hosts must reach the far site with no software installed on them
    Users must not authenticate individually for the site link

options.text: A remote access VPN, with client software installed on every host.
A remote access VPN reached through a browser-based portal per user.
A site-to-site VPN between the two edge routers.
Neither; IPsec cannot join two sites without a private circuit.

items.explanation: A permanent link that hosts use without knowing it exists, raised between two gateways rather than per user, is the definition of a site-to-site VPN: the routers carry the tunnel and every host behind them benefits. Options A and B both authenticate individual users and need something on the endpoint, which the requirement rules out twice over. Option D is wrong because carrying private traffic across the public internet is exactly what IPsec was designed for.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two properties does adding IPsec give this tunnel that GRE alone does not? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
Traffic between two offices currently crosses the internet inside a
GRE tunnel between the edge routers.

    Requirement now added
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Anyone capturing the traffic in transit must not be able to read it
    Any alteration made in transit must be detectable at the far end
    Each router must be able to confirm which peer it is talking to

options.text: Encapsulation, so one protocol can be carried inside another across the internet
A routable path between the two office networks
Confidentiality, so a capture taken in transit cannot be read
Integrity checking, so any alteration made in transit is detected
Compression of the payload before it is placed on the wire

items.explanation: IPsec adds protection rather than reachability: the payload is encrypted so a capture yields nothing readable, and an integrity check accompanies it so tampering is detected, with peer authentication establishing the tunnel in the first place. Option A names what GRE already does, which is precisely why the tunnel exists but is unprotected. Option B is also GRE's contribution. Option E describes a feature IPsec does not provide.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why is this content readable to anyone capturing between the two offices?

exhibit.content:
Capture taken at an internet exchange, between the two edge routers
No.  Time      Source          Destination     Protocol  Length  Info
41   8.220114  203.0.113.7     198.51.100.9    GRE       154     Encapsulated IP
42   8.220780  203.0.113.7     198.51.100.9    GRE       622     Encapsulated IP

Reassembled from the encapsulated payload of frames 41 and 42:

    POST /hr/salary-review HTTP/1.1
    Host: intranet.example.internal
    Authorization: Basic bmV0YWRtaW46V3IzbmNo

The tunnel between the two offices was built with GRE and nothing else.

options.text: GRE encrypts the header but leaves the encapsulated payload in clear.
GRE encapsulates traffic without encrypting it, so IPsec must be added.
The tunnel's MTU is too small for encryption to be applied to each packet.
GRE encryption is present but switched off by default and must be enabled.

items.explanation: GRE is a tunnelling protocol: it wraps one protocol inside another so the traffic can traverse a path it otherwise could not, and it offers no confidentiality whatsoever, which is why the credentials are legible in the capture. Pairing it with IPsec is the usual answer. Option A credits GRE with encrypting something, which it never does. Option C ties encryption to MTU, which affects fragmentation rather than protection. Option D invents an encryption feature GRE does not possess.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which VPN type is shown here?

exhibit.content:
home worker                              head office
       +-----------+                              +-----------+
       |  laptop   |======= internet =============|  FW-EDGE  |
       | VPN client|                              +-----+-----+
       +-----------+                                    |
                                                   office LAN

The laptop raises the tunnel when the user signs in with their own
credentials, and drops it when they sign out. No tunnel exists while the
laptop is switched off.

options.text: Remote access
Site-to-site
GRE without IPsec
No VPN at all

items.explanation: The tunnel is raised by an individual signing in, terminates on their own laptop and disappears when they sign out, which is what distinguishes remote access from a permanent gateway-to-gateway link. Option B would run between two routers and stay up regardless of who is working. Option C names an encapsulation rather than a VPN type, and nothing in the drawing indicates GRE. Option D is contradicted by the client and the tunnel both being shown.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which entry permits exactly that range and nothing beyond it?

exhibit.content:
R1 must permit traffic from every host in 192.168.40.64/26 and is
being given a standard access list to do it.

    192.168.40.64/26 runs from 192.168.40.64 to 192.168.40.127.

options.text: access-list 10 permit 192.168.40.64 0.0.0.31
access-list 10 permit 192.168.40.64 0.0.0.63

items.explanation: An access list takes a wildcard mask, which is the inverse of the subnet mask, so a /26 written as 255.255.255.192 becomes 0.0.0.63 and covers the sixty-four addresses from .64 to .127. Option A supplies the subnet mask itself, which IOS reads as a wildcard and which would match an unintended scatter of addresses. Option B is the wildcard for a /27 and reaches only halfway to .127. Option D is the wildcard for a /24 and permits the whole of 192.168.40.0.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why is the server at 192.168.30.55 still blocked?

exhibit.content:
R2# show access-lists
Standard IP access list 20
    10 deny   192.168.30.0, wildcard bits 0.0.0.255 (3184 matches)
    20 permit 192.168.30.55 (0 matches)
    30 permit any (92417 matches)

Line 20 was added so that the server at 192.168.30.55 would be exempt
from the block. It still cannot get through.

options.text: Line 10 denies the whole subnet first, so line 20 is never reached.
The host entry on line 20 needs a wildcard of 0.0.0.0 before it takes effect.
A standard access list cannot match a single host, only a whole network.
The permit any on line 30 overrides everything configured above it.

items.explanation: An access list is read from the top and stops at the first match, so 192.168.30.55 matches the deny on line 10 and is dropped before line 20 is considered; its counter of zero proves the line has never been reached. The exemption has to be placed above the deny to work. Option B invents a syntax requirement, since a bare address in a standard list already implies a host match. Option C is contradicted by line 20 being accepted at all. Option D reverses the order of evaluation.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why is traffic from 10.10.3.0/24 dropped when no line refers to it?

exhibit.content:
R3# show access-lists
Standard IP access list 30
    10 permit 10.10.1.0, wildcard bits 0.0.0.255 (4417 matches)
    20 permit 10.10.2.0, wildcard bits 0.0.0.255 (2298 matches)

Access list 30 is applied inbound on GigabitEthernet0/1. Hosts in
10.10.1.0/24 and 10.10.2.0/24 pass without trouble. Hosts in
10.10.3.0/24 arrive on the same interface and are dropped, though no
line mentions them.

options.text: The list has to be applied in both directions before return traffic passes.
R3 needs a route to 10.10.3.0/24 before the access list will evaluate it.
A deny statement for 10.10.3.0/24 is missing and has to be added explicitly.
Every access list ends in an implicit deny, so unmatched traffic drops.

items.explanation: Every access list carries an invisible deny any as its final entry, so a packet that matches no permit is discarded even though nothing visible mentions it; permitting 10.10.3.0/24 requires adding a line for it. Option A confuses direction of application with return traffic. Option B ties filtering to routing, but the list is evaluated on arrival regardless of whether a route exists. Option C has it backwards, since the drop is the default and it is the permit that would need adding.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which approach meets both requirements?

exhibit.content:
+----------+
   10.1.5.0/24 ---[ R-BRANCH ]--- WAN ---[ R-HQ ]---| FILE-SRV |
     PC-A among them                                | 10.9.9.20|
                                                    +----------+

PC-A at 10.1.5.44 must be stopped from reaching FILE-SRV at 10.9.9.20.
PC-A must keep full access to every other destination, and every other
host must keep full access to FILE-SRV.

options.text: A standard list near the source on R-BRANCH, matching PC-A's address.
An extended list near the source on R-BRANCH, matching PC-A and the server.
A standard list near the destination on R-HQ, matching PC-A's address.
An extended list near the destination on R-HQ, so the decision is made last.

items.explanation: Only an extended list can match a source and a destination together, which is what letting PC-A reach everything except one server requires, and an extended list belongs close to the source so the unwanted traffic never crosses the WAN. Options A and C both use a standard list, which matches the source alone and would cut PC-A off from everything reachable through that interface. Option D matches correctly but carries the traffic across the WAN before discarding it, wasting the circuit it was meant to protect.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two observations explain why staff lost SSH to every device? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
R5# show access-lists
Extended IP access list 110
    10 deny   tcp 10.20.0.0 0.0.255.255 any eq 22 (1204 matches)
    20 permit ip any any (58 matches)

The intent was to stop staff subnets reaching the management server at
10.90.1.10 over SSH. Staff now report that they cannot open an SSH
session to any device at all.

options.text: The source wildcard is too narrow to reach the staff subnets.
The destination reads any, so SSH to every host is denied rather than one.
Line 20 is never evaluated, because the deny above consumes every packet.
Naming host 10.90.1.10 as the destination would restore the intent.
An extended list cannot match a port, so the eq keyword is ignored.

items.explanation: The rule was meant to protect one management server, but its destination field says any, so every SSH session from those subnets is dropped wherever it was headed; replacing any with the server's own address narrows it to what was intended. Option A points at the source wildcard, which is wide but deliberately so. Option C is contradicted by line 20 showing fifty-eight matches. Option E denies port matching, which is what distinguishes an extended list from a standard one.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which line of FILTER-IN has never matched a packet?

exhibit.content:
R6# show access-lists
Extended IP access list FILTER-IN
    10 permit tcp any host 10.9.9.20 eq www (18422 matches)
    20 permit tcp any host 10.9.9.20 eq 443 (40119 matches)
    30 deny   tcp any host 10.9.9.20 (0 matches)
    40 permit ip any any (7733 matches)

options.text: Line 30
Line 10
Line 40
Line 20

items.explanation: Each entry carries a running match counter, and line 30 is the only one reading zero, meaning no traffic to that host has ever fallen through to it. Options B and D are the two permits carrying tens of thousands of matches between them. Option C is the final permit, which has matched 7,733 packets bound elsewhere. A counter of zero is worth noticing either way: it can mean the rule is unnecessary, or that something above it is matching first.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which command applies GUEST-FILTER as the requirement describes?

exhibit.content:
! R7 - relevant configuration
!
ip access-list extended GUEST-FILTER
 deny ip 192.168.99.0 0.0.0.255 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255
 permit ip any any
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 description guest VLAN gateway
 ip address 192.168.99.1 255.255.255.0
!

GUEST-FILTER must be evaluated on traffic as it arrives from the guest
VLAN, before R7 routes it anywhere.

options.text: R7(config)# ip access-group GUEST-FILTER in
R7(config-if)# ip access-group extended GUEST-FILTER in
R7(config-if)# ip access-list GUEST-FILTER in
R7(config-if)# ip access-group GUEST-FILTER in

items.explanation: A list is bound to an interface with ip access-group, entered under that interface, and in applies it to traffic arriving from the guest VLAN before routing. Option A has the right command but is entered in global configuration mode, where it does not exist. Option B inserts the extended keyword, which belongs to ip access-list when the list is created rather than to the command that binds it. Option C uses ip access-list, which opens the list for editing instead of binding it to the interface.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which line of access list 44 permits a host at 172.16.10.30?

exhibit.content:
R8# show access-lists
Standard IP access list 44
    10 permit 172.16.8.0, wildcard bits 0.0.3.255 (9021 matches)
    20 permit 172.16.20.7 (145 matches)
    30 deny   any (612 matches)

options.text: Line 20
Line 10
Line 30
No line permits it

items.explanation: The wildcard 0.0.3.255 on line 10 leaves the last two bits of the third octet free, so it covers 172.16.8.0 through 172.16.11.255, and 172.16.10.30 falls inside that range. Option A permits a single host at 172.16.20.7 and nothing else. Option C is the explicit deny that closes the list. Option D would be correct only if the wildcard were read as covering 172.16.8.0 alone rather than a block of four.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does list 120 have no effect on the traffic it was written for?

exhibit.content:
R9# show access-lists
Extended IP access list 120
    10 deny   tcp 172.20.4.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.9.9.30 eq 3389 (0 matches)
    20 permit ip any any (0 matches)

! R9 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 description toward the 172.20.4.0/24 client subnet
 ip access-group 120 out
!

Clients in 172.20.4.0/24 still reach 10.9.9.30, which sits beyond
GigabitEthernet0/1.

options.text: The list should match on the destination port rather than the source subnet.
Extended lists must be numbered above 199 before they can be applied outbound.
It is applied outbound on the interface the clients arrive on.
The permit on line 20 cancels the deny above it whenever both are unmatched.

items.explanation: Traffic from 172.20.4.0/24 enters R9 on Gi0/0 and leaves by Gi0/1, so an outbound list on Gi0/0 only sees traffic travelling the other way; both counters reading zero confirms nothing has ever been evaluated. Applying it inbound on Gi0/0, or outbound on Gi0/1, would work. Option A misplaces the fault in the matching, which is written correctly. Option B invents a numbering rule. Option D reverses how evaluation works, since a deny that matches stops the list.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What state is this port in, and what put it there?

exhibit.content:
SW1# show port-security interface GigabitEthernet0/5
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-shutdown
Violation Mode             : Shutdown
Aging Time                 : 0 mins
Aging Type                 : Absolute
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 1
Total MAC Addresses        : 1
Configured MAC Addresses   : 0
Sticky MAC Addresses       : 1
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 00d0.5842.7f22:10
Security Violation Count   : 1

options.text: It is forwarding normally, and the violation counter records an old event.
It is administratively shut down and needs a no shutdown command.
It has been err-disabled by a violation, since the mode is shutdown.
It is protecting itself by dropping frames while staying up.

items.explanation: Secure-shutdown is the status a port takes after a violation while the mode is set to shutdown, and the violation count of one confirms a single event caused it. Option A misreads the status, since Secure-shutdown means the port is not passing traffic at all. Option B describes an operator-issued shutdown, which would show the port as administratively down instead. Option D describes what the protect or restrict modes do, and this port is set to shutdown.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which violation mode satisfies every line of the requirement?

exhibit.content:
A hot-desking area is being secured with port security.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Traffic from an unexpected MAC address must be discarded
    The port must stay up so the authorised device keeps working
    Each violation must raise a log message and increment a counter
    No engineer visit should be needed to restore service

options.text: restrict, which drops the traffic, logs it and counts violations.
protect, which drops the offending traffic and leaves the port up.
shutdown, which err-disables the port the moment a violation occurs.
shutdown paired with an errdisable recovery timer for that cause.

items.explanation: Restrict is the only mode that does all three things at once: it discards frames from unexpected addresses, keeps the port forwarding for the authorised device, and both logs and counts each violation. Option B drops the traffic and stays up but does so silently, so the security team gets no record. Options C and D both take the port down, which stops the authorised device working, and the recovery timer in option D only shortens the outage rather than avoiding it.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is needed to bring Gi0/7 back into service for the replacement machine?

exhibit.content:
SW3#
*Aug 23 08:41:02.117: %PORT_SECURITY-2-PSECURE_VIOLATION: Security
violation occurred, caused by MAC address 00d0.5842.9a04 on port
GigabitEthernet0/7.
*Aug 23 08:41:02.120: %PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: psecure-violation error
detected on Gi0/7, putting Gi0/7 in err-disable state
SW3#

SW3# show port-security interface GigabitEthernet0/7
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-shutdown
Violation Mode             : Shutdown
Aging Time                 : 0 mins
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 1
Sticky MAC Addresses       : 1
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 00d0.5842.9a04:10
Security Violation Count   : 1

The workstation on Gi0/7 was replaced yesterday. The sticky address
still recorded on the port belongs to the machine that was taken away.
No errdisable recovery is configured on SW3.

options.text: Clear the switch's ARP cache so that the new workstation is learned again.
Raise the maximum MAC addresses to two so both machines are permitted.
Wait for the aging timer to expire, after which the port recovers itself.
Remove the stale sticky address, then shut and no shut the port.

items.explanation: The sticky entry still holds the old machine's address and the port is err-disabled, so both have to be dealt with: clear the learned address, then bounce the port, since err-disable does not clear on its own here. Option A confuses the ARP cache, which maps addresses at Layer 3 and has no bearing on port security. Option B would leave the departed machine permanently authorised and merely postpone the problem. Option C is ruled out by the aging time reading zero, which means aging is disabled.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which ports should be configured as trusted for DHCP snooping?

exhibit.content:
+---------------+
    clients --- [ SW-ACC ]--- Gi0/1 ---| DHCP server   |
     Gi0/3..Gi0/20                     | 10.10.10.10   |
                                       +---------------+

DHCP snooping is about to be enabled on SW-ACC for VLAN 10. Every client
port faces a desk; Gi0/1 is the only path toward the DHCP server.

options.text: The client-facing ports, so that requests from desks are forwarded.
GigabitEthernet0/1 alone, so replies from the server are accepted.
Every port in VLAN 10, since snooping needs to see the whole exchange.
None of them, because trust matters only where a relay agent is used.

items.explanation: Snooping discards server-sourced messages such as offers and acknowledgements arriving on untrusted ports, which is precisely how it blocks a rogue server plugged into a desk; the legitimate server sits beyond Gi0/1, so that uplink alone is trusted. Option A trusts the desks, which is what the feature exists to prevent. Option C trusts everything and disables the protection entirely. Option D ties trust to relay agents, when it applies wherever snooping runs.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two statements describe why no client has obtained an address? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
SW5# show ip dhcp snooping
Switch DHCP snooping is enabled
DHCP snooping is configured on following VLANs:
10
DHCP snooping is operational on following VLANs:
10
Insertion of option 82 is enabled
Verification of hwaddr field is enabled
Verification of giaddr field is enabled
DHCP snooping trust/rate is configured on the following Interfaces:

Interface                  Trusted    Allow option    Rate limit (pps)
-----------------------    -------    ------------    ----------------
GigabitEthernet0/1         no         no              unlimited
GigabitEthernet0/3         no         no              10
GigabitEthernet0/4         no         no              10

GigabitEthernet0/1 is the uplink toward the DHCP server. Since snooping
was enabled, no client on VLAN 10 has obtained an address.

options.text: The client ports need trusting so their requests reach the server.
The uplink toward the server is untrusted, so its replies are discarded.
Marking GigabitEthernet0/1 trusted resolves the fault.
Snooping has to be removed from the VLAN before leases will be issued.
The binding table has reached its limit and refuses new entries.

items.explanation: Every interface in the trust table reads no, including the uplink, and an untrusted port drops server-sourced messages, so requests leave the switch and nothing comes back; trusting Gi0/1 alone restores service while keeping the protection on the desk ports. Option A trusts the desks, which is what the feature exists to prevent. Option D abandons the protection rather than configuring it. Option E blames the binding table, which stays empty precisely because no lease has ever completed.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why did enabling dynamic ARP inspection break connectivity on VLAN 10?

exhibit.content:
! SW6 - relevant configuration
!
ip arp inspection vlan 10
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description uplink to distribution
 ip arp inspection trust
!

There is no ip dhcp snooping command anywhere in the configuration.
Since DAI was enabled, every host on VLAN 10 has lost connectivity, and
ARP requests from the desk ports are being discarded.

options.text: DAI checks each ARP against the snooping bindings, and none exist.
DAI needs an ARP access list before it will permit any traffic at all.
DAI must be enabled globally before it can be applied to a VLAN.
DAI operates only on extended-range VLANs, so VLAN 10 is unsupported.

items.explanation: Dynamic ARP inspection validates ARP on untrusted ports against the bindings that DHCP snooping records, so without snooping running there is no binding table, nothing validates, and every ARP from a desk port is discarded. Enabling ip dhcp snooping for the VLAN is the missing piece. Option B describes ARP ACLs, which handle statically addressed hosts as a supplement rather than a prerequisite. Option C invents a global command. Option D invents a VLAN range restriction.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What did SW7 detect on GigabitEthernet0/5?

exhibit.content:
SW7#
*Aug 23 09:14:22.418: %SW_DAI-4-DHCP_SNOOPING_DENY: 1 Invalid ARPs
(Req) on Gi0/5, vlan 10.([00d0.5842.7f22/10.10.10.99/0000.0000.0000/
10.10.10.1/09:14:22 UTC Mon Aug 23 2026])
SW7#

DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection are both operational on
VLAN 10. The binding table records 00d0.5842.7f22 holding the lease
for 10.10.10.55.

options.text: A host requesting an address from an unauthorised DHCP server.
A port carrying more MAC addresses than port security permits.
An ARP reply arriving on a port trusted for DHCP snooping.
An ARP claiming an address the binding table gives elsewhere.

items.explanation: The message names an invalid ARP request from 00d0.5842.7f22 claiming 10.10.10.99, while the binding table records that MAC holding 10.10.10.55, so the pairing contradicts the recorded lease and DAI discards it. This is the shape of an ARP spoofing attempt. Option A describes what DHCP snooping catches rather than DAI. Option B describes a port security violation, which logs under a different facility. Option C would be permitted, since trusted ports are exempt from inspection.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which interfaces would discard a DHCP offer arriving on them?

exhibit.content:
SW8# show ip dhcp snooping
Switch DHCP snooping is enabled
DHCP snooping is configured on following VLANs:
10,20
DHCP snooping is operational on following VLANs:
10,20
Insertion of option 82 is enabled
Verification of hwaddr field is enabled
Verification of giaddr field is enabled
DHCP snooping trust/rate is configured on the following Interfaces:

Interface                  Trusted    Allow option    Rate limit (pps)
-----------------------    -------    ------------    ----------------
GigabitEthernet0/1         yes        yes             unlimited
GigabitEthernet0/2         yes        yes             unlimited
GigabitEthernet0/9         no         no              15
GigabitEthernet0/10        no         no              15

options.text: Gi0/1 and Gi0/2, because their rate limit is unlimited.
Gi0/9 and Gi0/10, because both are listed as untrusted.
All four, since offers are only accepted from a relay agent.
None, because snooping records offers rather than discarding them.

items.explanation: The Trusted column decides: an untrusted port drops server-sourced messages, and Gi0/9 and Gi0/10 both read no. Option A names the two trusted uplinks, which accept offers, and reads the rate limit as though it governed trust. Option C introduces a relay agent the exhibit never mentions. Option D describes what happens on a trusted port, where the offer is recorded into the binding table rather than dropped.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which of the three stages refused the command?

exhibit.content:
An engineer signs in to a switch and the following happens.

    The username and secret are checked against the access control
    server, which confirms the account and permits the session.

    The engineer types a configuration command. The switch asks the
    server whether this account may run it. The server declines and the
    switch prints an error.

    A record is written showing which account attempted the command, on
    which device, and at what time.

options.text: Authentication, since the account was checked before anything else.
Authorization, which decides what a confirmed account may do.
Accounting, which recorded the attempt and blocked it as unapproved.
All three together, because the server evaluates them as one decision.

items.explanation: Authentication had already succeeded, which is why the session opened at all, and the refusal came when the switch asked whether that account was permitted this command, which is authorization. Option A confuses the two: proving identity says nothing about what follows. Option C describes accounting, which records what happened and never blocks anything. Option D merges three stages that a server deliberately evaluates in sequence.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does this pattern of behaviour indicate?

exhibit.content:
A contractor's account can sign in to every switch without trouble.
Once connected, the account can run show commands, but any attempt to
enter configuration mode is refused.

The refusal is consistent across every device and happens immediately,
with no delay while the switch waits for anything.

options.text: The account's credentials are wrong on some devices but not on others.
The accounting records are full, so the switches refuse further commands.
The account authenticates correctly but is not authorized for that level.
The access control server is unreachable, so the switches have fallen back.

items.explanation: Signing in successfully proves authentication works, and being blocked at a specific privilege proves the restriction lies in what the account is permitted to do, which is authorization applied consistently by the same policy. Option A is contradicted by the sign-in succeeding everywhere. Option B has accounting refusing commands, which it never does. Option D would produce a fallback or a timeout, and the exhibit rules that out by noting the refusal is immediate.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which question does accounting answer?

exhibit.content:
The security team is asked which record answers each question.

    Question
    ------------------------------------------------------------
    A  Was this really the person the account belongs to?
    B  Was this account allowed to run that particular command?
    C  Which commands did this account run last Tuesday, and when?

options.text: Question A
Question C
Question B
All three of them

items.explanation: Accounting is the record of what was done and when, so question C is the one it answers, and it is the reason a per-command log is worth collecting at all. Option A is authentication, which establishes who the account holder is at sign-in. Option C is authorization, which decides in the moment whether an action is permitted. Option D collapses three separate records that exist precisely because they answer different questions.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What would moving to WPA3-Personal change about this attack?

exhibit.content:
A shared office passphrase has been in use for two years and is
known to about sixty people.

    Observed
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Someone captured the association exchange of a joining client
    They then worked offline against that capture for several days
    They recovered the passphrase and joined the network
    No interaction with the network was needed during those days

The site runs WPA2-Personal. A move to WPA3-Personal is proposed.

options.text: Nothing, since WPA3-Personal still derives its keys from a shared phrase.
The capture would be prevented, because WPA3 encrypts the association itself.
The offline stage would no longer work, as SAE gives nothing to attack offline.
The attack would take longer, because WPA3 requires a passphrase of 20 characters.

items.explanation: The weakness is that WPA2's handshake yields material an attacker can grind against a wordlist at leisure, with no further contact. WPA3 replaces it with SAE, where each guess has to be tried against the network live, so days of offline work become impossible and slow online attempts are detectable. Option A misses that the exchange changed even though a phrase is still used. Option B protects the wrong stage. Option D invents a length rule and would only postpone the same attack.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which design is the Enterprise mode, and what does it give the site?

exhibit.content:
Two candidate designs for staff wireless at a site of 400 people

    Property                     Design 1              Design 2
    -------------------------    ------------------    ---------------
    Credential each user holds   one shared phrase     their own login
    Removing one leaver          change it for all     disable one
                                 400 people            account
    Backing store                none                  RADIUS server
    Per-user session keys        derived from the      derived per
                                 shared phrase         authentication

options.text: Design 1, because one phrase for the whole site is simpler to administer.
Design 2, since each user holds a credential that can be revoked alone.
Design 1, as a shared phrase still produces a separate key for each session.
Neither; both are Personal mode with different ways of storing the phrase.

items.explanation: Enterprise mode authenticates each user individually against a backing store such as RADIUS, which is why a leaver is handled by disabling one account rather than reissuing a phrase to 400 people. Option A describes Personal mode and treats its administrative simplicity as the distinguishing feature. Option C is true of both modes and so separates nothing. Option D denies the RADIUS row, which is exactly what marks Design 2 as Enterprise.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which generation is the earliest one that protects data with AES?

exhibit.content:
Wireless security generations as recorded in the site standard

    Generation   Data protection      Personal-mode key exchange
    ----------   ------------------   ------------------------------
    WPA          TKIP                 Pre-shared key, 4-way handshake
    WPA2         AES-CCMP             Pre-shared key, 4-way handshake
    WPA3         AES with SAE         Simultaneous Authentication of
                                      Equals

options.text: WPA
WPA3
WPA2
None of them use AES

items.explanation: The Data protection column shows WPA2 introducing AES-CCMP, which WPA3 then carries forward alongside its new key exchange. Option A is WPA, which uses TKIP, a stopgap built to run on hardware designed for the broken WEP. Option B is later than the earliest and changes the key exchange rather than the cipher family. Option D contradicts two rows of the table.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which problem do these findings describe?

exhibit.content:
An audit of 180 access switches, all built from the same design
document over four years by six engineers.

    Finding
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    41 switches carry an NTP server the standard no longer lists
    17 have a logging host that was decommissioned in 2024
    9 permit Telnet on their vty lines
    Every one of them was configured by hand, by someone following
    the same document

options.text: A hardware fault common to a batch of switches from one supplier.
Configuration drift, where devices diverge from the standard over time.
A routing problem, since the affected switches cannot reach the servers.
A licensing lapse that has reverted features to their defaults.

items.explanation: One design document, six engineers and four years produced 180 switches that no longer agree with the standard or with each other, which is configuration drift; it accumulates precisely because each change is applied by a person, once, from memory or from a document that has since moved on. Option A blames hardware for settings that were typed in. Option C describes reachability, and the finding is about which values are configured. Option D invents a licensing mechanism that does not rewrite an NTP server address.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does this outcome illustrate about automation?

exhibit.content:
A team introduces automation and pushes a corrected NTP and logging
baseline to all 180 access switches in one run.

    Outcome
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    The run completes in eleven minutes
    All 180 switches now match the standard exactly
    The template also carried a typo in the management ACL, which is
    now present on all 180 switches
    The previous manual process would have reached perhaps four
    switches in that time

options.text: That automation is unsuitable for changes affecting management access.
That the eleven-minute run was too fast and should have been throttled.
That the typo would have been avoided had the run been done by hand.
That it applies a mistake as widely and as quickly as a correction.

items.explanation: The same property that fixed 180 switches in eleven minutes carried the ACL typo to all 180 in the same run, because automation removes the delay that used to confine an error to whichever device someone was working on. That is an argument for reviewing and testing the template, not for going back to typing. Option A rules out a use it handles well. Option B treats speed as the fault rather than the absence of a check. Option C assumes a manual process would have caught it, when the same person wrote both.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What becomes of the overnight change?

exhibit.content:
The intended configuration for every access switch is held in a
version-controlled repository. Any change is proposed, reviewed and
merged there, and the automation applies whatever the repository holds.

    Question put to the team
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    "Someone made an emergency change directly on SW-ACC-14 at 02:00
     last night. What happens to it?"

options.text: The next run overwrites it, since the repository is the source of truth.
It is merged into the repository automatically at the next run.
It persists, because automation only adds configuration and never removes it.
The automation halts on that switch and reports a conflict for review.

items.explanation: When the repository holds the intended state and the automation applies whatever it holds, anything changed on the device outside that flow is undone the next time the job runs; keeping the fix means putting it through the repository. Option B has the device teaching the repository, which reverses the direction of authority. Option C describes an additive tool, and applying a declared state removes what is not declared. Option D describes a behaviour some tools can be configured for but not the default this arrangement implies.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which row records a cost of automating rather than a benefit?

exhibit.content:
Two ways of applying the same change to 180 switches

    Aspect                  By hand                Automated
    --------------------    -------------------    -----------------
    Time to complete        several days           minutes
    Variation between       likely, and grows      none; one source
    devices                 with each engineer     produces all
    Record of what changed  whatever was noted     the run itself
    Effect of an error      one device at a time   every device at once

options.text: Time to complete
Variation between devices
Effect of an error
Record of what changed

items.explanation: Three rows favour automation plainly, but the last one does not: an error reaching every device at once is worse than an error reaching one, and it is the row that justifies review, testing and staged rollout. Option A shows days becoming minutes. Option B shows variation disappearing. Option D shows an ad hoc note replaced by the run itself as the record, which is a gain in traceability.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How does the work differ between the two deployments?

exhibit.content:
A new guest VLAN and its access policy must be added at 60 sites.

    Traditional deployment    each device holds its own configuration
                              and is reached over SSH
    Controller-based          devices are joined to a controller that
                              holds the intended policy centrally

options.text: Both require 60 separate sessions; only the transport used differs.
The controller-based case still needs a visit per site to join each device.
The traditional case needs 60 changes; the controller-based one needs one.
The traditional case is faster, since no controller has to distribute it.

items.explanation: In a traditional deployment the intent lives on each device, so it has to be expressed 60 times with 60 chances to differ; with a controller the intent is declared once and the controller renders it onto every joined device. Option A denies the difference the models exist to create. Option B confuses joining a device, which happens once at onboarding, with making a policy change. Option D reverses which is faster and treats distribution as though it were manual.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which part of the device's operation has moved to the controller?

exhibit.content:
In a traditional network, each router runs OSPF, builds its own
link-state database, and computes its own best paths. In a
controller-based fabric, a central component works out the paths and
programs the devices to forward accordingly.

    Question
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Which part of a device's operation has moved in the second case?

options.text: The control plane, which decides how traffic should be forwarded.
The data plane, which moves each frame from one port to another.
The management plane, which handles logins and configuration access.
All three, since a joined device retains no local function.

items.explanation: Working out paths and deciding what the forwarding tables should contain is the control plane, and that is what the controller has taken over; each device still moves packets itself. Option B names the part that necessarily stays on the device, since forwarding happens in its hardware at line rate. Option C names logins and access, which the exhibit does not discuss. Option D overstates it: the separation is the whole point, and a device with no data plane would forward nothing.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does this behaviour show about the model?

exhibit.content:
A campus runs a controller-based fabric. The controller becomes
unreachable from the fabric switches after a failure in the management
network.

    Observed while the controller is unreachable
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Traffic between hosts already communicating continues to flow
    Existing policy stays in force on the switches
    A request to add a new segment cannot be carried out

options.text: The fabric has failed, since a controller-based network cannot run without one.
The controller was never required, as the switches clearly operate alone.
Forwarding has moved into the controller, which is why nothing new can start.
Forwarding continues from what is programmed, but changes cannot be made.

items.explanation: The switches keep forwarding because their tables and policy are already programmed into hardware, but nothing new can be expressed while the component holding the intent is out of reach, which is the dependency centralisation creates and the reason controllers are deployed redundantly. Option A overstates the outage, since traffic plainly continues. Option B understates the dependency by ignoring the failed request. Option C places forwarding in the controller, which the continuing traffic disproves.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. According to this table, what makes consistency different between the two models?

exhibit.content:
Traditional             Controller-based
    ----------    --------------------    ---------------------------
    Policy is     configured on each      declared once and pushed
    expressed     device separately       to the devices
    A change      touches every device    is made in one place
    Consistency   depends on the person   is a property of the system
    Interface     device CLI              API and controller

options.text: Traditional devices enforce it in hardware; controllers only recommend it.
It rests on the engineer traditionally, and on the system otherwise.
Both models leave it to the engineer; only the interface used differs.
Controllers abandon consistency in exchange for making changes faster.

items.explanation: The Consistency row states it plainly: configured device by device it depends on whoever does the work, whereas a single declared policy rendered onto every device makes agreement a property of how the system operates rather than of anyone's diligence. Option A inverts the table. Option C denies the row's distinction. Option D presents the two as a trade-off, when the table lists consistency and speed as gains together.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which API does each of the two actions use?

exhibit.content:
+--------------------------------------+
        |   provisioning portal, ticketing,    |
        |   monitoring and analytics tools     |
        +--------------------------------------+
                          |  API  A
        +--------------------------------------+
        |             CONTROLLER               |
        +--------------------------------------+
                          |  API  B
        +--------------------------------------+
        |   switches, routers, access points   |
        +--------------------------------------+

A ticketing system asks the controller to create a segment. The
controller then instructs forty switches to implement it.

options.text: Both use API A, since the controller mediates every request that arrives.
The ticketing request uses A, northbound; the switches are reached over B.
The ticketing request uses B, and the controller reaches the switches over A.
Both use API B, because every action ends at a device in the end.

items.explanation: Northbound faces the applications above the controller, so a ticketing system calls in over API A, and southbound faces the infrastructure below it, so the controller programs the switches over API B. The names describe direction relative to the controller rather than importance. Option C reverses the two, which is the usual slip. Option A ignores that the controller must also speak downward. Option D looks at where the effect lands rather than which interface each call crosses.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which description matches what this switch is doing?

exhibit.content:
A fabric switch receives a frame and forwards it in hardware within
microseconds, using tables it did not compute for itself. A central
component worked out what those tables should contain and programmed
them, and it recomputes them whenever the topology changes.

options.text: It runs both planes locally, with the central component only monitoring it.
It runs the control plane locally while the data plane is centralised.
It runs neither plane; the central component forwards the traffic itself.
It runs the data plane locally while the control plane sits centrally.

items.explanation: Forwarding a frame in hardware in microseconds is the data plane and stays on the switch, while deciding what the tables should hold is the control plane and has moved to the central component; that division is what separation of the planes means. Option A denies the separation the exhibit describes. Option B reverses the two, which would put per-frame forwarding across the network. Option C leaves the switch doing nothing, contradicted by it forwarding the frame.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which layer is the underlay, and what does it carry?

exhibit.content:
A campus fabric carries traffic between two hosts.

    Layer          What it consists of
    -----------    --------------------------------------------
    Layer one      The physical switches, their links, and the
                   routing that lets each device reach every
                   other device's loopback
    Layer two      Tunnels built between those loopbacks, in
                   which the hosts' own traffic is carried

options.text: Layer one is the underlay, carrying the tunnels that hold host traffic.
Layer two is the underlay, since host traffic is what the fabric exists for.
Layer one is the overlay, because it is the physical network beneath.
Neither; underlay and overlay describe the same links seen from two angles.

items.explanation: The underlay is the real network of switches, links and routing whose only job is to let every device reach every other, and the overlay is the set of tunnels built across it in which host traffic actually travels. Option B swaps them by reasoning from purpose rather than position. Option C names the right layer but calls it the overlay, inverting the terms. Option D collapses a distinction that exists precisely so host addressing can change without the physical network being touched.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two components does this arrangement contain? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
+---------+   +---------+
                     | SPINE-1 |   | SPINE-2 |
                     +----+----+   +----+----+
                          | \_______/ |
                          |  ________/|
                     +----+-/---+  +--+------+
                     |  LEAF-1  |  |  LEAF-2 |
                     +----------+  +---------+

Every leaf connects to every spine. A controller holds the policy for
the whole arrangement and programs each device. Host traffic between
leaves is carried in tunnels between the leaf loopbacks, over the
routed links shown.

options.text: An underlay: the routed spine-and-leaf links carrying loopback reachability
A three-tier campus hierarchy of core, distribution and access layers
A WAN circuit supplied and billed by a service provider
An overlay: tunnels between the leaf loopbacks carrying host traffic
A collapsed core, since the two spines aggregate the leaf switches

items.explanation: The drawing holds both halves of a fabric: the routed links between spines and leaves form the underlay whose job is to let every device reach every other, and the tunnels built between leaf loopbacks form the overlay in which host traffic actually travels. Option B names a campus hierarchy this is not. Option C introduces a provider circuit the drawing never shows. Option E borrows a campus term for spines that aggregate nothing in that sense.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which API does the engineer's script use?

exhibit.content:
+--------------------------------------+
        |   provisioning portal, ticketing,    |
        |   monitoring and analytics tools     |
        +--------------------------------------+
                          |  API  A
        +--------------------------------------+
        |             CONTROLLER               |
        +--------------------------------------+
                          |  API  B
        +--------------------------------------+
        |   switches, routers, access points   |
        +--------------------------------------+

An engineer writes a script that runs on the monitoring server and asks
the controller for a list of every device it manages.

options.text: API A, the northbound interface the controller offers to applications.
API B, the southbound interface toward the managed devices.
Neither, since a read-only request bypasses both interfaces.
Both in turn, as the request is relayed down to each device.

items.explanation: The script runs above the controller and asks it for information, so it calls in over the northbound API, which is what the controller publishes for applications and tools. Option B is the interface the controller uses to reach the switches, which the script never touches. Option C invents an exemption for reads, when a query is an ordinary API call. Option D assumes the controller must poll every device, but it answers from what it already holds.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which capability produced this alert?

exhibit.content:
A monitoring platform has been collecting interface counters,
control-plane telemetry and flow records from the campus for nine months.

    Reported this morning
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    "Utilisation on the DIST-1 to CORE-1 uplink is 4.2 standard
     deviations above the pattern observed for a Monday at 09:00 over
     the preceding thirty-six weeks. No configuration change is
     recorded. Investigate."

No threshold for this interface was ever configured by an engineer.

options.text: A generative model, which composed the wording of the alert from telemetry.
A static threshold, crossed once utilisation passed a configured percentage.
A predictive model, which learned the pattern and flagged a departure.
A scheduled report, comparing this morning's figures against yesterday's.

items.explanation: The alert is expressed as a deviation from a baseline built over thirty-six weeks of history rather than a fixed percentage, which is what a model trained on past behaviour produces; nobody set a threshold, and that is precisely the point of learning one. Option A confuses how the message was phrased with what detected the condition. Option B is ruled out by no threshold having been configured. Option D compares two days, which could not yield a figure in standard deviations.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which kind of capability is the assistant demonstrating here?

exhibit.content:
An engineer types the following into an assistant built into the
management platform:

    "Give me the configuration for a new branch router: two LAN
     subnets on 10.44.0.0/22, OSPF area 0 to the WAN link, and a
     floating static as backup."

The assistant returns a complete, syntactically valid configuration in
about two seconds.

options.text: Predictive, since it anticipates the settings the branch will need.
Generative, since it produces new configuration text from a description.
Anomaly detection, comparing the request against known branch designs.
Automation scheduling, queueing the configuration for a later window.

items.explanation: Producing configuration text that did not previously exist, from a description given in ordinary language, is a generative capability; nothing here forecasts a future state or scores an observation against a baseline. Option A borrows the word predictive for ordinary anticipation, where in this context it means forecasting from learned patterns. Option C describes comparing something observed against normal behaviour, and no observation has been made. Option D describes when a change runs rather than where the text came from.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does this part of the draft illustrate about generated configuration?

exhibit.content:
The assistant's draft for the branch router included:

    interface GigabitEthernet0/3
     description backup circuit
     ip address 203.0.113.6 255.255.255.252
    !
    ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.5 130

The branch router model in question has two Gigabit Ethernet interfaces,
numbered 0/0 and 0/1. There is no GigabitEthernet0/3 on the platform,
and the backup circuit terminates on a serial interface.

options.text: The model was given the wrong prompt, which is the sole cause of the error.
Generated configuration is unusable in practice and should not be attempted.
The syntax error would have been caught by the device on paste.
Output can be plausible and still wrong, so it needs checking before use.

items.explanation: Every line is valid IOS and reads exactly like a real backup circuit, yet it names an interface the platform does not have and puts the circuit on the wrong media, so the fault is invisible to anything that only checks syntax. That is the reason generated configuration is reviewed against the actual inventory before it is applied. Option A blames the prompt, which never claimed a third interface. Option B overcorrects into dismissing a useful drafting aid. Option C expects a syntax check to catch a semantically wrong but well-formed command.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which request creates Loopback10 without disturbing the existing members?

exhibit.content:
A controller exposes its interface configuration at

    /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces          the collection
    /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=Loopback0
                                                       one member

Loopback0 already exists. A new Loopback10 is to be added, and the
existing members must be left exactly as they are.

options.text: PUT to the collection, carrying the full set of interfaces as it should end up.
GET the collection, edit the returned body by hand, and send it back.
POST to the collection, which adds a member alongside the existing ones.
PATCH the individual member path for Loopback10, which does not yet exist.
