items.explanation: Create maps onto POST against the collection, and the server places the new member inside it without the client needing to know or resend what is already there. Option A would work only if the body listed every existing interface too, and anything omitted would be removed. Option B describes that same replacement carried out manually, with a race against any other change in between. Option D patches a resource that does not exist yet, so there is nothing to modify.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does this response indicate?

exhibit.content:
GET /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces HTTP/1.1
Host: 10.9.9.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJuZXRhZG1pbiJ9
Accept: application/yang-data+json

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="restconf"

The path is correct and the same path returned data yesterday from the
same client.

options.text: The token is missing, expired or no longer accepted.
The path requested does not exist on this controller.
The controller understood the request and refuses to carry it out.
The body of the request was malformed and could not be parsed.

items.explanation: A 401 concerns who is asking rather than what was asked, and the WWW-Authenticate header inviting a bearer credential confirms it; since the same path worked yesterday, an expired token is the likeliest cause. Option B describes a 404, which the working path rules out. Option C describes a 403, where the caller is known but not permitted. Option D describes a 400, and this request carries no body at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why did the description and the address disappear from Loopback0?

exhibit.content:
PUT /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=Loopback0 HTTP/1.1
Host: 10.9.9.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJuZXRhZG1pbiJ9
Content-Type: application/yang-data+json

{
  "ietf-interfaces:interface": {
    "name": "Loopback0",
    "enabled": false
  }
}

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

Before the request, Loopback0 carried a name, a description, an IPv4
address and an enabled flag. Afterwards only the name and the enabled
flag remain.

options.text: The controller rejected the request and rolled the resource back to defaults.
PATCH was needed, since only PATCH can remove a field explicitly.
The Content-Type header did not match the encoding the body actually used.
PUT replaces the whole resource, so fields left out of the body are removed.

items.explanation: PUT states what the resource should be in its entirety, so the controller made it match the body exactly and the fields absent from that body ceased to exist; PATCH is the verb for changing part of a resource and leaving the rest alone. The 204 confirms the request succeeded, which is what makes this destructive rather than an error. Option A is contradicted by that success. Option B reverses which verb removes fields. Option C blames a header that matches the body correctly.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two approaches fail the stated requirements? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
An automation host will call a controller's API several thousand
times an hour.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    The long-lived credential must not travel on every single request
    Access must lapse on its own after a period without renewal
    A leaked value must be revocable without changing the account
    Nothing may be placed in the request URL, which is logged upstream

options.text: A bearer token presented in a header until it expires
Basic authentication, sending the account credential on every request
An API key appended to the request URL as a query parameter
A token that can be revoked without changing the underlying account
A credential exchanged once at the start and then held by the client

items.explanation: Basic authentication puts the long-lived account credential on every one of several thousand requests an hour, which the first line forbids, and an API key in the URL lands in the logs upstream, which the fourth line forbids by name. Option A meets all four. Option D describes the revocation the third line asks for. Option E describes obtaining a token once, which is the behaviour the first line is written around.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is the Accept header telling the controller?

exhibit.content:
GET /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces HTTP/1.1
Host: 10.9.9.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJuZXRhZG1pbiJ9
Accept: application/yang-data+json

options.text: That the controller must store its configuration in JSON form.
That the body being sent with this request is encoded as JSON.
That the client wants the response encoded as JSON.
That only controllers able to parse JSON may answer this request.

items.explanation: Accept describes what the client is willing to receive, so the controller returns JSON rather than XML; the companion header Content-Type describes what the client is sending, and confusing the two is the usual slip. Option B states the Content-Type meaning, and this request has no body in any case. Option A treats a transport encoding as a storage format. Option D reads it as a capability filter rather than a preference for this exchange.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which CRUD operation has this request performed?

exhibit.content:
DELETE /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=Loopback99 HTTP/1.1
Host: 10.9.9.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJuZXRhZG1pbiJ9

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

options.text: Delete, removing Loopback99 from the controller.
Read, retrieving the current state of Loopback99.
Update, changing one field on Loopback99.
Create, adding Loopback99 to the collection.

items.explanation: The verb is DELETE against a single member path, and the 204 reports success with nothing left to return, which is the ordinary response to a removal. Option B maps to GET, which would return a body describing the resource. Option C maps to PUT or PATCH, both of which carry a body saying what to change. Option D maps to POST against the collection rather than DELETE against a member.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which mechanism matches this way of working?

exhibit.content:
A team is choosing how to push configuration to 180 switches.

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Nothing may be installed on the switches themselves
    The control host initiates the work; devices are never asked to poll
    Connections use SSH or the device API, already open for management
    Running the same job twice must not change a device the second time

options.text: A tool needing a small agent on each switch, reporting to a central master.
Ansible, which is agentless and pushes over SSH or the device API.
A tool where each device pulls its own configuration on a timer.
Any of them, since every current tool works in essentially this way.

items.explanation: Nothing installed on the devices, work started from a control host and carried over connections already open for management describes an agentless push model, which is how Ansible operates; its modules are also written to be idempotent, so a repeated run changes nothing. Option A requires the agent the first line forbids. Option C describes a pull model, where devices initiate rather than the control host. Option D denies a distinction the requirement is written around.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does running this playbook do?

exhibit.content:
---
- name: Access layer baseline
  hosts: access_switches
  gather_facts: false
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure Loopback0 exists and is up
      cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
        config:
          - name: Loopback0
            enabled: true
        state: merged

options.text: It collects facts from every switch and writes them into a report.
It removes Loopback0 from any switch on which it is found.
It runs against one named switch rather than against a group.
It ensures Loopback0 exists and is enabled on the access switches.

items.explanation: The hosts line targets the access_switches group, the task names the desired outcome, and state merged tells the module to bring the device to that state without touching anything else, so a switch already correct is left alone. Option A is contradicted by gather_facts being false and by there being no reporting task. Option B would need a state that removes rather than merges. Option C misreads a group name as a single hostname.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What has this command actually done?

exhibit.content:
$ terraform plan

Terraform used the selected providers to generate the following
execution plan. Resource actions are indicated with the following
symbols:
  + create

Terraform will perform the following actions:

  # iosxe_interface.loopback10 will be created
  + resource "iosxe_interface" "loopback10" {
      + name        = "Loopback10"
      + description = "automation test"
      + enabled     = true
    }

Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

options.text: Previewed the difference between the declared state and what exists.
Applied the change to the device and reported exactly what it altered afterwards.
Checked the file for syntax errors without contacting anything.
Reversed the previous run, removing what that run had created.

items.explanation: A plan is a dry run: the tool reads the declared desired state, compares it against what it has recorded and against the device, and prints the actions that would close the gap, which is why the summary counts what would be added rather than what was. Option B describes apply, the separate step that follows. Option C describes a purely local check, but a plan consults the provider to see what exists. Option D describes a destroy.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What will happen to Loopback20 when this runs?

exhibit.content:
$ terraform apply

  # iosxe_interface.loopback20 will be updated in-place
  ~ resource "iosxe_interface" "loopback20" {
        name        = "Loopback20"
      ~ description = "old text" -> "branch uplink test"
        enabled     = true
    }

Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.

options.text: It will be created, since the resource is listed in the plan.
It will be destroyed and rebuilt with the new description.
Its description will be changed and nothing else about it.
Nothing, because the summary counts no resources to add.

items.explanation: The tilde marks a change in place and sits against the description line alone, while name and enabled are shown unchanged, so a single attribute is updated and the interface is never removed. The summary agrees: nothing to add, one to change, nothing to destroy. Option A misreads an update as a creation. Option B describes a replacement, which would count one to add and one to destroy. Option D reads only the add column.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does the payload record about the second entry in the interfaces array?

options.text: It is enabled and carries a single address.
It is disabled but still carries a single address.
It is enabled and carries no addresses at all.
It is disabled and carries no addresses at all.

items.explanation: The second object in the array sets enabled to false and gives addresses an empty pair of brackets, so both readings point the same way: the interface is down and holds nothing. Option A describes the first entry instead, which is the ordinary wrong-element read when arrays are indexed by eye. Option B takes the correct enabled value but the wrong address list. Option C reverses both fields at once.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which two of these readings of the JSON document are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: addresses on the first interface is an array holding one string.
location holds the JSON null value rather than an empty string.
management is an array of three settings rather than an object.
port holds the string "443" rather than a number.
interfaces holds a single object rather than a list of them.

items.explanation: Square brackets mark an array and the one element inside them is quoted, so addresses is an array of one string, and location reads null, which is JSON's own keyword for an absent value and is distinct from an empty pair of quotes. Option C misreads braces as brackets, since management groups named settings and is an object. Option D calls an unquoted 443 a string, when JSON numbers are never quoted. Option E ignores the brackets around the two interface objects.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does the parser reject this document?

options.text: The vlans array may not hold bare numbers; each value needs quoting.
An object cannot be nested inside another object in JSON.
JSON booleans are written true and false, in lower case.
The last key in an object must be followed by a trailing comma.

items.explanation: JSON spells its booleans entirely in lower case, so True is not a keyword the parser recognises and the document fails at that line; the capitalised form comes from Python and is a frequent slip when a file is written by hand. Option A is wrong because unquoted numbers are exactly how JSON expresses them. Option B is contradicted by the uplink object, which nests legitimately. Option D inverts the rule, since a trailing comma is itself invalid.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How many interface objects does this payload describe?

options.text: Two
One
Four
None; interfaces holds an object

items.explanation: The interfaces array holds two brace-delimited objects, one per interface, each with its own name, enabled flag and address list. Option B counts only the first. Option C counts the key/value pairs inside one object rather than the objects themselves. Option D misreads the square brackets as braces, and the difference matters: an array can grow to hold more interfaces where a single object could not.
